lesson:
# Computer Programming — Week 1

Two lectures: (1) solving problems with a computer, from machine language to
high-level languages, the compilation chain, and the structure of a C program;
(2) the components of a computer, software types, and above all **algorithms and
flowcharts**.

---

## 1. From machine language to high-level languages

The processor only executes **machine code**: strings of 0s and 1s.
**Assembly** puts mnemonics on those instructions but stays tied to one
architecture. A **high-level language (HLL)** finally lets you write programs
that are **independent of a particular type of computer**: this is
**portability**.

```diagram
{
  "title": "The same function at three levels: high-level language, assembly, machine code.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "hll", "x": 250, "y": 40, "w": 380, "h": 40, "label": "int square(int num) { return num * num; }", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "asm", "x": 250, "y": 130, "w": 380, "h": 40, "label": "push rbp · mov rbp, rsp · imul eax, edi, edi · pop rbp · ret", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "mc", "x": 250, "y": 220, "w": 380, "h": 40, "label": "0111000001101000101010010010010100…", "tone": "violet", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "l1", "x": 540, "y": 40, "shape": "text", "label": "high-level language\nportable", "size": 11 },
    { "id": "l2", "x": 540, "y": 130, "shape": "text", "label": "assembly\none architecture", "size": 11 },
    { "id": "l3", "x": 540, "y": 220, "shape": "text", "label": "machine code\nwhat the CPU runs", "size": 11 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "hll", "to": "asm", "label": "compiler" },
    { "from": "asm", "to": "mc", "label": "assembler" }
  ]
}
```

Portability is aided by an **agreed standard** (for example **C99**). A
**compiler** (**gcc**, **icc**) translates the HLL program into executable
machine code.

## 2. Why C?

Because it **produces code that runs nearly as fast as assembly while still
being a high-level language**.

Cited uses: operating systems, compilers, assemblers, text editors, print
spoolers, network drivers, interpreters, utilities.

## 3. Executing a program

The full chain, from source code to results:

```diagram
{
  "title": "Executing a program: edit, compile, link, run.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "prog", "x": 60, "y": 40, "w": 100, "h": 36, "shape": "ellipse", "label": "programmer", "size": 12 },
    { "id": "ed", "x": 210, "y": 40, "w": 100, "h": 36, "label": "text editor", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "src", "x": 360, "y": 40, "w": 100, "h": 40, "shape": "note", "label": "source\n(.c)", "tone": "sky", "size": 12 },
    { "id": "cc", "x": 360, "y": 120, "w": 100, "h": 36, "label": "compiler", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "obj", "x": 360, "y": 200, "w": 100, "h": 40, "shape": "note", "label": "object\n(.o)", "tone": "sky", "size": 12 },
    { "id": "lib", "x": 160, "y": 280, "w": 100, "h": 36, "shape": "note", "label": "library", "tone": "neutral", "size": 12 },
    { "id": "ld", "x": 360, "y": 280, "w": 100, "h": 36, "label": "linker", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "exe", "x": 360, "y": 360, "w": 100, "h": 40, "shape": "note", "label": "executable", "tone": "emerald", "size": 12 },
    { "id": "run", "x": 360, "y": 440, "w": 100, "h": 36, "label": "runner", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "res", "x": 540, "y": 440, "w": 100, "h": 40, "shape": "note", "label": "results", "tone": "emerald", "size": 12 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "prog", "to": "ed" }, { "from": "ed", "to": "src" }, { "from": "src", "to": "cc" }, { "from": "cc", "to": "obj" },
    { "from": "obj", "to": "ld" }, { "from": "lib", "to": "ld" }, { "from": "ld", "to": "exe" }, { "from": "exe", "to": "run" }, { "from": "run", "to": "res" }
  ]
}
```

Four stages: you **edit** the source; the **compiler** produces an **object**
file; the **linker** combines that object with the **libraries** to produce the
**executable**; the **runner** executes it.

## 4. A minimal C program

```c
#include <stdio.h>
main()
{
    printf("hello, world\n");
}
```

Output:

```
hello, world
```

- `#include <stdio.h>` is a **preprocessor directive**: it inserts the header of
  the standard input/output library, needed to use `printf`.
- `main()` is the **entry point**: execution begins there.
- **Braces** `{ }` delimit the body; every **statement** ends with a
  **semicolon**.
- `\n` is an **escape sequence**: a newline.

---

## 5. Components of a computer

A **computer** is an electronic device that performs **arithmetic and logical**
operations. Four blocks:

```diagram
{
  "title": "The four blocks of a computer: input devices, CPU (control unit, ALU, registers), main memory, output devices.",
  "groups": [
    { "x": 330, "y": 70, "w": 250, "h": 110, "label": "CPU (VLSI)", "tone": "amber" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "in", "x": 80, "y": 70, "w": 120, "h": 50, "label": "input devices\nkeyboard · mouse", "tone": "sky", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "cu", "x": 275, "y": 85, "w": 110, "h": 40, "label": "control unit\n(CU)", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 11 },
    { "id": "alu", "x": 395, "y": 85, "w": 100, "h": 40, "label": "ALU", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 11 },
    { "id": "reg", "x": 335, "y": 115, "shape": "text", "label": "registers (general · special purpose)", "size": 10 },
    { "id": "out", "x": 590, "y": 70, "w": 120, "h": 50, "label": "output devices\nmonitor", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "mem", "x": 330, "y": 210, "w": 200, "h": 40, "label": "main memory", "tone": "violet", "filled": true },
    { "id": "mt", "x": 330, "y": 128, "shape": "text" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "in", "to": "cu", "label": "data · instructions" },
    { "from": "alu", "to": "out", "label": "results" },
    { "from": "mem", "to": "mt", "arrow": "both", "label": "data bus · address bus" }
  ]
}
```

- **CPU**: a **VLSI** integrated circuit containing the **arithmetic and logic
  unit (ALU)**, the **control unit (CU)** and **registers** (general and
  special purpose). The **CU** generates the control signals; the **ALU** does
  the computation. The CPU talks to memory over the **data bus** and the
  **address bus**.
- **Input devices**: the user feeds data and instructions (keyboard, mouse).
- **Output devices**: the computer returns its results (monitor).

### Memory

```diagram
{
  "title": "Memory: primary (RAM, ROM) addressed directly by the CPU; secondary (disk, flash) as a data reservoir.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "m", "x": 300, "y": 30, "w": 120, "h": 36, "label": "Memory", "tone": "violet", "filled": true },
    { "id": "p", "x": 170, "y": 110, "w": 130, "h": 36, "label": "Primary", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "s", "x": 450, "y": 110, "w": 220, "h": 50, "label": "Secondary\nhard disk · flash drives…", "tone": "sky", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "ram", "x": 100, "y": 200, "w": 120, "h": 50, "label": "RAM\n(volatile)", "size": 12 },
    { "id": "rom", "x": 250, "y": 200, "w": 120, "h": 50, "label": "ROM\n(non-volatile)", "size": 12 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "m", "to": "p", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "m", "to": "s", "arrow": "none" },
    { "from": "p", "to": "ram", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "p", "to": "rom", "arrow": "none" }
  ]
}
```

- **Primary memory**: the CPU addresses it directly (data + address bus). **RAM**
  is **volatile** (current instructions and data); **ROM** is **non-volatile**.
- **Secondary memory**: large capacity, non-volatile, acts as a **data
  reservoir**.

## 6. Software

- **System software**: interacts with the hardware and manages resources —
  **operating system**, **loader**, **linker**, **translator**.
  OS: Linux, Windows, UNIX, macOS.
- **Translator**: turns an HLL program (C, C++, Java...) into machine language.
- **Linker**: links the object codes of the subroutines/functions into an
  executable.
- **Loader**: loads a program from secondary memory into primary memory so it
  can run.
- **Application software**: word processing, image editing, spreadsheet,
  database software...

---

## 7. Algorithms

An **algorithm** is a **finite set of unambiguous instructions** which, when
executed, performs a task correctly.

- It uses **English-like** statements, step by step.
- It has **no fixed writing style**.
- It must be **finite** and **unambiguous**.
- It is **independent of the programming language**.

**Example — average of three numbers:**

```
Step 0  START
Step 1  INPUT first number into A
Step 2  INPUT second number into B
Step 3  INPUT third number into C
Step 4  COMPUTE SUM = A + B + C
Step 5  COMPUTE AVG = SUM / 3
Step 6  DISPLAY AVG
Step 7  END
```

```flowchart
{
  "title": "Average of three numbers: a purely sequential (imperative) flowchart.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "s", "kind": "start", "label": "START" },
    { "id": "a", "kind": "io", "label": "INPUT A" },
    { "id": "b", "kind": "io", "label": "INPUT B" },
    { "id": "c", "kind": "io", "label": "INPUT C" },
    { "id": "sum", "kind": "process", "label": "SUM = A + B + C" },
    { "id": "avg", "kind": "process", "label": "AVG = SUM / 3" },
    { "id": "d", "kind": "io", "label": "DISPLAY AVG" },
    { "id": "e", "kind": "end", "label": "END" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "s", "to": "a" }, { "from": "a", "to": "b" }, { "from": "b", "to": "c" }, { "from": "c", "to": "sum" },
    { "from": "sum", "to": "avg" }, { "from": "avg", "to": "d" }, { "from": "d", "to": "e" }
  ]
}
```

**Example — maximum of two numbers (conditional):**

```
Step 0  START
Step 1  INPUT A
Step 2  INPUT B
Step 3  IF A > B THEN
            MAX = A
        ELSE
            MAX = B
        END IF
Step 4  DISPLAY MAX
Step 5  END
```

```flowchart
{
  "title": "Maximum of two numbers: the decision diamond has two exits, yes and no, that merge again before DISPLAY.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "s", "kind": "start", "label": "START" },
    { "id": "in", "kind": "io", "label": "INPUT A, B" },
    { "id": "d", "kind": "decision", "label": "Is A > B ?" },
    { "id": "ma", "kind": "process", "label": "MAX = A" },
    { "id": "mb", "kind": "process", "label": "MAX = B" },
    { "id": "out", "kind": "io", "label": "DISPLAY MAX" },
    { "id": "e", "kind": "end", "label": "END" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "s", "to": "in" }, { "from": "in", "to": "d" },
    { "from": "d", "to": "ma", "branch": "yes" }, { "from": "d", "to": "mb", "branch": "no" },
    { "from": "ma", "to": "out" }, { "from": "mb", "to": "out" }, { "from": "out", "to": "e" }
  ]
}
```

**Example — sum of the even numbers among N (iterative):**

```
Step 0  START
Step 1  INPUT N
Step 2  I = 1
Step 3  SUM = 0
Step 4  REPEAT WHILE I <= N
            INPUT NUM
            REM = NUM mod 2
            IF REM == 0 THEN
                SUM = SUM + NUM
            END IF
            I = I + 1
        END WHILE
Step 5  DISPLAY SUM
Step 6  END
```

```flowchart
{
  "title": "Sum of the even numbers among N inputs: the loop is a decision whose yes branch comes back up to the test.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "s", "kind": "start", "label": "START" },
    { "id": "n", "kind": "io", "label": "INPUT N" },
    { "id": "init", "kind": "process", "label": "I = 1\nSUM = 0" },
    { "id": "loop", "kind": "decision", "label": "I <= N ?" },
    { "id": "num", "kind": "io", "label": "INPUT NUM" },
    { "id": "rem", "kind": "process", "label": "REM = NUM mod 2" },
    { "id": "even", "kind": "decision", "label": "REM == 0 ?" },
    { "id": "add", "kind": "process", "label": "SUM = SUM + NUM" },
    { "id": "inc", "kind": "process", "label": "I = I + 1" },
    { "id": "out", "kind": "io", "label": "DISPLAY SUM" },
    { "id": "e", "kind": "end", "label": "END" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "s", "to": "n" }, { "from": "n", "to": "init" }, { "from": "init", "to": "loop" },
    { "from": "loop", "to": "num", "branch": "yes" }, { "from": "loop", "to": "out", "branch": "no" },
    { "from": "num", "to": "rem" }, { "from": "rem", "to": "even" },
    { "from": "even", "to": "add", "branch": "yes" }, { "from": "even", "to": "inc", "branch": "no" },
    { "from": "add", "to": "inc" }, { "from": "inc", "to": "loop" },
    { "from": "out", "to": "e" }
  ]
}
```

### The three programming constructs

Every piece of logic reduces to three kinds of statement:

| construct | role | algorithm keyword |
|---|---|---|
| **imperative** | do an action, in order | `COMPUTE`, `INPUT`, `DISPLAY`, `=` |
| **conditional** | choose based on a condition | `IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... END IF` |
| **iterative** | repeat while a condition holds | `REPEAT WHILE ... END WHILE` |

---

## 8. Flowcharts

A **flowchart** is a **graphical tool** that shows the **flow of control**
within a sequence of statements.

### Notations

```flowchart
{
  "title": "The flowchart symbols used in this course.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t", "kind": "start", "label": "Terminal", "x": 80, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "io", "kind": "io", "label": "Input / Output", "x": 250, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "p", "kind": "process", "label": "Process", "x": 430, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "d", "kind": "decision", "label": "Decision ?", "x": 610, "y": 40 }
  ],
  "edges": []
}
```

| symbol | shape | role |
|---|---|---|
| **Terminal** | oval / rounded rectangle | start and end of the flowchart |
| **Input/output** | parallelogram | an input or output operation |
| **Process** | rectangle | a processing operation (imperative logic) |
| **Decision** | diamond | a condition; **two exits** (true / false) |
| **Connector** | circle | link two points on the same page |
| **Off-page connector** | pentagon | link two points on different pages |
| **Arrows** | arrowed lines | the order of the flow |

### Flowchart — division avoiding division by zero

```flowchart
{
  "title": "Division avoiding division by zero: when B is 0 the no branch skips straight to END.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "s", "kind": "start", "label": "START" },
    { "id": "in", "kind": "io", "label": "INPUT A, B" },
    { "id": "d", "kind": "decision", "label": "Is B != 0 ?" },
    { "id": "q", "kind": "process", "label": "Q = A / B" },
    { "id": "out", "kind": "io", "label": "DISPLAY Q" },
    { "id": "e", "kind": "end", "label": "END" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "s", "to": "in" }, { "from": "in", "to": "d" },
    { "from": "d", "to": "q", "branch": "yes" }, { "from": "d", "to": "e", "branch": "no" },
    { "from": "q", "to": "out" }, { "from": "out", "to": "e" }
  ]
}
```

### To remember

- A **decision** (diamond) has **exactly two exits**, one for *true*, one for
  *false*.
- The **process** (rectangle) carries the **imperative** logic; the **I/O**
  (parallelogram) carries `INPUT` / `DISPLAY`.
- **Before writing a program**, develop the **algorithm** and/or the
  **flowchart** for it.
- Algorithm and flowchart are **language-independent** and give two views of the
  same reasoning: textual for one, graphical for the other.

questions.question_text: What is meant by the portability of a program?
questions.choice_a: The ability to run a program with no operating system
questions.choice_b: The ability of a program to run with no RAM
questions.choice_c: The ability to physically move a computer without turning it off
questions.choice_d: The ability to write programs that are independent of a particular type of computer
questions.explanation: High-level languages let the programmer write programs that are independent of particular types of computer. That is what portability means.

questions.question_text: How can the portability of a program be aided?
questions.choice_a: By compiling the program on as many machines as possible
questions.choice_b: By using an agreed standard when writing the program, such as C99
questions.choice_c: By writing directly in machine language
questions.choice_d: By using no external libraries
questions.explanation: Portability can be aided by using an agreed standard when writing the program, such as C99. The standard fixes a common behavior that all conforming compilers must respect.

questions.question_text: What is the role of a compiler such as gcc or icc?
questions.choice_a: To execute the program line by line without translating it
questions.choice_b: To detect errors while the program runs
questions.choice_c: To link the program to the system libraries only
questions.choice_d: To convert a program written in a high-level language into executable machine code
questions.explanation: A compiler such as gcc or icc is used to convert the high-level program into machine code that can be executed by the computer.

questions.question_text: In what order do the levels of program representation follow one another?
questions.choice_a: High-level language, then machine code, then assembly code
questions.choice_b: High-level language, then assembly code, then machine code
questions.choice_c: Assembly code, then high-level language, then machine code
questions.choice_d: Machine code, then assembly code, then high-level language
questions.explanation: The translation chain goes down from the high-level language (HLL) to assembly code, then to machine code, the only form the processor executes directly.

questions.question_text: In what form does the processor actually execute a program?
questions.choice_a: As source text, interpreted on the fly
questions.choice_b: As machine code, strings of 0s and 1s
questions.choice_c: As high-level language, line by line
questions.choice_d: As assembly code, with mnemonics
questions.explanation: The processor only executes machine code: strings of 0s and 1s. Assembly merely puts mnemonics on those instructions, and a high-level language must be compiled before it can run.

questions.question_text: What is the main reason given for using C?
questions.choice_a: It is the only language able to access the network
questions.choice_b: It needs no compilation
questions.choice_c: It prevents all memory errors by construction
questions.choice_d: It produces code that runs nearly as fast as assembly while still being a high-level language
questions.explanation: C is chosen mainly because it produces code that runs nearly as fast as code written in assembly, while still being a high-level programming language.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT cited in the course as a typical use of C?
questions.choice_a: Network drivers and print spoolers
questions.choice_b: Operating systems
questions.choice_c: Compilers and assemblers
questions.choice_d: Collaborative online spreadsheets
questions.explanation: The uses cited are: operating systems, language compilers, assemblers, text editors, print spoolers, network drivers, language interpreters and utilities.

questions.question_text: In the chain of executing a program, what does the compiler produce from the source code?
questions.choice_a: The final executable directly
questions.choice_b: An object file
questions.choice_c: The program's results
questions.choice_d: A shared-library file
questions.explanation: The chain is: the programmer writes the source in a text editor, the compiler produces an object file, the linker combines that object with the libraries to produce the executable, and the runner executes it to give the results.

questions.question_text: In the program-execution chain, what does the linker take as input and produce as output?
questions.choice_a: It takes the source file and produces an object file
questions.choice_b: It takes the object file plus the libraries and produces the executable
questions.choice_c: It takes the executable and produces the program's results
questions.choice_d: It takes the high-level code and produces assembly code
questions.explanation: The linker has two inputs on the diagram: the object file produced by the compiler, and the libraries. It combines them into the single executable file.

questions.question_text: What tool does the programmer use in the very first stage of the chain?
questions.choice_a: The linker, to prepare the libraries
questions.choice_b: A text editor, to produce the source file
questions.choice_c: The compiler, applied straight from the keyboard
questions.choice_d: The debugger, to set breakpoints
questions.explanation: The chain begins with the programmer using a text editor to write the source file containing the C code.

questions.question_text: The line #include <stdio.h> is handled by which part of the toolchain, and to what effect?
questions.choice_a: By the linker, which links the stdio library into the executable
questions.choice_b: By the compiler, which treats it as a normal statement
questions.choice_c: By the preprocessor, which inserts the standard input/output header before compilation proper
questions.choice_d: By the loader, which loads stdio into memory at run time
questions.explanation: #include, like #define and #ifdef, is a preprocessor directive: it is processed before compilation. #include <stdio.h> pastes the contents of the standard I/O header at that point, so printf is declared.

questions.question_text: In a C program, where does execution begin?
questions.choice_a: At the first #include directive
questions.choice_b: At the first line of the file, whatever it is
questions.choice_c: At the last function defined in the file
questions.choice_d: At the main function
questions.explanation: Execution of a C program begins at the main function. That is its entry point, regardless of where it sits in the file.

questions.question_text: What role do the braces { } play in a C program?
questions.choice_a: They delimit a block of statements, such as the body of a function
questions.choice_b: They declare an array
questions.choice_c: They mark the start and end of a string
questions.choice_d: They mark a comment
questions.explanation: Braces delimit a block. In the minimal program they enclose the body of the main function, that is, the set of statements it executes.

questions.question_text: You compile a program that calls a function declared in a header but defined in no source file or library. Which stage of the chain reports the error?
questions.choice_a: The preprocessor, when it expands the #include
questions.choice_b: The compiler, because the call has no matching definition in that file
questions.choice_c: The linker, because it cannot resolve the symbol against any object or library
questions.choice_d: The runner, because the function is missing at run time
questions.explanation: The compiler only needs a declaration to accept the call and emit the object file. Resolving the call to an actual definition is the linker's job; a missing definition is the classic 'undefined reference' link error.

questions.question_text: An algorithm reads N, then while a counter stays <= N it reads a number and adds it to a sum only when it is even. Which of the three constructs does it use?
questions.choice_a: Imperative only
questions.choice_b: Imperative and conditional only
questions.choice_c: Imperative and iterative only
questions.choice_d: All three: imperative, conditional and iterative
questions.explanation: Reads and assignments are imperative, the 'while counter <= N' is iterative, and the 'only when it is even' test is conditional.

questions.question_text: Trace this algorithm: I = 0; SUM = 0; REPEAT WHILE I < 3 { INPUT X; SUM = SUM + X; I = I + 1 }; DISPLAY SUM. The inputs are 4, 1, 7. What is displayed?
questions.explanation: The loop runs three times (I = 0, 1, 2), accumulating 4 + 1 + 7 = 12 into SUM.

questions.question_text: A flowchart: START -> INPUT A, B -> <Is A > B ?> with yes -> [MAX = A] and no -> [MAX = B], both joining DISPLAY MAX -> END. With A = 3 and B = 9, which branch runs and what is displayed?
questions.choice_a: The 'yes' branch; it displays 3
questions.choice_b: The 'no' branch; it displays 9
questions.choice_c: The 'yes' branch; it displays 9
questions.choice_d: Neither branch; the flowchart has no valid path
questions.explanation: A > B is 3 > 9, which is false, so the 'no' branch sets MAX = B = 9, and both branches merge into DISPLAY MAX.

exercises.prompt: What are the four components of a computer covered in the lecture?
choices: Input devices, the CPU, main memory and output devices
The keyboard, the monitor, the hard disk and the motherboard
The ALU, the CU, the RAM and the ROM
The compiler, the linker, the loader and the OS
exercises.explanation: A computer = input devices -> CPU <-> main memory -> output devices.

exercises.prompt: What does the CPU contain?
choices: The ALU, the control unit (CU) and registers
Only the data bus and the address bus
exercises.explanation: The CPU is a VLSI circuit: arithmetic and logic unit (ALU) + control unit (CU) + general and special purpose registers.

exercises.prompt: What is the role of the control unit (CU)?
choices: Generate the control signals sent to the components
exercises.explanation: The CU generates and distributes the control signals; the ALU is what performs the arithmetic and logic operations.

exercises.prompt: Through what does the CPU communicate directly with main memory?
choices: The data bus and the address bus
exercises.explanation: The CPU accesses main memory directly via the data bus and the address bus.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is correct?
choices: RAM is volatile, ROM is non-volatile
RAM is non-volatile, ROM is volatile
RAM and ROM are both volatile
RAM and ROM are secondary memory
exercises.explanation: Primary memory splits into RAM (volatile: current instructions and data) and ROM (non-volatile).

exercises.prompt: What is secondary memory (hard disk, flash drive) used for?
choices: As a non-volatile, large-capacity data reservoir
exercises.explanation: Secondary memory is non-volatile and acts as a data reservoir; the CPU cannot address it directly.

exercises.prompt: What does the loader do?
choices: It loads a program from secondary memory into main memory so it can run
It links object codes into an executable
exercises.explanation: Loader = loading from secondary memory into an area of main memory. The linker, by contrast, assembles the object codes.

exercises.prompt: What does the linker do?
choices: It links the object codes of the subroutines and forms an executable
It loads the program into main memory
exercises.explanation: The linker combines the object codes (and the libraries) into a single executable file.

exercises.prompt: A translator (compiler) turns...
choices: A high-level language program into machine language
Machine language into a high-level language
exercises.explanation: A translator turns an HLL program (C, C++, Java...) into machine language.

exercises.prompt: Which one is system software (not application software)?
exercises.explanation: System software: OS, loader, linker, translator. Spreadsheet / image editing / word processor are application software.

exercises.prompt: Which primary memory is volatile: the RAM or the ROM?
exercises.explanation: RAM is volatile: its contents are lost when power is cut. ROM is non-volatile.

exercises.prompt: What is an algorithm?
choices: A finite set of unambiguous instructions that performs a task correctly
An electronic diagram of the CPU
exercises.explanation: Algorithm = a finite set of unambiguous instructions which, when executed, accomplish the task. It is language-independent.

exercises.prompt: Which properties must an algorithm have?
exercises.explanation: An algorithm must be finite and its instructions unambiguous. It has no fixed writing style.

exercises.prompt: What are the three programming constructs?
exercises.explanation: Every piece of logic reduces to imperative statements (actions), conditional ones (IF/ELSE) and iterative ones (loops).

exercises.prompt: `IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... END IF` is which construct?
exercises.explanation: IF/ELSE picks a branch based on a condition: it is the conditional construct.

exercises.prompt: `REPEAT WHILE ... END WHILE` is which construct?
exercises.explanation: REPEAT WHILE repeats a block while a condition holds: iterative construct.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the condition. Algorithm MAXIMUM: "Step 3  IF ___ THEN  MAX = A  ELSE  MAX = B".
exercises.explanation: We take A as the maximum when A is strictly greater than B: IF A > B THEN MAX = A.

exercises.prompt: In the "sum of even numbers" algorithm, which instruction computes the remainder used to test whether NUM is even?
exercises.explanation: REM = NUM mod 2; if REM == 0, NUM is even.

exercises.prompt: An algorithm does: INPUT A, INPUT B, INPUT C; SUM = A + B + C; AVG = SUM / 3; DISPLAY AVG. What does it compute?
choices: The sum of the even numbers
The quotient of A by B
exercises.explanation: SUM is the sum of the three inputs, AVG = SUM / 3 is their average.

exercises.prompt: Put the algorithm that displays the average of three numbers in order.
exercises.explanation: Read the three numbers, compute the sum, then the average, then display it.

exercises.prompt: Put the algorithm that displays the maximum of A and B in order.
exercises.explanation: Read A and B, compare them, assign MAX in the right branch, then display it.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of executing a program in order, from source code to result.
steps: The programmer writes the source code in the editor
The compiler turns the source into an object file
The linker combines the object with the libraries
The runner executes the executable and gives the results
exercises.explanation: Editor -> source; compiler -> object; linker (+ libraries) -> executable; runner -> results.

exercises.prompt: Write the algorithm that displays the average of three numbers A, B and C.
exercises.hint: 8 lines, as in the lecture: START, 3 INPUT, SUM, AVG, DISPLAY, END.
exercises.explanation: Three reads, one sum, one division by 3, one display.

exercises.prompt: Write the algorithm that displays the maximum of A and B, using IF / ELSE / END IF.
exercises.hint: 10 lines: START, INPUT A, INPUT B, IF ... THEN, MAX = A, ELSE, MAX = B, END IF, DISPLAY MAX, END.
exercises.explanation: Compare A and B and assign MAX in the matching branch.

exercises.prompt: Write the division algorithm Q = A / B that only divides when B is not zero.
exercises.hint: 8 lines: START, INPUT A, INPUT B, IF B != 0 THEN, Q = A/B, DISPLAY Q, END IF, END.
exercises.explanation: The division only happens in the B != 0 branch; otherwise nothing is done and the algorithm ends.

exercises.prompt: Which flowchart symbol marks the start and the end?
exercises.explanation: The terminal symbol (oval / rounded rectangle) marks START and END.

exercises.prompt: Which symbol represents an input or output operation?
exercises.explanation: The parallelogram = input/output (INPUT, DISPLAY). The rectangle = process.

exercises.prompt: Which symbol represents a processing operation?
exercises.explanation: The rectangle carries the imperative logic (assignments, computations).

exercises.prompt: Which symbol represents a condition?
exercises.explanation: The diamond represents a decision: a condition evaluated to true or false.

exercises.prompt: How many exits does a decision diamond have?
choices: Two: one for true, one for false
As many as the program has branches
exercises.explanation: A decision has exactly two exit points, for the condition being true and false.

exercises.prompt: What is the off-page connector (pentagon) used for?
choices: Linking two points of a flowchart on different pages
Marking the end of the flowchart
exercises.explanation: The off-page connector links two points when the flowchart spans several pages; the plain connector (circle) links two points on the same page.

exercises.prompt: Which shape represents a decision in a flowchart?
exercises.explanation: A decision is drawn as a diamond, with two exits true / false.

exercises.prompt: Build the flowchart that displays the average of three numbers A, B and C.
exercises.hint: Everything is linear: start, three inputs, two processes, one output, end.
exercises.explanation: No decision: the flow goes straight down from START to END.

exercises.prompt: Build the flowchart that computes Q = A / B while avoiding division by zero.
exercises.hint: One decision "Is B != 0 ?": yes -> divide and display; no -> go straight to the end.
exercises.explanation: The "no" branch skips the computation and joins END; the "yes" branch divides, displays, then END.

exercises.prompt: Build the flowchart that displays the maximum of A and B.
exercises.hint: Decision "Is A > B ?": yes -> MAX = A; no -> MAX = B; both branches join DISPLAY MAX.
exercises.explanation: The two branches of the decision merge (join point) before the display.

exercises.prompt: With the inputs A = 6 and B = 0, what does this flowchart display?
choices: Nothing: it reaches END without displaying
exercises.explanation: B != 0 is false, so the no branch is taken straight to END: Q is never computed nor displayed.

exercises.prompt: With the inputs A = 6 and B = 3, what does this flowchart display?
exercises.explanation: B != 0 is true: Q = A / B = 2 is computed and displayed.

# Computer Programming — Week 2 · Overview of C & Constants

**Cours** : Chapter 2, *Overview of C* (slides 2_1) et le début du Chapter 3,
*Constants, Variables and Data Types* (slides 2_2) : **character set**,
**tokens**, **keywords**, **identifiers**, les **constants** (integer, real,
character, string, escape sequences) et les **variables**.

> **En bref.** Un programme C a **une seule** `main()` et suit toujours le même
> squelette (documentation → link → definition → global → `main` →
> subprograms). On l'**édite**, le **compile** (`cc prog.c`), le **link** avec
> la system library et on l'**exécute** (`a.out`). Les plus petites unités du
> code sont les **tokens** : keywords (32, en minuscules), identifiers (lettre
> ou `_` d'abord), constants, strings, operators, special symbols. Au quiz :
> savoir dire si un **identifier** est valide, quel est le **type d'une
> constante**, et ce que fait une **escape sequence**.

## 2. Les programmes d'exemple du chapitre

| Fig. | Programme | Ce qu'il montre |
|---|---|---|
| 2.2 | `printf("I see, I remember");` | un `main()` minimal, une seule instruction |
| 2.4 | `number = 100; amount = 30.75 + 75.35;` puis `%d` et `%5.2f` | déclarations `int`/`float`, sortie **`100`** puis **`106.10`** |
| 2.5 | investment problem, `#define PERIOD 10`, `PRINCIPAL 5000.00`, `while (year <= PERIOD)` | **symbolic constants**, boucle `while`, `value = amount + inrate * amount` |
| 2.7 | `int mul(int a, int b);` puis `c = mul(a, b);` | une **user-defined function** déclarée avant `main` |
| 2.8 | `#include <math.h>`, `y = cos(x);` | une **math function** (il faut **`-lm`** au link) |

```c
/* Fig. 2.7 : a program using a user-defined function */
int mul(int a, int b);          /* DECLARATION (prototype) */

main()
{
    int a, b, c;
    a = 5;
    b = 10;
    c = mul(a, b);
    printf("multiplication of %d and %d is %d", a, b, c);
}

int mul(int x, int y)           /* DEFINITION, après main */
{
    int p;
    p = x * y;
    return (p);
}
```

> Les slides utilisent le style pré-ANSI (`main()` sans type de retour). En C
> moderne on écrit `int main(void)` et on termine par `return 0;`.

|---|---|---|

  à l'**accolade fermante** correspondante.
- **C is free-form** : `a = b; x = y + 1; z = a + x;` peut tenir sur une ligne.
  L'indentation ne sert qu'à la lisibilité.

## 5. Character set et tokens

Le **character set** du C est rangé en **4 catégories** :

| Catégorie | Contenu |
|---|---|
| **Letters** | `A…Z`, `a…z` |
| **Digits** | `0…9` |
| **Special characters** | `, . ; ' " | / \ ~ _ ! ? $ % # & ^ * - + < > ( ) [ ] { }` |
| **White spaces** | blank space, horizontal tab, carriage return, new line, form feed |

Un **token** est la **plus petite unité individuelle** d'un programme C (comme
les mots et la ponctuation dans un texte).

## 6. Keywords

Les **keywords** ont un **sens fixe qu'on ne peut pas changer** et s'écrivent
**en minuscules**. ANSI C en a **32** :

| | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `auto` | `do` | `goto` | `signed` | `unsigned` |
| `break` | `double` | `if` | `sizeof` | `void` |
| `case` | `else` | `int` | `static` | `volatile` |
| `char` | `enum` | `long` | `struct` | `while` |
| `const` | `extern` | `register` | `switch` | |
| `continue` | `float` | `return` | `typedef` | |
| `default` | `for` | `short` | `union` | |

> **Piège :** `main`, `printf`, `scanf`, `include`, `define` ne sont **pas** des
> keywords. `main` est un identifier, `printf` une fonction de bibliothèque,
> `#include`/`#define` des directives du préprocesseur.

## 7. Identifiers

Les **identifiers** sont les noms **définis par l'utilisateur** : variables,
fonctions, tableaux (`int my_name;`, `void CalculateTotal(int value)`).

**Règles :**

1. Le **premier caractère** est une **lettre** ou **`_`**.
2. Uniquement **lettres, chiffres et `_`**.
3. Seuls les **31 premiers caractères** sont significatifs (ANSI ; 63 en C99).
4. Pas un **keyword**.
5. Pas d'**espace** (white space).
6. **Case sensitive** : `Ss ≠ ss`, `Vmax ≠ vmax`.
7. Aucun **opérateur** (`R*S+T`) ni **signe de ponctuation** (`#@x%!!`).

| Nom | Valide ? | Pourquoi |
|---|---|---|
| `times10` | ✅ | lettre d'abord |
| `get_next_char` | ✅ | `_` autorisé |
| `_done` | ✅ | `_` en premier autorisé |
| `int_type` | ✅ | contient un keyword mais n'en **est** pas un |
| `10times` | ❌ | commence par un chiffre |
| `get-next-char` | ❌ | `-` est un opérateur |
| `char` | ❌ | keyword |
| `Price$` | ❌ | `$` interdit |
| `Group one` | ❌ | espace |

### Integer constants

| Base | Règle | Exemples | Invalide |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Decimal** | chiffres 0–9, signe optionnel | `0`, `321`, `-22`, `+99` | `25,012` (virgule), `$1000`, `20 000` |
| **Octal** | **commence par `0`**, chiffres 0–7 | `0436`, `0`, `071` | `089` (8 et 9 interdits) |
| **Hexadecimal** | **commence par `0x`/`0X`**, 0–9 et A–F | `0X2`, `0x9F`, `0x2af` | `0xG1` |

- La plus grande valeur dépend de la **machine** (16 bits, 32 bits…).
- **Qualifiers** : `56789U` = **unsigned**, `9876543L` = **long**,
  `987612347UL` = **unsigned long** (minuscules acceptées : `u`, `l`, `ul`).

> **Piège :** `0436` n'est **pas** 436 : c'est de l'**octal** = 4·64 + 3·8 + 6
> = **286** en décimal.

### Real (floating-point) constants

- **Decimal notation** : `0.083`, `-0.75`, `435.36`, `+247.0`, et aussi `215.`,
  `.95`, `-.71`, `+.5`.
- **Exponential (scientific) notation** : `mantissa e exponent`, l'exposant est
  un **entier** : `0.65e4` (= 6500), `12e-2` (= 0.12), `1.5e+5`, `3.18E3`,
  `-1.2e-1`.
- **Invalides** : `1.5E+2.5` (exposant non entier), `7.1e 4` (espace).

### Character et string constants

| | Écriture | Valeur |
|---|---|---|
| **Single character** | entre **apostrophes** : `'5'`, `'X'`, `';'`, `' '` | a une **valeur entière** (code **ASCII**) |
| **String** | entre **guillemets** : `"Hello!"`, `"1987"`, `"5+3"`, `"X"` | **pas** de valeur entière |

- `'5' != 5` : `'5'` vaut **53** (ASCII), `5` vaut 5.
- `printf("%d", 'a');` → **97** ; `printf("%c", 97);` → **a**.
- `'X'` (un char) ≠ `"X"` (une string d'un caractère, terminée par `\0`).

### Backslash characters (escape sequences)

| Séquence | Effet | Séquence | Effet |
|---|---|---|---|
| `\a` | **beep** (alert) | `\v` | vertical tab |
| `\b` | backspace | `\\` | backslash |
| `\f` | form feed (imprimante) | `\"` | guillemet |
| `\n` | **new line** | `\'` | apostrophe |
| `\r` | carriage return | `\0` | **NULL** (fin de string) |
| `\t` | horizontal **tab** | `\ooo` / `\xhh` | octal / hexadecimal |

### Enumeration

```c
enum Language { Korean, Malay, English, Arabic };
/*                0       1       2       3     */
```

## 9. Variables

Une **variable** est un **nom de donnée** associé à une **case mémoire** dont la
**valeur peut changer**.

| Étape | Exemple | Sens |
|---|---|---|
| **Declaration** | `int num;` | précise le **type** |
| **Definition / assignment** | `num = 5;` | donne une **valeur** |

On **déclare avant d'utiliser** :

```c
int inches, feet, fathoms;   /* int   */
float x, y;                  /* float */
char c;                      /* char  */
```

**Trois classes de data types** en ANSI C :

| Classe | Exemples |
|---|---|
| **Primary (fundamental)** | `int`, `char`, `float`, `double`, `long double`, `void` |
| **User-defined** | `typedef`, `enum` |
| **Derived** | arrays, functions, structures, pointers |

```flowchart
    { "id": "err", "kind": "io", "label": "\"Error: Division by zero\"" },
    { "id": "x", "kind": "process", "label": "x = a / den" },
    { "id": "out", "kind": "io", "label": "DISPLAY x" },
    { "id": "e", "kind": "end", "label": "END" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "s", "to": "in" }, { "from": "in", "to": "p" }, { "from": "p", "to": "d" },
    { "from": "d", "to": "err", "branch": "yes" }, { "from": "d", "to": "x", "branch": "no" },
    { "from": "x", "to": "out" }, { "from": "out", "to": "e" }, { "from": "err", "to": "e" }
  ]
}
```

| Cas | a | b | c | b − c | x |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | 250 | 85 | 25 | 60 | **4.166667** |
| (b) | 300 | 70 | 70 | **0** | erreur |

Autre exercice du chapitre : afficher l'équation d'une droite
`ax + by = c` avec a = 5, b = 8, c = 18 →
`printf("%dx + %dy = %d\n", a, b, c);` → `5x + 8y = 18`.

### Exo 5 — afficher chaque type

| Variable | Initialisée à | Format | Sortie |
|---|---|---|---|
| `int int_val` | `0` | `%d` | `0` |
| `float float_val` | `0.0` | `%f` | `0.000000` |
| `char char_val` | `'0'` | `%c` | `0` (le caractère ; en `%d` ce serait **48**) |
| `double double_val` | `0.0` | `%lf` | `0.000000` |

---

## Pièges d'exam

- **Une seule `main()`** ; deux = illégal.
- `0436` est **octal**, `0x2af` **hexadécimal** ; `25,012` et `$1000` sont
  **invalides**.
- Exposant **entier** obligatoire : `1.5E+2.5` invalide.
- `'5'` (char, ASCII 53) ≠ `5` (int) ≠ `"5"` (string).
- Identifier : **lettre ou `_` d'abord**, pas de `-`, `$`, espace, ni keyword ;
  **case sensitive**.
- Les keywords sont **en minuscules** ; `main` n'en est pas un.
- `cc prog.c` → **`a.out`** ; `-o name` renomme ; **`-lm`** pour `<math.h>`.

## À retenir

- Squelette : documentation → link → definition → global → **main** →
  subprograms.
- Tokens : keywords, identifiers, constants, strings, special symbols,
  operators.
- Constants : integer (dec / **0**ctal / **0x**hex, suffixes `U L UL`), real
  (décimal ou `mantisse e exposant`), character (`'x'`, valeur ASCII), string
  (`"x"`).
- Escape sequences : `\n` new line, `\t` tab, `\a` beep, `\0` NULL, `\\`, `\"`.
- Variable = nom d'une case mémoire ; **déclarer** (type) avant **définir**
  (valeur).

questions.question_text: In what order do the sections of a C source file appear?
questions.choice_a: main() function, then link section, then definitions, then subprograms
questions.choice_b: Documentation, link, definition, global declaration, main(), subprograms
questions.choice_c: Subprograms first, then main(), then the #include directives
questions.choice_d: There is no fixed order in C; sections may appear anywhere
questions.explanation: The canonical order is: documentation, link (#include), definition (#define), global declaration, the main() function, then the subprogram section with the user-defined functions.

questions.question_text: How many main() functions may a C program contain, and what happens there?
questions.choice_a: Exactly one; execution of the program begins there
questions.choice_b: At least one; execution begins at whichever is defined first
questions.choice_c: Any number; they run one after another
questions.choice_d: Zero or one; with none, execution starts at the first function
questions.explanation: Every C program has exactly one main(). It is the entry point: execution begins at its opening brace regardless of where it sits in the file.

questions.question_text: What does printf("%5.2f", 3.14159); print?
questions.choice_c: 3.14 (with one leading space)
questions.explanation: %.2f rounds to two decimals -> 3.14 (four characters). The width 5 pads it with one leading space to reach a total width of 5. Width is a minimum, never a truncation.

questions.question_text: A program runs printf("%d\n", 100); then printf("%5.2f", 30.75 + 75.35);. What is the output?
questions.explanation: First line prints 100 and a newline. 30.75 + 75.35 = 106.10, printed by %5.2f as 106.10 (already 6 characters, so the width 5 adds no padding).

questions.question_text: In the command cc prog.c -lm, what is -lm for?
questions.choice_a: It turns on all compiler warnings
questions.choice_b: It links the math library, needed for <math.h> functions like cos and sqrt
questions.choice_c: It names the output file 'm'
questions.choice_d: It compiles without linking
questions.explanation: -lm links libm, the math library. Functions declared in <math.h> live there and are not linked by default.

questions.question_text: You run cc prog.c with no -o option. What is the executable called?
questions.choice_a: prog
questions.choice_b: prog.exe
questions.choice_c: prog.out
questions.choice_d: a.out
questions.explanation: Without -o, the compiled and linked program is written to a.out. cc -o name prog.c chooses the name instead.

questions.question_text: What does the preprocessor do with the line #define PI 3.1416 ?
questions.choice_a: It creates a read-only float variable named PI
questions.choice_b: It substitutes the text 3.1416 for every PI in the source, before compilation
questions.choice_c: It tells the linker to include a constant named PI
questions.choice_d: Nothing; #define is only a comment to the reader
questions.explanation: #define is a textual substitution performed by the preprocessor before the compiler runs. It has no type, no '=', and no trailing semicolon.

questions.question_text: A program calls mul(5, 10) inside main(), but mul is defined AFTER main(). What is needed for this to compile cleanly?
questions.choice_a: A prototype 'int mul(int a, int b);' before main()
questions.choice_b: Nothing; C always scans the whole file first
questions.choice_c: mul must be marked 'static'
questions.choice_d: mul must be moved into a separate #include file
questions.explanation: The compiler reads top to bottom. A function used before its definition needs a prototype (declaration) earlier, typically in the global declaration section.

exercises.prompt: int num; int r = scanf("Enter radius: %d", &num); float area = PI * (r * r); -- what is wrong?
choices: The area is computed from r, which is scanf's return value (the count of items read, 1), not from num
PI cannot be used in a multiplication
scanf is unable to read an integer
area must be declared as double, never float
exercises.explanation: Two bugs: (1) the format string embeds the prompt text 'Enter radius: ', so the user must type it back literally -- print it with printf instead; (2) r holds scanf's return value (1 on success), so PI * r * r is always PI, never the circle area. Use num.

exercises.prompt: float b = 70, c = 70; float denominator = b - c; if (denominator == 0) { ... } -- what is the concern with 'denominator == 0'?
choices: Comparing a floating-point result to 0 with == is fragile; a tiny rounding error would slip past the guard and the division would still run
A float can never be compared with an integer literal
The condition is always true, so the division never happens
exercises.explanation: Here 70.0f - 70.0f is exactly 0.0 so the guard happens to fire, but in general an == test against a float is unsafe. Guard the inputs (b != c) or test against a small tolerance.

exercises.prompt: A program has #define PI 3.1416 at the top but its body only does sum = x + y;. What can be said?
choices: PI is defined but never used -- the macro is dead code
sum cannot be a global variable
main must take argc and argv
exercises.explanation: An unused #define is harmless but pointless -- it signals either a leftover or an unfinished computation. sum is an int, printed correctly with %d.

exercises.prompt: In scanf("%d", &n), why is the & needed in front of n?
accept: to pass the address of n
so scanf can write into n
it passes the address of n so scanf can store the value there
because scanf needs a pointer to n
to give scanf the address of the variable
exercises.explanation: C passes arguments by value, so scanf receives a copy. &n passes n's address instead, letting scanf write the read value back into n.

exercises.prompt: Build the flowchart that reads a radius R and displays the area of the circle (AREA = PI * R * R).
exercises.hint: Linear: start, one input, one process, one output, end. No decision.
exercises.explanation: No decision is needed: read R, compute PI * R * R, display it.

exercises.prompt: Write the algorithm that computes x = a / (b - c), dividing only when b - c is not zero.
exercises.hint: 9 lines: START, INPUT a, INPUT b, INPUT c, IF b - c != 0 THEN, x = a / (b - c), DISPLAY x, END IF, END.
exercises.explanation: The division sits inside the b - c != 0 branch. With b - c = 0 (e.g. a=300, b=70, c=70) nothing is displayed and the algorithm ends.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of building and running a C program with the UNIX cc command in order.
steps: Write prog.c in a text editor
The linker writes the executable to a.out
exercises.explanation: cc prog.c does compilation and linking in one step; with no -o the result is a.out, which you then execute.

exercises.prompt: Into how many categories is the C character set grouped?
choices: 4: letters, digits, special characters, white spaces
exercises.explanation: Letters, digits, special characters, white spaces.

exercises.prompt: What is a C token?
choices: The smallest individual unit of a C program
exercises.explanation: Keywords, identifiers, constants, strings, special symbols, operators.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is NOT a C keyword?
exercises.explanation: main est un identifier ; les 32 keywords s'écrivent en minuscules et ont un sens fixe.

exercises.prompt: Match each name with its validity as an identifier.
pairs: valid: may start with an underscore
valid: contains a keyword but is not one
exercises.explanation: Lettre ou _ d'abord, puis lettres, chiffres, _ ; pas de keyword ; pas d'espace.

exercises.prompt: Which integer constant is written in OCTAL?
exercises.explanation: Octal = commence par 0, chiffres 0–7 ; 0x = hexadécimal.

exercises.prompt: What is the decimal value of the octal constant 0436?
Which real constant is INVALID?
exercises.explanation: L'exposant doit être un entier ; 7.1e 4 (espace) est aussi invalide.

exercises.prompt: Which integer constant is INVALID?
exercises.explanation: Ni virgule, ni espace, ni $ dans une constante entière.

exercises.prompt: What does printf("%d", 'a'); print?
exercises.explanation: Une character constant a une valeur entière : son code ASCII ('A' = 65, '0' = 48).

exercises.prompt: Which statement about '5', 5 and "5" is correct?
choices: '5' is a char (ASCII 53), 5 is an int, "5" is a string
exercises.explanation: Une string n'a pas de valeur entière associée.

exercises.prompt: Match each escape sequence with its effect.
exercises.explanation: Backslash character constants (escape sequences).

exercises.prompt: int num; then num = 5; — what are these two steps called?
exercises.explanation: La déclaration donne le type, l'affectation donne la valeur.

exercises.prompt: Match each class of data types with an example.
exercises.explanation: ANSI C supports three classes of data types.

exercises.prompt: How many main() functions may a C program contain?
exercises.explanation: Utiliser plus d'une main() est illégal ; l'exécution commence à main.

exercises.prompt: Order the sections of a C program from top to bottom.
exercises.explanation: Fig. 2.9 : seule main() est obligatoire.

exercises.prompt: cc ebg1.c compiles and links a program. What is the default name of the executable on UNIX?
exercises.explanation: cc -o name source.c pour choisir un autre nom ; -lm pour la math library.

Keywords, identifiers, constants, strings, special symbols, operators.

name: Week 1
lesson:
# Database Design — Week 1

Lectures 01–02 — *Introduction & Course Overview*, *Introduction to DBMS*.
Data and information, the DBMS concept, the eight advantages of a database,
basic terminology, the three-level ANSI-SPARC architecture, data independence,
types of users, the role of the DBA and the database system architecture.

---

## 1. Data, information, DBMS

**Data** is raw, unorganized facts, observations or symbols: numbers (50, 62),
text ("apple"), an image, an audio clip, a video. **Without context, data is
useless.** Once it is processed, organized, structured or presented in a
context that makes it useful, it becomes **information**.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Data becomes information once it is processed and given a context.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "d", "x": 90, "y": 40, "w": 160, "h": 56, "label": "Data\nStudent_1 = 50/100\nStudent_2 = 25/100", "tone": "neutral" },
    { "id": "p", "x": 320, "y": 40, "h": 48, "label": "process\norganise · structure", "shape": "ellipse", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "i", "x": 550, "y": 40, "w": 160, "h": 56, "label": "Information\nStudent_1 = Pass\nStudent_2 = Fail", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "d", "to": "p" },
    { "from": "p", "to": "i" }
  ]
}
```

The acronym **DBMS** breaks down as:

| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Data** | a fact that can be recorded or stored | a person's name, age, gender, weight |
| **Database** | a collection of logically related data | the books database of a library, the student database of a university |
| **Management** | manipulation, searching and security of the data | viewing a result on a website, searching exam papers |
| **System** | the programs or tools used to manage the database | SQL Server Studio Express, Oracle |

A **DBMS** is therefore **software designed to define, manipulate, retrieve and
manage the data in a database**. Examples: MS SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, SQLite,
MongoDB.

It is a **computerized record-keeping system**, required wherever data needs to
be stored: e-commerce (Amazon, eBay), streaming (Prime, Hotstar), social media,
banking and insurance, airlines and railways, universities and schools, library
management, human resources, hospitals and medical stores, government
organizations.

## 2. The eight advantages of a DBMS

The slides illustrate every advantage with the same `Faculty` record for
*Prof. Lee* stored by several departments of a college. Keep that picture in
mind: without a DBMS, each department keeps **its own file**.

### 2.1 Reduce data redundancy (duplication)

Four departments, four copies of the same row.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Without a DBMS the same data is stored at four different places.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t1", "x": 150, "y": 45, "shape": "table", "label": "Computer", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","8235","DB"]], "mark": [1] },
    { "id": "t2", "x": 470, "y": 45, "shape": "table", "label": "Business", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","8235","DB"]], "mark": [1] },
    { "id": "t3", "x": 150, "y": 265, "shape": "table", "label": "Electrical", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","8235","DB"]], "mark": [1] },
    { "id": "t4", "x": 470, "y": 265, "shape": "table", "label": "Mechanical", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","8235","DB"]], "mark": [1] },
    { "id": "db", "x": 310, "y": 155, "w": 150, "h": 60, "shape": "cylinder", "label": "DBMS\none central copy", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "t1", "to": "db", "tone": "emerald" },
    { "from": "t2", "to": "db", "tone": "emerald" },
    { "from": "t3", "to": "db", "tone": "emerald" },
    { "from": "t4", "to": "db", "tone": "emerald" }
  ]
}
```

A DBMS removes the redundancy by **storing the data centrally**: one copy that
every department reads.

### 2.2 Remove data inconsistency

Redundancy leads straight to inconsistency: Prof. Lee changes his mobile number,
the Computer department updates its file… and the other three copies now
disagree. The **same data exists in different states** depending on where you
look.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Same data having different states (values): the mobile number was changed in one file only.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t1", "x": 150, "y": 45, "shape": "table", "label": "Computer", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","2237","DB"]], "mark": [1] },
    { "id": "t2", "x": 470, "y": 45, "shape": "table", "label": "Business", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","5235","DB"]], "mark": [1] },
    { "id": "t3", "x": 150, "y": 140, "shape": "table", "label": "Electrical", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","8235","DB"]], "mark": [1] },
    { "id": "t4", "x": 470, "y": 140, "shape": "table", "label": "Mechanical", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","9235","DB"]], "mark": [1] },
    { "id": "n", "x": 310, "y": 225, "w": 360, "h": 34, "shape": "note", "label": "Which mobile number is the right one? Nobody knows.", "tone": "rose" }
  ],
  "edges": []
}
```

By eliminating the redundancy, the DBMS **keeps the data in a consistent
state**: there is only one value to update.

### 2.3 Data isolation

Data is scattered across **various files**, possibly in **different formats**,
so retrieving the appropriate data is difficult. The DBMS lets us access
(retrieve) the right data easily.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Three files, three formats: answering \"everything about Prof. Lee\" means opening all of them.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "q", "x": 70, "y": 120, "w": 110, "h": 56, "shape": "ellipse", "label": "Everything\nabout Prof. Lee?", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "f1", "x": 380, "y": 40, "shape": "table", "label": "File 1", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","1234","DB"]] },
    { "id": "f2", "x": 380, "y": 130, "shape": "table", "label": "File 2", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Post","Salary","Load"],["Prof. Lee","Professor","50,000","15"]] },
    { "id": "f3", "x": 380, "y": 220, "shape": "table", "label": "File 3", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Teaching","Knowledge","Rating"],["Prof. Lee","Good","Excellent","9"]] }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "q", "to": "f1", "dashed": true },
    { "from": "q", "to": "f2", "dashed": true },
    { "from": "q", "to": "f3", "dashed": true }
  ]
}
```

> The slides also give the transactional meaning of the word: **isolation** is
> the property that determines *when and how* the changes made by one operation
> become visible to other concurrent users and systems. It only matters in a
> **concurrency** situation. Week 2 comes back to it with ACID.

### 2.4 Guaranteed atomicity

**Atomicity: a transaction executes either 0 % or 100 %.** A transfer of 500
from account A to account B is *two* steps; if the system fails after step 1,
the money has vanished.

```diagram
{
  "title": "A transfer is two steps. Atomicity guarantees both happen, or neither.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "a", "x": 90, "y": 50, "w": 130, "h": 54, "label": "Person A\nAccount A\nBal : 2000", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "b", "x": 550, "y": 50, "w": 130, "h": 54, "label": "Person B\nAccount B\nBal : 1000", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "s1", "x": 320, "y": 30, "shape": "text", "label": "Transfer 500", "bold": true },
    { "id": "s2", "x": 320, "y": 100, "w": 300, "h": 40, "shape": "note", "label": "Step 1 : debit 500 from Account A\nStep 2 : credit 500 into Account B", "tone": "neutral" },
    { "id": "ok", "x": 160, "y": 190, "w": 300, "h": 52, "shape": "note", "label": "Both steps done (100 %)\nA = 1500, B = 1500 → sum still 3000", "tone": "emerald" },
    { "id": "ko", "x": 500, "y": 190, "w": 340, "h": 52, "shape": "note", "label": "Failure after step 1 (50 %)\nA = 1500, B = 1000 → sum 2500, inconsistent", "tone": "rose" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "a", "to": "b", "tone": "sky" },
    { "from": "s2", "to": "ok", "tone": "emerald" },
    { "from": "s2", "to": "ko", "tone": "rose", "dashed": true }
  ]
}
```

The sum of both accounts is 3000 before the transfer and must be 3000 after it.
A half-executed transaction would leave 2500: the DBMS **rolls back** step 1
instead.

### 2.5 Allow to implement integrity constraints

Business rules can be enforced by the database itself.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Integrity constraints: business rules checked by the DBMS on every write.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "f", "x": 190, "y": 40, "shape": "table", "label": "Faculty", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile_No","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","8256974180","DB"]] },
    { "id": "s", "x": 190, "y": 140, "shape": "table", "label": "Student", "size": 12, "rows": [["Student_Name","Branch","Backlog","SPI"],["Irmun","Juan","0","8.5"]] },
    { "id": "c1", "x": 540, "y": 50, "w": 240, "h": 36, "shape": "note", "label": "should contain exactly 10 digits", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "c2", "x": 540, "y": 150, "w": 240, "h": 36, "shape": "note", "label": "should be between 0 and 10", "tone": "amber" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "c1", "to": "f", "tone": "amber" },
    { "from": "c2", "to": "s", "tone": "amber" }
  ]
}
```

Other examples from the slides: *do not allow to store an amount less than 0 in
a balance*.

### 2.6 Sharing of data among multiple users & 2.7 restricting unauthorized access

More than one user can access the **same data at the same time** — and only
the users who are **authorized** to.

```diagram
{
  "title": "One central copy, shared by the college's departments; a faculty from another university is refused.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "u1", "x": 80, "y": 40, "w": 120, "h": 44, "shape": "ellipse", "label": "Computer dept.", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "u2", "x": 80, "y": 110, "w": 120, "h": 44, "shape": "ellipse", "label": "Business dept.", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "u3", "x": 80, "y": 180, "w": 120, "h": 44, "shape": "ellipse", "label": "Mechanical dept.", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "db", "x": 360, "y": 110, "shape": "table", "label": "Faculty (DBMS)", "size": 12, "rows": [["Emp_Name","Address","Mobile","Subject"],["Prof. Lee","Busan","8253","DB"]] },
    { "id": "x", "x": 610, "y": 110, "w": 120, "h": 52, "shape": "ellipse", "label": "Faculty of\nanother univ.", "tone": "rose" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "u1", "to": "db", "tone": "sky", "label": "read" },
    { "from": "u2", "to": "db", "tone": "sky", "label": "update" },
    { "from": "u3", "to": "db", "tone": "sky", "label": "read" },
    { "from": "x", "to": "db", "tone": "rose", "dashed": true, "label": "denied" }
  ]
}
```

### 2.8 Providing backup and recovery services

The DBMS provides facilities to **back up** the database (auto or manual,
regular) and to **restore** it in case of failure or corruption.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Backup and recovery: a regular copy, restored after a failure (flood, virus…).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "db", "x": 90, "y": 60, "w": 120, "h": 64, "shape": "cylinder", "label": "Database", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "bk", "x": 430, "y": 60, "w": 200, "h": 64, "shape": "cylinder", "label": "Backup\nDVD · tape · remote server", "tone": "neutral", "filled": true }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "db", "to": "bk", "label": "backup (regular)", "via": [[90, 20], [430, 20]] },
    { "from": "bk", "to": "db", "label": "restore after failure", "via": [[430, 100], [90, 100]], "tone": "emerald" }
  ]
}
```

### Summary of the eight advantages

| # | Advantage | One line |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Reduce data redundancy | avoid duplication by storing data centrally |
| 2 | Remove data inconsistency | no redundancy ⇒ no contradictory copies |
| 3 | Data isolation | a user easily retrieves the proper data |
| 4 | Guaranteed atomicity | a transaction executes 0 % or 100 % |
| 5 | Integrity constraints | business rules enforced (balance ≥ 0, 10-digit mobile) |
| 6 | Sharing of data | several users access the same data simultaneously |
| 7 | Restricting unauthorized access | a user only reaches what is authorized to them |
| 8 | Backup and recovery | regular backups, restore if the database corrupts |

## 3. Basic terms

- **Data**: raw, unorganized facts that need to be processed
  (Student_1 = 50/100, Student_2 = 25/100).
- **Information**: data processed, organized, structured or presented in a
  context that makes it useful (Student_1 = Pass, Student_2 = Fail).
- **Metadata**: *data about data* — for a table: its name, its column names,
  the data types, the authorized users and their access privileges.
- **Data dictionary**: an information repository that contains the **metadata**.
- **Data warehouse**: an information repository that stores the **data** itself.

> *Exercise from the slides — why are the data dictionary and the data warehouse
> stored in different places?* Because they change at very different rates and
> serve different readers: the metadata is small, changes only when the schema
> changes and is consulted by the DBMS on every query; the data is large and
> changes constantly.

- **Field**: a character or group of characters that has a specific meaning —
  each value of `Emp_Name`, `Address`, `Mobile_No`… is a field.
- **Record / tuple**: a collection of logically related fields — the four
  fields `(Emp_Name, Address, Mobile_No, Subject)` of one professor form one
  record of the `Faculty` table.

## 4. The three-level ANSI-SPARC architecture

Database systems are made up of complex data structures. To ease the user's
interaction, the developers **hide the internal, irrelevant details** from the
users: this is **data abstraction**. ANSI-SPARC formalises it in three levels.

| Level | Question it answers | Described by | Who works there |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Internal (physical)** | *how* the data is stored on the storage device: structure of records on disk — files, pages, blocks, indexes, ordering of records | the **internal schema** | the DBMS, storage details hidden from programmers |
| **Conceptual (logical)** | *what* data is stored and *what relationships* exist among it; hides the low-level complexities of physical storage | the **conceptual schema** | the **DBA** decides what data to keep; programmers generally work here |
| **External (view)** | the **part** of the database a given end user is concerned with, i.e. how data is viewed by each user; different users need different views, so there can be many | the **external schemas** | end users (via a GUI, unaware of storage) and application programmers |

Example: a `STUDENT` database contains `STUDENT` and `COURSE` tables that are
visible to the users, who have no idea how they are stored. At the internal
level the records are blocks of storage (bytes, gigabytes…); at the conceptual
level they are fields and attributes with their data types and the relationships
between them; at the view level a user just interacts with a GUI.

### Mapping and data independence

The process of **transforming requests and results between the three levels**
is called **mapping**: a request goes down through the levels, the result comes
back up.

**Data independence** is the ability to modify a schema definition at one level
**without affecting the schema definition at the next higher level**.

```diagram

  "title": "Mapping (request down, result up) and the two kinds of data independence.",
```

| | Physical data independence | Logical data independence |
|---|---|---|
| definition | modify the **physical** schema without any change in the logical (conceptual) schema or the application programs | modify the **conceptual** schema without any change in the application programs |
| when | occasionally, to **improve performance** | whenever the **logical structure** of the database changes |
| typical changes | file structures, compression techniques, hashing algorithms, storage devices | adding a field, splitting a table… |
| difficulty | easy: nothing above depends on the storage details | hard: programs depend heavily on the logical structure of the data they access, so a logical change usually forces program changes |

## 5. Types of database users

| Type | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Naive users (end users)** | unsophisticated users with zero knowledge of the database system; interact through sophisticated software or tools | a clerk in a bank |
| **Application programmers** | write software using tools such as Java, .Net, PHP | software developers |
| **Sophisticated users** | interact with the database **without an application program**, through query tools like SQL | an analyst |
| **Specialized users (DBA)** | write specialized database application programs, use administration tools | the database administrator |

## 6. Role of the DBA (Database Administrator)

1. **Schema definition** — defines the logical schema of the database.
2. **Storage structure and access method definition** — decides how the data
   is represented in the database and how it is accessed.
3. **Defining security and integrity constraints**.
4. **Granting of authorization for data access** — which user needs access to
   which part of the database.
5. **Liaison with users** — provides the necessary data to the users.
6. **Assisting application programmers** in developing their programs.
7. **Monitoring performance** — changes the physical or logical schema when
   needed to keep performance good.
8. **Backup and recovery** — backs the database up (DVD, tape, remote servers)
   and recovers the system after a failure such as a flood or a virus attack.

## 7. Database system architecture

The whole picture: each type of user reaches the DBMS through their own tool;
inside, a **query processor** turns requests into low-level operations and a
**storage manager** executes them against the data on disk.

### Query processor

- **DDL interpreter** — processes the DDL statements (`CREATE`, `ALTER`,
  `DROP`) and records the definitions in the **data dictionary**.
- **DML compiler & organizer** — translates a DML statement into a low-level
  evaluation plan and picks the cheapest one (query optimisation).
- **Compiler & linker** — turns an application program, including the DML
  embedded in it, into object code.
- **Query evaluation engine** — actually executes the low-level instructions
  produced by the DML compiler.

### Storage manager

The interface between the low-level data on disk and the queries.

- **Buffer manager** — brings blocks from disk into main memory and decides
  what to keep cached.
- **File manager** — manages the disk-space allocation and the on-disk data
  structures.
- **Authorization & integrity manager** — checks that users have the rights
  they claim and that updates respect the integrity constraints.
- **Transaction manager** — keeps the database consistent despite failures and
  concurrent access (atomicity, isolation).

### Disk storage

The database on disk holds four kinds of data: the **data** itself, the
**indices**, the **data dictionary** (metadata) and **statistical data** (used
by the query optimiser).

---

## To remember

- Data = raw facts; information = data given a context. A DBMS is software to
  **define, manipulate, retrieve and manage** the data of a database.
- Eight advantages: no redundancy, no inconsistency, easy retrieval
  (isolation), atomicity (0 % or 100 %), integrity constraints, sharing,
  access control, backup & recovery.
- Metadata = data about data; data **dictionary** holds the metadata, data
  **warehouse** holds the data. Field = one value; record/tuple = one row.
- ANSI-SPARC: **external** (views, one per user) / **conceptual** (what data,
  what relationships — the DBA's level) / **internal** (how it is stored).
  Hiding details = data abstraction; translating between levels = mapping.
- Data independence: **physical** = change storage without touching the
  logical schema; **logical** = change the logical schema without touching the
  programs (much harder).
- Users: naive (clerk) · application programmers · sophisticated (analyst, SQL)
  · specialized (DBA). The DBA defines the schema, storage, security,
  authorizations, helps users and programmers, monitors performance, does backups.
- Architecture: query processor (DDL interpreter, DML compiler, query
  evaluation engine) over a storage manager (buffer, file, authorization &
  integrity, transaction managers) over the disk (data, indices, data
  dictionary, statistics).

questions.question_text: How does the course define a database management system (DBMS)?
questions.choice_a: A network protocol for transferring data
questions.choice_b: Software designed to define, manipulate, retrieve and manage the data in a database
questions.choice_c: A standardized query language
questions.choice_d: Hardware dedicated to storing enterprise data
questions.explanation: A DBMS is software for creating and managing databases: it defines, manipulates, retrieves and manages the data. Examples: MS SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, SQLite, MongoDB.

questions.question_text: How does the course describe a DBMS overall?
questions.choice_a: A data-oriented programming language
questions.choice_b: A specialized operating system
questions.choice_c: A computerized record-keeping system
questions.choice_d: An automatic backup service
questions.explanation: The DBMS is presented as a computerized record-keeping system, required wherever data needs to be stored: e-commerce, streaming, social media, banking, transport, universities, libraries, HR, hospitals, government.

questions.question_text: How does a DBMS reduce data redundancy?
questions.choice_a: By storing data centrally rather than duplicating it in each department
questions.choice_b: By forbidding several users from writing at the same time
questions.choice_c: By automatically compressing every table
questions.choice_d: By deleting the oldest records
questions.explanation: Without a DBMS, the same data (Prof. Lee, Busan, 8235, DB) ends up stored in four different departments. The DBMS removes that redundancy by storing data centrally.

questions.question_text: Why does removing redundancy eliminate data inconsistency?
questions.choice_a: Because the DBMS spell-checks the entered values
questions.choice_b: Because users are authenticated
questions.choice_c: Because backups are automatic
questions.choice_d: Because data stored in a single place can no longer exist in different states across copies
questions.explanation: When the same data is duplicated in four places, a partial update leaves diverging values (a mobile number changed in one place only). By eliminating redundancy, inconsistency is eliminated: the DBMS keeps data in a consistent state.

questions.question_text: What does the atomicity of a transaction guarantee?
questions.choice_a: The transaction can always be undone after commit
questions.choice_b: The transaction always executes in under a second
questions.choice_c: The transaction executes either 0% or 100%, never partially
questions.choice_d: The transaction uses only one table at a time
questions.explanation: Atomicity means a transaction executes 0% or 100%. In the example of a 500 transfer between two accounts, if the debit happens without the credit, the sum of the accounts goes from 3000 to 2500: the state becomes inconsistent.

questions.question_text: In the example of a 500 transfer between two accounts, what are the two steps of the transaction?
questions.choice_a: Debit 500 from account A, then credit 500 to account B
questions.choice_b: Check the balance, then send a notification
questions.choice_c: Copy account A, then delete account B
questions.choice_d: Lock both accounts, then unlock them
questions.explanation: The transaction has two steps: step 1, debit 500 from account A; step 2, credit 500 to account B. The sum of the two accounts must be 3000 both before and after the transfer.

questions.question_text: What example of an integrity constraint does the course give?
questions.choice_a: A mobile number must contain exactly 10 digits, an SPI must be between 0 and 10
questions.choice_b: A password must be changed every 90 days
questions.choice_c: A table must not exceed one million rows
questions.choice_d: An employee name must start with a capital letter
questions.explanation: The DBMS lets business rules be enforced as integrity constraints: the Mobile_No field must contain exactly 10 digits, and a student's SPI must be between 0 and 10.

questions.question_text: What is data isolation in the context of the DBMS?
questions.choice_a: A property that determines when and how one operation's changes become visible to other concurrent users
questions.choice_b: Forbidding a user from connecting remotely
questions.choice_c: The physical separation of disks between departments
questions.choice_d: Encrypting each table with a distinct key
questions.explanation: Without a DBMS, data is scattered across files of various formats, making it hard to retrieve. Isolation is the property that determines when and how changes made by one operation become visible to other concurrent users and systems: it is a concurrency issue.
