questions.choice_c: Ten
questions.choice_d: Three
questions.explanation: The summary lists eight advantages: reduce redundancy, remove inconsistency, data isolation, guaranteed atomicity, integrity constraints, sharing among several users, restricting unauthorized access, backup and recovery.

questions.question_text: Which advantage of a DBMS protects against data loss in case of failure?
questions.choice_a: The backup and recovery services
questions.choice_b: The reduction of redundancy
questions.choice_c: The integrity constraints
questions.choice_d: The atomicity of transactions
questions.explanation: The DBMS provides facilities to back up and restore the database in case of failure. A regular backup, automatic or manual, can restore the database if it becomes corrupted.

questions.question_text: How does a DBMS handle simultaneous access by several users to the same data?
questions.choice_a: It lets more than one user access the same data at the same time
questions.choice_b: It creates a private copy of the data for each user
questions.choice_c: It refuses all concurrent access to avoid conflicts
questions.choice_d: It queues the users, one at a time
questions.explanation: Sharing data among several users is an advantage of the DBMS: it lets more than one user access the same data simultaneously, where separate files would force duplication or block access.

questions.question_text: What is metadata?
questions.choice_a: Data stored outside the database, in a flat file
questions.choice_b: Data duplicated for backup purposes
questions.choice_c: Data about data: table name, column name, type, access privileges
questions.choice_d: Data generated automatically by a query
questions.explanation: Metadata is data about data. For a table, it is the table name, the column names, the data types, the authorized user and their access privileges.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between a data dictionary and a data warehouse?
questions.choice_a: The dictionary contains the metadata, the warehouse stores the data itself
questions.choice_b: Both store exactly the same thing in different places
questions.choice_c: The dictionary stores the data, the warehouse the metadata
questions.choice_d: The dictionary is physical, the warehouse is logical
questions.explanation: The data dictionary is an information repository containing the metadata (table name, column names, types, privileges). The data warehouse is an information repository that stores the data itself.

questions.question_text: What is a field?
questions.choice_a: A complete row of a table
questions.choice_b: A character or group of characters that has a specific meaning
questions.choice_c: The name given to a table
questions.choice_d: The set of all columns of a database
questions.explanation: A field is a character or group of characters that has a specific meaning. In the Faculty table, the values of Emp_Name, Address, Mobile_No are all fields.

questions.question_text: What is a record (or tuple)?
questions.choice_a: A collection of logically related fields
questions.choice_b: A query saved for reuse
questions.choice_c: A set of logically related tables
questions.choice_d: A constraint applied to a column
questions.explanation: A record, also called a tuple, is a collection of logically related fields. The collection of fields Emp_Name, Address, Mobile_No and Subject forms a record of the Faculty table.

questions.question_text: What are the three levels of the ANSI-SPARC architecture?
questions.choice_a: External (view), conceptual (logical) and internal (physical)
questions.choice_b: Application, presentation and session
questions.choice_c: Client, server and database
questions.choice_d: Primary, secondary and tertiary
questions.explanation: The ANSI-SPARC architecture has three levels: external or view (how data is viewed by each user), conceptual or logical (what data is stored and what relationships exist), and internal or physical (how data is actually stored).

questions.question_text: What question does the internal (physical) level answer?
questions.choice_a: Who is authorized to modify the data
questions.choice_b: What data is stored and what relationships exist among it
questions.choice_c: How each user views the data
questions.choice_d: How the data is actually stored on the storage device
questions.explanation: The internal level describes how data is stored on the storage device. It deals with physical storage: the structure of records on disk (files, pages, blocks, indexes) and the ordering of records. It is described by the internal schema.

questions.question_text: At which level of the ANSI-SPARC architecture does the DBA work to decide what data to keep?
questions.choice_a: At the external (view) level
questions.choice_b: At the internal (physical) level
questions.choice_c: At none of these levels
questions.choice_d: At the conceptual (logical) level
questions.explanation: The conceptual level answers the question of what data is stored and what relationships exist among it, hiding the low-level complexities of physical storage. This is the level where the DBA works to determine what data to keep in the database.

questions.question_text: Who uses the external (view) level of the ANSI-SPARC architecture?
questions.choice_a: Only the SQL compiler
questions.choice_b: Only the system administrator
questions.choice_c: Only the storage engine
questions.choice_d: End users and application programmers
questions.explanation: The external level describes only the part of the database that concerns a given user. Different users need different views, hence many possible views. It is used by end users and application programmers.

questions.question_text: What is data abstraction?
questions.choice_a: The deletion of obsolete data
questions.choice_b: Hiding the irrelevant internal details from the user
questions.choice_c: Automatic conversion between data types
questions.choice_d: A statistical summary of a table's data
questions.explanation: Database systems are made of complex data structures. To ease the user's interaction with the database, developers hide the irrelevant internal details: this process is called data abstraction.

questions.question_text: What is mapping in the three-level architecture?
questions.choice_a: The assignment of disk blocks to records
questions.choice_b: The association of a primary key with a foreign key
questions.choice_c: The process of transforming requests and results between the three levels
questions.choice_d: The conversion of an ER model into a relational model
questions.explanation: The process of transforming requests and results between the three levels is called mapping. It lets a request formulated at a view be translated down to the physical level, and the result back up.

questions.question_text: How is data independence defined?
questions.choice_a: The ability to modify a schema definition at one level without affecting the schema definition at the next higher level
questions.choice_b: The fact that each user has their own copy of the data
questions.choice_c: The absence of relationships between a database's tables
questions.choice_d: The possibility of storing data on several servers
questions.explanation: Data independence is the ability to modify a schema definition at one level without affecting the schema definition at the next higher level.

questions.question_text: What is physical data independence?
questions.choice_a: The physical separation of production and test servers
questions.choice_b: The ability to modify the physical schema without changing the logical schema or the application programs
questions.choice_c: The ability to modify the conceptual schema without changing the programs
questions.choice_d: The fact that data is stored on a nonvolatile medium
questions.explanation: Physical data independence is the ability to modify the physical schema without requiring a change to the logical schema or the application programs. Internal changes are sometimes needed to improve performance: file structures, compression techniques, hashing algorithms, storage devices.

questions.question_text: Why is logical data independence harder to achieve than physical data independence?
questions.choice_a: Because the logical schema can never be modified
questions.choice_b: Because the DBMS forbids any change to the conceptual level
questions.choice_c: Because the storage hardware changes too often
questions.choice_d: Because application programs depend heavily on the logical structure of the data they manipulate
questions.explanation: Logical data independence is the ability to modify the conceptual schema without changing the application programs. But programs depend heavily on the logical structures of the data they access: any change to the logical structure therefore often forces the programs to change.

questions.question_text: Which modifications would count as a change at the internal level?
questions.choice_a: Creating a view for a new user
questions.choice_b: Modifying a business rule
questions.choice_c: Adding a new table to the schema
questions.choice_d: A change of file structure, compression technique, hashing algorithm or storage device
questions.explanation: Possible modifications at the internal level are changes in file structures, compression techniques, hashing algorithms, storage devices, etc. They are occasionally necessary to improve performance.

questions.question_text: How is a naive user characterized?
questions.choice_a: A user who administers access rights
questions.choice_b: A user who develops applications in Java or PHP
questions.choice_c: A user who writes complex SQL queries
questions.choice_d: A user with no knowledge of the database system, interacting through software or a tool
questions.explanation: Naive users, or end users, are unsophisticated users with zero knowledge of the database system. They interact with the database through sophisticated software or tools. Example given: a bank teller.

questions.question_text: What characterizes a sophisticated user?
questions.choice_a: They do not know what a database is
questions.choice_b: They are responsible for the system's backups
questions.choice_c: They interact with the system without an application program, using query tools such as SQL
questions.choice_d: They write the company's application programs
questions.explanation: A sophisticated user interacts with the database system without an application program. They use query tools such as SQL. Example given: an analyst.

questions.question_text: What are the four types of database users identified?
questions.choice_a: Readers, writers, administrators and auditors
questions.choice_b: Beginners, intermediate, advanced and expert
questions.choice_c: Naive users, application programmers, sophisticated users and specialized users (DBA)
questions.choice_d: Internal, external, conceptual and physical
questions.explanation: The four types are: naive or end users (bank teller), application programmers (Java, .Net, PHP developers), sophisticated users (analysts using SQL), and specialized users or DBA.

questions.question_text: What tool does an application programmer use according to the course's taxonomy?
questions.choice_a: Languages such as Java, .Net or PHP
questions.choice_b: Only interactive SQL queries
questions.choice_c: Only database administration tools
questions.choice_d: Software with a graphical interface designed for the uninitiated
questions.explanation: Application programmers are programmers who write software using tools such as Java, .Net or PHP. Example given: a software developer.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is part of the DBA's role?
questions.choice_a: Defining the logical schema of the database
questions.choice_b: Designing the application's graphical interface
questions.choice_c: Entering customer data every day
questions.choice_d: Writing the business application programs
questions.explanation: The DBA's roles include: schema definition, definition of storage structures and access methods, definition of security and integrity constraints, granting of authorization for data access, liaison with users, assisting programmers, monitoring performance, backup and recovery.

questions.question_text: What does the DBA do under performance monitoring?
questions.choice_a: Rewrite the developers' application programs
questions.choice_b: Delete the least-consulted data
questions.choice_c: Modify the physical or logical schema if needed to keep performance good
questions.choice_d: Automatically add extra hardware
questions.explanation: The DBA ensures that better performance is maintained by making a change to the physical or logical schema if required.

questions.question_text: Which DBA responsibility concerns users' access to data?
questions.choice_a: Creating a system account for every company employee
questions.choice_b: Encrypting all network communications
questions.choice_c: Defining the company's password policy
questions.choice_d: Determining which user needs access to which part of the database and granting the authorization
questions.explanation: Granting of authorization for data access means, for the DBA, determining which user needs access to which part of the database.

questions.question_text: On what media does the DBA perform backups according to the course?
questions.choice_a: Only the database's system disk
questions.choice_b: Only the server's RAM
questions.choice_c: Media such as DVD, CD, magnetic tape or remote servers
questions.choice_d: Only encrypted USB sticks
questions.explanation: The DBA backs up the database on storage devices such as DVD, CD, magnetic tape or remote servers, and restores the system from these backups in case of failure, such as a flood or a virus attack.

exercises.prompt: Into which two main parts is the DBMS organised (above the disk)?
choices: The query processor and the storage manager
The internal schema and the external schema
The data dictionary and the data warehouse
exercises.explanation: The query processor turns statements into evaluation plans; the storage manager is the interface between those plans and the low-level data on disk.

exercises.prompt: Which query-processor component picks the cheapest evaluation plan for a DML statement?
exercises.explanation: The DML compiler translates the statement into low-level instructions and organises/optimises them into the cheapest plan.

exercises.prompt: What does the query evaluation engine do?
choices: It executes the low-level instructions produced by the DML compiler
It parses CREATE / ALTER / DROP statements
It caches disk blocks in memory
It grants access privileges to users
exercises.explanation: The evaluation engine actually runs the plan the DML compiler produced.

exercises.prompt: The DDL interpreters process which kind of statement?
exercises.explanation: DDL = Data Definition Language; the interpreters record the resulting definitions in the data dictionary.

exercises.prompt: Which storage-manager component brings disk blocks into main memory and decides what to cache?
exercises.explanation: The buffer manager is responsible for moving blocks between disk and memory and for the cache-replacement decisions.

exercises.prompt: Which storage-manager component checks users' rights and that updates respect the integrity constraints?
exercises.explanation: The authorization & integrity manager enforces both access control and integrity constraints.

exercises.prompt: Which storage-manager component keeps the database consistent despite failures and concurrent access?
exercises.explanation: The transaction manager provides atomicity and isolation, so a crash or concurrent updates never leave the database inconsistent.

exercises.prompt: What four kinds of data does the database on disk hold, according to the architecture?
choices: Data, indices, data dictionary, statistical data
exercises.explanation: The statistical data is what the query optimiser reads to estimate plan costs.

exercises.prompt: Through which interface does a sophisticated user reach the DBMS?
exercises.explanation: Naive users -> application interfaces; application programmers -> application programs; sophisticated users -> query tools; DBA -> administration tools.

exercises.prompt: Put the levels of the ANSI-SPARC architecture in order, from the one the end user sees down to physical storage.
exercises.explanation: The end user sees only a view; the conceptual level says what data and relationships exist; the internal level says how it is stored; the database sits on disk.

exercises.prompt: A transfer of 500 from account A to account B. Put the two steps of the transaction in order.
exercises.explanation: Atomicity means both steps happen or neither does; a failure between them would leave the accounts inconsistent.

exercises.prompt: Put the path of a user query through the DBMS architecture in order.
steps: The user issues a request through a query tool or application interface
The query processor compiles and optimises it into an evaluation plan
The query evaluation engine executes the plan
The storage manager fetches the required blocks from disk
The result is mapped back up to the user's view
exercises.explanation: Request goes down through the query processor and storage manager; the result is mapped back up the three levels to the user.

exercises.prompt: Build the flowchart of an atomic fund transfer: debit A, credit B, then COMMIT if both succeeded, otherwise ROLLBACK.
exercises.hint: One decision 'Both steps succeeded ?': yes -> COMMIT; no -> ROLLBACK; both reach END.
exercises.explanation: COMMIT makes the transfer permanent; ROLLBACK undoes the debit so the database returns to its previous consistent state. That is atomicity: 0% or 100%.

name: Week 2
lesson:
# Database Design — Week 2

Lectures 03–04 — *ACID Properties, Data Models* and *E-R Diagrams – 1*.
Tables and schemas, levels of abstraction, the ACID properties, what a data
model is, the classic data models (hierarchical, network, E-R, relational,
object-oriented, object-relational, semi-structured), then the first half of
E-R diagrams: entities, attributes and their types, relationships.

---

## 1. Tables, schema, instance

Data in a database is typically organized into **tables**, made of **rows** and
**columns**. Each **row** is a single record (an *instance* of data); each
**column** is a specific attribute or characteristic of that data.

```diagram
{
  "title": "The elements of a database table.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t", "x": 300, "y": 120, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "cols": [60, 90, 130], "rows": [["ID","Name","Date of Birth"],["1","Kim","2001-03-04"],["2","Lee","2000-11-30"],["3","Park","2002-06-15"]], "mark": [2] },
    { "id": "corner", "x": 172, "y": 82, "shape": "text" },
    { "id": "hdr", "x": 270, "y": 78, "shape": "text" },
    { "id": "key", "x": 172, "y": 87, "shape": "text" },
    { "id": "row", "x": 430, "y": 131, "shape": "text" },
    { "id": "lt", "x": 80, "y": 20, "w": 130, "h": 30, "shape": "note", "label": "Table (Relation)", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "lf", "x": 470, "y": 20, "w": 130, "h": 30, "shape": "note", "label": "Field (Column)", "tone": "violet" },
    { "id": "lk", "x": 60, "y": 87, "w": 70, "h": 30, "shape": "note", "label": "Key", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "lr", "x": 570, "y": 131, "w": 130, "h": 30, "shape": "note", "label": "Record (Tuple)", "tone": "emerald" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "lt", "to": "corner", "tone": "sky" },
    { "from": "lf", "to": "hdr", "tone": "violet" },
    { "from": "lk", "to": "key", "tone": "amber" },
    { "from": "lr", "to": "row", "tone": "emerald" }
  ]
}
```

A **schema** is a description of a particular collection of data, using a
given data model — the **structure or form of the database without any data in
it**. An **instance** is the actual content of the database at a given moment.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Schema vs instances: the plan of a house vs the houses built from it; the template of a table vs the data-filled table.",
  "groups": [
    { "x": 380, "y": 80, "w": 560, "h": 96, "label": "Schema", "tone": "amber" },
    { "x": 380, "y": 225, "w": 560, "h": 150, "label": "Instances", "tone": "emerald" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "h1", "x": 230, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "Real world", "bold": true },
    { "id": "h2", "x": 540, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "Database", "bold": true },
    { "id": "sr", "x": 230, "y": 88, "w": 260, "h": 40, "shape": "note", "label": "Plan for a standard house", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "sd", "x": 540, "y": 88, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "amber", "cols": [70, 80, 90], "rows": [["P-ID","Name","Prename"]] },
    { "id": "ir", "x": 230, "y": 225, "w": 260, "h": 70, "shape": "note", "label": "Built standard houses\nhouse #1 · house #2 · house #3\n(same plan, different owners)", "tone": "emerald" },
    { "id": "id", "x": 540, "y": 225, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "emerald", "cols": [70, 80, 90], "rows": [["P-ID","Name","Prename"],["102356","Smith","John"],["102357","Potter","Harry"],["523646","Wood","Lucinda"]] }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "sr", "to": "ir", "dashed": true, "label": "built from" },
    { "from": "sd", "to": "id", "dashed": true, "label": "filled in" }
  ]
}
```

The schema exists at three levels — the same three levels as the ANSI-SPARC
architecture of Week 1:

| Schema | Describes | Who works there |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical schema** | how the data stored in blocks of storage is described | the DBMS (hidden from programmers) |
| **Logical schema** | which types of data records are stored in which data structures; the implementation details of those structures are hidden (they live at the physical level) | programmers and database administrators |
| **View schema** | how the end user interacts with the database system | end users |

### Levels of abstraction

```diagram
{
  "title": "Levels of abstraction: many views, one conceptual schema, one physical schema.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "v1", "x": 270, "y": 30, "w": 80, "h": 32, "label": "View 1", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "v2", "x": 390, "y": 30, "w": 80, "h": 32, "label": "View 2", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "v3", "x": 510, "y": 30, "w": 80, "h": 32, "label": "View 3", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "c", "x": 390, "y": 130, "w": 180, "h": 38, "label": "Conceptual schema", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "p", "x": 390, "y": 230, "w": 180, "h": 38, "label": "Physical schema", "tone": "violet", "filled": true },
    { "id": "db", "x": 390, "y": 320, "w": 110, "h": 50, "shape": "cylinder", "label": "Database", "filled": true },
    { "id": "n1", "x": 90, "y": 30, "w": 150, "h": 44, "shape": "note", "size": 11, "label": "how users see the data\n(external schemas)", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "n2", "x": 90, "y": 130, "w": 150, "h": 44, "shape": "note", "size": 11, "label": "single schema defining\nthe logical structure", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "n3", "x": 90, "y": 230, "w": 150, "h": 44, "shape": "note", "size": 11, "label": "describes the files\nand indexes used", "tone": "violet" },
    { "id": "d1", "x": 640, "y": 80, "w": 190, "h": 44, "shape": "note", "size": 11, "label": "views are generated on\ndemand from the real data", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "d2", "x": 640, "y": 130, "w": 190, "h": 34, "shape": "note", "size": 11, "label": "← conceptual database design", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "d3", "x": 640, "y": 230, "w": 190, "h": 34, "shape": "note", "size": 11, "label": "← physical database design", "tone": "violet" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "v1", "to": "c", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "v2", "to": "c", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "v3", "to": "c", "arrow": "none" },
    { "from": "c", "to": "p", "arrow": "none" },
    { "from": "p", "to": "db", "arrow": "none" }
  ]
}
```

- **Conceptual database design** = producing the conceptual schema.
- **Physical database design** = producing the physical schema.

Example, a university database:

```
Conceptual schema:
    Students(sid: string, name: string, login: string, age: integer, gpa: real)
    Courses(cid: string, cname: string, credits: integer)
    Enrolled(sid: string, cid: string, grade: string)

Physical schema:
    Relations stored as unordered files
    Index on the first column of Students

External schema (view):
    Course_info(cid: string, enrollment: integer)
```

## 2. ACID properties

A **transaction** is a unit of work on the database. Four *desirable
properties* must hold for every transaction — **ACID**:

| Property | Statement | Ensured by |
|---|---|---|
| **Atomicity** | the transaction is performed **in its entirety or not at all** | the **transaction-recovery subsystem** of the DBMS |
| **Consistency** | the database **always remains consistent** | the **database program / the programmer** |
| **Isolation** | a transaction **does not interfere** with other transactions | the **concurrency-control subsystem** |
| **Durability** | the changes of **committed** transactions **must persist** | the **recovery subsystem** |

```diagram
{
  "title": "Which subsystem of the DBMS guarantees which ACID property.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "a", "x": 80, "y": 40, "w": 130, "h": 48, "label": "Atomicity\nall or nothing", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "d", "x": 250, "y": 40, "w": 130, "h": 48, "label": "Durability\ncommits persist", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "i", "x": 420, "y": 40, "w": 130, "h": 48, "label": "Isolation\nno interference", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "c", "x": 590, "y": 40, "w": 130, "h": 48, "label": "Consistency\nconstraints hold", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "rec", "x": 165, "y": 160, "w": 200, "h": 40, "label": "Transaction-recovery\nsubsystem", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "cc", "x": 420, "y": 160, "w": 190, "h": 40, "label": "Concurrency-control\nsubsystem", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "prog", "x": 610, "y": 160, "w": 150, "h": 40, "label": "Database program\n(the programmer)", "tone": "emerald" },
    { "id": "log", "x": 165, "y": 260, "w": 130, "h": 54, "shape": "cylinder", "label": "Log\nold values", "tone": "sky", "filled": true }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "a", "to": "rec", "tone": "sky" },
    { "from": "d", "to": "rec", "tone": "sky" },
    { "from": "i", "to": "cc", "tone": "amber" },
    { "from": "c", "to": "prog", "tone": "emerald" },
    { "from": "rec", "to": "log", "arrow": "both", "tone": "sky", "label": "uses" },
    { "from": "rec", "to": "cc", "arrow": "both", "dashed": true, "label": "cooperate" }
  ]
}
```

### Atomicity

- Ensured by the **transaction-recovery subsystem**.
- The recovery technique must **undo any effect of a failed (aborted)
  transaction** — done by using the **log** and **writing back the old
  values**.
- Cooperation with the **concurrency-control subsystem** is also necessary.

### Consistency

- Each transaction should bring the database **from one consistent state to
  another consistent state**.
- A **consistent state** = the database satisfies the **integrity constraints**
  specified in the schema, as well as any other constraints that should hold.
- It is the **responsibility of the database program (the programmer)**.
- Transactions can use **abort** instructions, leading to **rollbacks**
  (handled by the recovery subsystem).

### Isolation

- Ensured by the **concurrency-control subsystem**.
- Ideally we avoid all the anomalies of concurrent execution:

| Anomaly | What happens |
|---|---|
| **dirty write** | a transaction overwrites a value another uncommitted transaction has written |
| **dirty read** | a transaction reads a value written by a transaction that has not committed yet (and may roll back) |
| **non-repeatable read** | the same row read twice in one transaction gives two different values because another transaction modified it in between |
| **phantom** | the same query run twice returns a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or deleted rows |

- Full isolation may be **too expensive** in terms of efficiency, so it is often
  **relaxed** in one way or another: the **isolation levels**.
- One of the most difficult and interesting issues of transaction management.

### Durability (permanency)

- Ensured by the **recovery subsystem**.
- After a crash, the **log** is used to **restore committed transactions**
  and **roll back uncommitted ones**.
- The **cache** complicates the restoration (a committed change may still be
  sitting in memory, not yet on disk, when the crash happens).

```diagram
{
  "title": "After a crash the log lets the recovery subsystem redo what was committed and undo what was not.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t1", "x": 140, "y": 40, "w": 250, "h": 40, "label": "T1 — committed before the crash", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "t2", "x": 140, "y": 120, "w": 250, "h": 40, "label": "T2 — still running at the crash", "tone": "rose", "filled": true },
    { "id": "crash", "x": 330, "y": 80, "shape": "text", "label": "✕ CRASH", "bold": true, "tone": "rose" },
    { "id": "log", "x": 450, "y": 80, "w": 120, "h": 60, "shape": "cylinder", "label": "Log", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
```

## 3. Data models

A **data model** is a **collection of conceptual tools for describing data,
data relationships, data semantics and consistency constraints**. It provides a
way to describe the *design* of a database: how data is related, stored,
retrieved and modified, using a set of symbols and terminology that the members
of an organisation can understand before communicating.

### Basic building blocks

| Block | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Entity** | anything about which data is to be collected and stored; represents a particular type of object in the real world |
| **Entity set** | a set of entities of the same type that share the same properties |
| **Attribute** | a characteristic of an entity |
| **Constraint** | a restriction placed on the data; constraints help ensure data integrity |
| **Relationship** | an association among entities |

### Hierarchical model

Classifies the data into a **tree-like structure with a single parent (root)
for each record**. Sibling records are arranged in a certain sequence — the
physical order in which the database is stored. It depicts a set of **1:M
relationships between a parent and its children's segments**.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| very simple and fast to traverse a tree-like structure | complex relationships are not supported |
| any change in the parent node is automatically reflected in the child node, so data integrity is maintained | a child node cannot have **two parents**: such a relationship cannot be represented |
| | if a parent node is deleted, the child node is **automatically deleted** |

### Network model

An **expansion of the hierarchical model**, the most prevalent model prior to
the relational model. The main difference: **a record can have several
parents** — the hierarchical *tree* is replaced by a **graph**.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Network model: Student has two parents, CSE Department and Library — impossible in the hierarchical model.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "col", "x": 330, "y": 30, "w": 110, "label": "College", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "cse", "x": 190, "y": 115, "w": 130, "label": "CSE Department", "tone": "neutral", "filled": true },
    { "id": "lib", "x": 470, "y": 115, "w": 110, "label": "Library", "tone": "neutral", "filled": true },
    { "id": "stu", "x": 330, "y": 200, "w": 110, "label": "Student", "tone": "rose", "filled": true },
    { "id": "n", "x": 560, "y": 200, "w": 150, "h": 36, "shape": "note", "size": 11, "label": "two parents:\nallowed in a graph", "tone": "rose" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "col", "to": "cse" }, { "from": "col", "to": "lib" },
    { "from": "cse", "to": "stu" }, { "from": "lib", "to": "stu" }
  ]
}
```

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| data may be obtained more quickly than with the hierarchical approach: the data is more linked, there may be **more than one path** to a node, so information can be accessed in a variety of ways | as relationships are added the system gets **increasingly complicated**; a user needs a full understanding of the model to operate it |
| data integrity is present thanks to the parent-child connection: changes to the parent record are mirrored in the child record | any modification (update, deletion, insertion) is quite **difficult** |

visual form** so stakeholders can grasp it easily, and developers understand
the system. The **E-R diagram** is the visual tool used to depict an E-R model.
It is made up of **three parts**:

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| **Simple**: conceptually very easy to build — if we know the relationship between the attributes and the entities, we can draw the diagram | **No industry standard for notation**: one developer might use notations other developers do not understand |
| **Effective communication tool**: widely used by database designers to communicate their ideas | **Hidden information**: it is a high-level view, so some details may be lost or hidden |
| **Easy conversion to any model**: maps well to the relational model (E-R → tables) and can also be converted to the network or hierarchical model | |

### Relational model

The **most common** model. Data is kept in **two-dimensional tables** (rows
and columns); the tables are also called **relations**.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Relational model: tables linked through shared key columns.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "s", "x": 150, "y": 70, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "emerald", "label": "student", "rows": [["student_id","name","age"],["1","Akon","17"],["2","Bkon","16"],["3","Ckon","17"],["4","Dkon","18"]] },
    { "id": "j", "x": 480, "y": 70, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "emerald", "label": "subject", "rows": [["subject_id","name","teacher"],["1","Java","Mr. J"],["2","C++","Miss C"],["3","C#","Mr. C Hash"],["4","Php","Mr. P H P"]] },
    { "id": "m", "x": 315, "y": 270, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "emerald", "label": "marks", "rows": [["student_id","subject_id","marks"],["1","1","98"],["1","2","78"],["2","1","76"],["3","2","88"]] }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "s", "to": "m", "label": "student_id", "via": [[150, 190], [250, 190]] },
    { "from": "j", "to": "m", "label": "subject_id", "via": [[480, 190], [380, 190]] }
  ]
}
```

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| **Simple**: simpler than the network and hierarchical models | **Hardware overheads**: hiding the complexity requires more powerful computers and storage |
| **Scalable**: add as many rows and columns as needed | **Bad design**: it is so easy to design and use that users need not know how the data is stored — which can lead to a poor database that slows down as it grows |
| **Structural independence**: the structure can change without changing the way the data is accessed | |

### Object-oriented (OO) model

A database is a **collection of objects** (reusable software parts) with
related characteristics and operations. Several kinds: a **multimedia
database** holds media (photos) that would be impossible to store in a
relational database; a **hypertext database** lets any object link to any other
object (good for large heterogeneous data, not for numerical analysis). Because
it integrates but is not limited to tables, the OO model is the best-known
**post-relational** (or *hybrid*) paradigm. Most used with OO languages: Java,
Kotlin, C#, Node JS, Swift.

```diagram
{
  "title": "An object bundles attributes and operations; an object-relational table can hold a complex, structured value in a column.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "h1", "x": 150, "y": 8, "shape": "text", "label": "Object-oriented: object", "bold": true },
    { "id": "h2", "x": 470, "y": 8, "shape": "text", "label": "Object-relational: table with a complex type", "bold": true },
    { "id": "o", "x": 150, "y": 110, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "violet", "cols": [180], "rows": [["Employee"],["emp_id : int"],["name : string"],["salary : float"],["raise_salary()"],["get_details()"]] },
    { "id": "t", "x": 470, "y": 80, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "rows": [["emp_id","name","address (composite type)"],["1","Kim","{ street, city, zip }"],["2","Lee","{ street, city, zip }"]] }
  ],
  "edges": []
}
```

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| complex data sets can be saved and retrieved quickly and easily | object databases are **not widely adopted** |
| object IDs are assigned automatically | high complexity can cause **performance problems** |
| works well with OO programming languages; semantic content is added; support for complex objects; visual representation includes semantic content | high system overheads slow transactions |

### Object-relational (OR) model

A **hybrid of the relational and object-oriented models**, created to bridge
the gap between them. It allows sophisticated features such as creating
complicated data types from existing ones. Its issue: it may become complicated
and difficult to manage, so a thorough comprehension of the paradigm is
essential.

| Object-oriented database | Object-relational database |
|---|---|
| represents information as **objects**, as in OOP; depends on OOP | depends on the relational **and** the OO data model: a hybrid |
| relationships represented by **references via the object identifier (OID)** | connections between two relations represented by **foreign key** attributes referencing the primary key of another relation |
| handles larger and more complex data than an RDBMS | handles comparatively simpler data |
| less efficient | comparatively more efficient |
| the data-management language is typically incorporated into a programming language such as C++ | data-manipulation languages such as **SQL, QUEL, QBE**, based on relational calculus |

### Semi-structured model

Emerged from the relational model. **We cannot tell the difference between data
and schema**: for web-based data, the website's structure and its data are not
distinguishable. Some entities may be missing attributes, others may have extra
ones — greater flexibility of storage. Examples of semi-structured sources:
emails, XML and other markup languages, binary executables, TCP/IP packets,
zipped files, data integrated from different sources, web pages.

**Database design** is a collection of processes that facilitate the designing,
development, implementation and maintenance of enterprise database management
systems. The **E-R diagram** (Entity-Relationship diagram) is a **graphical
(pictorial) representation of a database** that uses different symbols to
represent the different objects of the database.

### Entity

An **entity** is a person, a place or an object. It is represented by a
**rectangle** containing the name of the entity. Entities of a college
database: Student, Professor/Faculty, Course, Department, Result, Class,

### Relationship

A **relationship** is an association (connection) between several entities. It
is placed **between two entities**, with a **line connecting it to each
entity**, and is represented by a **diamond** containing the relationship's
name.

```er
{
  "title": "A relationship (diamond) between two entities.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "s", "kind": "entity", "label": "Student", "x": 100, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "i", "kind": "relationship", "label": "Issue", "x": 320, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "b", "kind": "entity", "label": "Book", "x": 540, "y": 40 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "s", "to": "i" }, { "from": "i", "to": "b" }
  ]
}
```

A **descriptive attribute** is an attribute **of the relationship** (not of an
entity): the date at which a book is issued belongs to the `Issue`
relationship, not to `Student` nor to `Book`.

## To remember

- Table = rows (records / tuples) × columns (fields / attributes). **Schema** =
  the structure without data; **instance** = the content at one moment.
  Physical / logical / view schema = the three ANSI-SPARC levels.
- **ACID**: Atomicity (all or nothing — recovery subsystem, log, old values),
  Consistency (integrity constraints hold — the programmer), Isolation (no
  interference — concurrency control; anomalies: dirty write/read,
  non-repeatable read, phantom; relaxed via isolation levels), Durability
  (commits persist — recovery subsystem, log redo/undo after a crash).
- A **data model** = conceptual tools to describe data, relationships,
  semantics and constraints. Blocks: entity, entity set, attribute, constraint.
- Models: **hierarchical** (tree, one parent, 1:M), **network** (graph, several
  parents), **E-R** (high-level, visual, three parts), **relational** (tables =
  relations, the most common), **OO** (objects, OID references), **OR**
  (hybrid, foreign keys), **semi-structured** (schema and data mixed: XML,
  emails, web pages).
- E-R: **rectangle** = entity, **oval** = attribute, **diamond** = relationship.
  Key attribute **underlined**. Composite = sub-ovals; multi-valued = **double
  oval**; derived = **dashed oval**. Every entity needs a primary key.
  Descriptive attribute = attribute of a relationship. Binary = 2 entities,
  ternary = 3.

questions.question_text: Data in a database is typically organised into tables. What does one row represent?
questions.choice_a: A single attribute of the data
questions.choice_b: A single record or instance of data
questions.choice_c: The whole schema
questions.choice_d: An index
questions.explanation: Each row is one record / instance; each column is a specific attribute or characteristic of that data.

questions.question_text: What is a schema?
questions.choice_a: The data currently stored in the database
questions.choice_b: A description of a collection of data in a given data model — the structure or form of the database with no data in it
questions.choice_c: A backup copy of the database
questions.choice_d: A query written in SQL
questions.explanation: The schema is the definition of the structure; an instance is the actual content at a moment in time.

questions.question_text: At which schema level is the storage of data in blocks described?
questions.choice_a: View schema
questions.choice_b: Logical schema
questions.choice_c: Physical schema
questions.choice_d: External schema
questions.explanation: The physical schema describes how the data stored in blocks of storage is organised.

questions.question_text: Who works at the logical schema level?
questions.choice_a: End users only
questions.choice_b: Programmers and database administrators
questions.choice_c: The hardware vendor
questions.choice_d: Nobody; it is generated automatically
questions.explanation: At the logical level, data is described as record types stored in data structures; the internal implementation details are hidden here (they live at the physical level).

questions.question_text: The view schema generally describes:
questions.choice_a: How indexes are built
questions.choice_b: End-user interaction with the database system
questions.choice_c: The disk block size
questions.choice_d: The transaction log format
questions.explanation: Different views (also called the external schema) describe how particular users see the data; they are generated on demand from the real data.

questions.question_text: In the university-database example, 'Course_info(cid, enrollment)' is part of which schema?
questions.choice_a: The physical schema
questions.choice_b: The conceptual schema
questions.choice_c: An external schema (a view)
questions.choice_d: The internal schema
questions.explanation: The conceptual schema holds Students, Courses and Enrolled; the physical schema stores relations as unordered files with an index; Course_info is a view.

questions.question_text: What does the 'A' in ACID stand for, and what does it require?
questions.choice_a: Availability — the database is always online
questions.choice_b: Atomicity — a transaction is performed in its entirety or not at all
questions.choice_c: Authorization — only permitted users may write
questions.choice_d: Auditing — every change is logged for review
questions.explanation: Atomicity is ensured by the transaction-recovery subsystem, which must undo any effects of a failed (aborted) transaction, using the log to write back the old values.

questions.question_text: Which subsystem ensures atomicity by undoing a failed transaction's effects?
questions.choice_a: The concurrency-control subsystem
questions.choice_b: The transaction-recovery subsystem, using the log to write back old values
questions.choice_c: The query optimiser
questions.choice_d: The buffer manager
questions.explanation: Cooperation with the concurrency-control subsystem is also necessary.

questions.question_text: Consistency (the 'C' in ACID) is primarily the responsibility of:
questions.choice_a: The database program — that is, the programmer
questions.choice_b: The disk controller
questions.choice_c: The end user
questions.choice_d: The network layer
questions.explanation: Each transaction should bring the database from one consistent state (integrity constraints satisfied) to another; transactions may use abort instructions, leading to rollbacks handled by the recovery subsystem.

questions.question_text: Isolation is ensured by which subsystem?
questions.choice_a: The recovery subsystem
questions.choice_b: The concurrency-control subsystem
questions.choice_c: The DDL interpreter
questions.choice_d: The file manager
questions.explanation: Ideally we avoid all anomalies (dirty writes and reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms); because full isolation is expensive it is often relaxed via isolation levels.

questions.question_text: Why is full isolation often relaxed in practice?
questions.choice_a: It is illegal in some countries
questions.choice_b: It can be too expensive in terms of efficiency, so isolation levels trade some guarantees for speed
questions.choice_c: Modern hardware makes it unnecessary
questions.choice_d: Because atomicity already covers it
questions.explanation: Concurrency control is one of the most difficult and interesting issues in transaction management.

questions.question_text: Durability guarantees that:
questions.choice_a: The database never runs out of disk space
questions.choice_b: The changes of committed transactions must persist, even after a crash
questions.choice_c: Every transaction eventually commits
questions.choice_d: Uncommitted data is visible to all users
questions.explanation: After a crash the log is used to restore committed transactions and roll back uncommitted ones; the cache complicates the restoration.

questions.question_text: A data model is:
questions.choice_a: A physical layout of disk blocks
questions.choice_b: A collection of conceptual tools for describing data, data relationships, data semantics and consistency constraints
questions.choice_c: A specific SQL query
questions.choice_d: A backup strategy
questions.explanation: A data model provides a way to describe the design of a database; it is widely used in DBMSs to show how data is related, stored, retrieved and modified.

questions.question_text: In data-model terms, an 'entity' is:
questions.choice_a: A single column of a table
questions.choice_b: Anything about which data is to be collected and stored — a particular type of real-world object
questions.choice_c: A restriction placed on the data
questions.choice_d: A relationship between two tables
questions.explanation: A set of entities of the same type that share the same properties is an entity set; a characteristic of an entity is an attribute.

questions.question_text: What is a constraint, and why does it matter?
questions.choice_a: A synonym for an attribute
questions.choice_b: A restriction placed on the data; it helps ensure data integrity
questions.choice_c: The maximum number of rows in a table
questions.choice_d: The primary key of an entity
questions.explanation: Constraints are important because they help to ensure data integrity.

questions.question_text: Which relationship cardinalities does the course list?
questions.choice_a: 1:1, 1:M and M:N
questions.choice_b: Only 1:1 and M:N
questions.choice_d: Weak, strong and derived
questions.explanation: A relationship describes an association among entities; the types are one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many.

questions.question_text: The hierarchical model organises data as:
questions.choice_a: A set of two-dimensional tables
questions.choice_b: A tree-like structure with a single parent / root for each record, siblings in a set sequence
questions.choice_c: A graph where records can have several parents
questions.choice_d: A collection of objects
questions.explanation: It depicts a set of 1:M relationships between a parent and its children's segments.

questions.question_text: A stated disadvantage of the hierarchical model is that:
questions.choice_a: It is slow to traverse
questions.choice_b: It does not support complex relationships / more than one parent per child (so no M:N), and deleting a parent deletes its children
questions.choice_c: Changes in a parent are not reflected in children
questions.choice_d: It cannot store text
questions.explanation: Advantages: simple and fast to traverse; any change in the parent node is automatically reflected in the child, maintaining integrity.

questions.question_text: The network model differs from the hierarchical model mainly because:
questions.choice_a: It uses tables instead of a tree
questions.choice_b: A record can have several parents — it replaces the hierarchical tree with a graph
questions.choice_c: It has no relationships at all
questions.choice_d: It stores only numeric data
questions.explanation: It was the most prevalent model before the relational model; e.g. a Student node can have both a CSE Department parent and a Library parent.

questions.question_text: A disadvantage of the network model is that:
questions.choice_a: Data can only be reached by a single path
questions.choice_b: As more relationships are added the system becomes complex, and any update, deletion or insertion is quite difficult
questions.choice_c: It cannot maintain a parent-child relationship
questions.choice_d: It has no data integrity
questions.explanation: Advantage: because data is more linked and there may be more than one path to a node, information can be accessed in several ways, and the parent-child link gives integrity.

questions.question_text: The Entity-Relationship model is described as:
questions.choice_a: A low-level physical storage model
questions.choice_b: A high-level data-model diagram that expresses the real-world problem in visual form so stakeholders and developers can grasp the system
questions.choice_c: A query language
questions.choice_d: A backup format
questions.explanation: The ER diagram is the visual tool used to depict an ER model; it is made up of entities, attributes and relationships.

questions.question_text: A disadvantage of the Entity-Relationship model is:
questions.choice_a: It cannot be converted to the relational model
questions.choice_b: There is no industry standard for the notation, and some information may be hidden in the high-level view
questions.choice_c: It is conceptually very hard to build
questions.choice_d: It cannot represent relationships
questions.explanation: Advantages: conceptually simple, an effective communication tool, and it maps well to the relational model (and others).

questions.question_text: In the relational model, tables are also referred to as:
questions.choice_a: Segments
questions.choice_b: Relations
questions.choice_c: Objects
questions.choice_d: Nodes
questions.explanation: Data is kept as a two-dimensional table of rows and columns; tables (relations) are the foundation of the relational paradigm.

questions.question_text: 'Structural independence' in the relational model means:
questions.choice_a: The database has no structure
questions.choice_b: You can change the database structure without changing the way the data is accessed (the DBMS can still access the data)
questions.choice_c: Every table is independent and cannot be joined
questions.choice_d: The hardware is independent of the software
questions.explanation: Advantages of the relational model: simple, scalable (add rows and columns freely), and structural independence.

questions.question_text: A disadvantage of the relational model, per the course, is:
questions.choice_a: It cannot scale
questions.choice_b: Hardware overheads — hiding the complexity requires more powerful computers and storage — and its ease of design can lead to a poor database that slows down as it grows
questions.choice_c: It has no way to enforce integrity
questions.choice_d: It cannot represent 1:M relationships
questions.explanation: Because users need not know how data is stored, the ease of design can produce a bad schema.

questions.question_text: In the object-oriented (OO) data model, how are relationships represented?
questions.choice_a: By foreign-key attributes
questions.choice_b: By references via the object identifier (OID)
questions.choice_c: By a parent pointer in a tree
questions.choice_d: By a diamond symbol
questions.explanation: An OO database is a collection of objects (attributes + operations); OIDs are assigned automatically and it works well with OOP languages such as Java, C# and Swift.

questions.question_text: The object-relational (OR) model is:
questions.choice_a: A pure object database with no tables
questions.choice_b: A hybrid of the relational and object-oriented models, created to bridge the gap between them, allowing complex data types built on existing ones
questions.choice_c: An older name for the hierarchical model
questions.choice_d: A model with no schema
questions.explanation: The trade-off is that it may become complicated and difficult to manage, so a thorough understanding of it is essential.

questions.question_text: Which comparison of OO and OR databases is correct?
questions.choice_a: OO uses foreign keys; OR uses the OID
questions.choice_b: OO represents relationships by references via the OID and handles larger, more complex data but is less efficient; OR represents relationships by foreign keys and is comparatively more efficient
questions.choice_c: OO and OR are identical
questions.choice_d: OR handles more complex data than OO
questions.explanation: OR databases have data-manipulation languages such as SQL, QUEL and QBE based on relational calculus.

questions.question_text: The semi-structured model is characterised by:
questions.choice_a: A rigid, fixed schema for every entity
questions.choice_b: Data and schema that cannot be clearly told apart; some entities may miss attributes while others have extra ones
questions.choice_c: Storage only as two-dimensional tables
questions.choice_d: A single parent per record
questions.explanation: It emerged from the relational model and allows greater storage flexibility; examples include emails, XML and other markup languages, TCP/IP packets and web pages.

questions.question_text: Which is an example of a semi-structured data source?
questions.choice_a: A normalised SQL table
questions.choice_b: XML (and other markup languages), emails, web pages
questions.choice_c: A B-tree index
questions.choice_d: A transaction log
questions.explanation: In web-based data sources we often cannot distinguish the website's structure from its data.

questions.question_text: In an E-R diagram, an entity is represented by:
questions.choice_a: An oval
questions.choice_b: A diamond
questions.choice_c: A rectangle containing the entity name
questions.choice_d: An underlined word
questions.explanation: An entity is a person, a place or an object; examples in a college database: Student, Faculty, Course, Department, Result, Class, Subject.

questions.question_text: In an E-R diagram, an attribute is represented by:
questions.choice_a: A rectangle
questions.choice_b: An oval containing the attribute name, joined to its entity by a line
questions.choice_c: A diamond
questions.choice_d: A double line
questions.explanation: An attribute is a property or detail about an entity, e.g. RollNo, Student Name, Branch, Semester, Address for the Student entity.

questions.question_text: In an E-R diagram, a relationship is represented by:
questions.choice_a: A rectangle
questions.choice_b: An oval
questions.choice_c: A diamond containing the relationship's name, on the line between two entities
questions.choice_d: An arrow
questions.explanation: A relationship is an association (connection) between several entities; e.g. Student —Issue— Book.

questions.question_text: How is a primary-key attribute shown, and how many must an entity have?
questions.choice_a: Shown in a double oval; an entity may have several
questions.choice_b: Underlined; every entity must have exactly one primary-key attribute
questions.choice_c: Shown in bold; an entity has zero or one
questions.choice_d: Shown in a rectangle; an entity has exactly two
questions.explanation: Each and every entity must have one primary-key attribute (e.g. RollNo for Student, BookNo for Book).

questions.question_text: What is a composite attribute?
questions.choice_a: An attribute with more than one value
questions.choice_b: An attribute that can be divided into subparts, e.g. Name into first / middle / last, or Address into street / city
questions.choice_c: An attribute whose value is calculated from others
questions.choice_d: An attribute shared by two entities
questions.explanation: A simple attribute (e.g. RollNo, CPI) cannot be divided into subparts.

questions.question_text: Which pair correctly contrasts single-valued and multi-valued attributes?
questions.choice_a: RollNo is multi-valued; PhoneNo is single-valued
questions.choice_b: RollNo is single-valued (one value); PhoneNo / EmailID are multi-valued (a person may have several)
questions.choice_c: Both are always single-valued
questions.choice_d: Multi-valued attributes cannot be stored in a database
questions.explanation: A single-valued attribute has one value; a multi-valued attribute has more than one.

questions.question_text: What is a derived attribute?
questions.choice_a: An attribute stored manually in the database
questions.choice_b: An attribute whose value is derived or calculated from other attributes, e.g. Age from Birthdate and the current date
questions.choice_c: An attribute that belongs to a relationship
questions.choice_d: The primary key of a weak entity
questions.explanation: Birthdate is a stored attribute (entered manually); Age is derived from it.

questions.question_text: A descriptive attribute is:
questions.choice_a: An attribute that describes an entity in words
questions.choice_b: An attribute of the relationship (not of an entity), e.g. IssueDate on the Issue relationship between Student and Book
questions.choice_c: A synonym for a composite attribute
questions.choice_d: Any attribute written in a comment
questions.explanation: Attributes of the relationship are called descriptive attributes.

questions.question_text: A relationship between exactly two entities is called:
questions.choice_a: A unary relationship
questions.choice_b: A binary relationship
questions.choice_c: A ternary relationship
questions.choice_d: A composite relationship
questions.explanation: Student —Issue— Book is binary. A relationship between three entities (e.g. Faculty —Guide— Student with a Project) is ternary.

questions.question_text: A relationship between three entities is called:
questions.choice_a: A binary relationship
questions.choice_b: A ternary relationship
questions.choice_c: A triple key
questions.choice_d: A composite entity
questions.explanation: Example: Faculty and Student linked through a Guide relationship that also involves a Project entity.

questions.question_text: What is 'Database Design' as defined at the start of Lecture 4?
questions.choice_a: The act of writing SQL SELECT statements
questions.choice_b: A collection of processes that facilitate the designing, development, implementation and maintenance of enterprise database management systems
questions.choice_c: Choosing which disk to buy
questions.choice_d: Drawing the user interface
questions.explanation: An E-R diagram is one graphical tool used within that design process.
