lesson:
# Computer Programming — Week 4 · Operators and Expressions

**Cours** : Chapter 4, *Operators and Expressions* (slides 4_1 et 4_2) : les
**8 catégories d'opérateurs**, l'**integer / real / mixed-mode arithmetic**,
`++` / `--` en **prefix** et **postfix**, les **shorthand assignments**
(`+=`…), le **conditional operator** `?:`, les **bitwise**, **comma** et
**sizeof** operators, l'**évaluation** d'une expression (**precedence** et
**associativity**), les **type conversions** (implicit / explicit cast) et les
**math functions**.

> **En bref.** `/` entre deux `int` **tronque** (14/4 = 3) et `%` donne le
> **reste** (14 % 4 = 2, signe du **dividende**). `++m` incrémente **puis**
> utilise ; `m++` utilise **puis** incrémente. Dans une expression sans
> parenthèses, `* / %` passent **avant** `+ -`, de gauche à droite. Dans une
> expression mixte, le type « **lower** » est converti vers le « **higher** »
> (`int` → `float` → `double`). Un **cast** `(float) a / b` évite la division
> entière. Au quiz : savoir **dérouler** une expression pas à pas.

---

## 1. Les catégories d'opérateurs

```diagram
{
  "title": "Les 8 catégories d'opérateurs du C.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t", "x": 300, "y": 30, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "label": "C operators", "rows": [["Catégorie","Opérateurs","Exemple"],["Arithmetic","+  -  *  /  %","a % b"],["Relational","<  <=  >  >=  ==  !=","a <= b"],["Logical","&&  ||  !","a > 0 && b > 0"],["Assignment","=  +=  -=  *=  /=  %=","x += 2"],["Increment / decrement","++  --","++m, m--"],["Conditional","? :","x = (a > b) ? a : b"],["Bitwise","&  |  ^  <<  >>  ~","a << 2"],["Special","  ,   sizeof   &   *   .   ->","sizeof(int)"]], "mark": [1,2,3,4], "cols": [170,190,170] }
  ],
  "edges": []
}
```

**Key concepts** : un **operator** est un symbole qui réalise une opération
mathématique ou logique ; une **expression** est une combinaison d'**operands**
et d'operators qui se **réduit à une seule valeur**.

## 2. Arithmetic operators

| Opérateur | Sens |
|---|---|
| `+` | addition ou **unary plus** |
| `-` | soustraction ou **unary minus** |
| `*` | multiplication |
| `/` | division |
| `%` | **modulo** (reste de la division) — **uniquement entre entiers** |

### Integer arithmetic (les deux opérandes sont entiers)

Avec **a = 14, b = 4** :

| Expression | Résultat | Remarque |
|---|---|---|
| `a - b` | 10 | |
| `a + b` | 18 | |
| `a * b` | 56 | |
| `a / b` | **3** | partie décimale **tronquée** |
| `a % b` | **2** | reste |

- Division entière : si les deux opérandes ont le **même signe**, on tronque
  **vers zéro** : `6/7 = 0`, `-6/-7 = 0`. Mais `-6/7` vaut 0 **ou** −1 :
  **machine dependent**.
- Modulo : le signe du résultat est **toujours celui du premier opérande**
  (le dividende) : `-14 % 3 = -2`, `-14 % -3 = -2`, `14 % -3 = 2`.

### Real et mixed-mode arithmetic

| Mode | Exemple | Résultat |
|---|---|---|
| **Real** (deux réels) | `6.0 / 7.0` | 0.857143 |
| | `-2.0 / 3.0` | −0.666667 |
| **Mixed-mode** (un réel + un entier) | `15 / 10.0` | **1.5** |
| **Integer** (deux entiers) | `15 / 10` | **1** |

> Dès qu'**un** opérande est réel, le calcul est réel.

### Worked-out problem 4.1 : jours → mois et jours

```c
months = days / 30;      /* quotient : nombre de mois entiers */
days   = days % 30;      /* reste    : jours restants          */
```

| Entrée | `days / 30` | `days % 30` | Sortie |
|---|---|---|---|
| 265 | 8 | 25 | Months = 8 Days = 25 |
| 364 | 12 | 4 | Months = 12 Days = 4 |
| 45 | 1 | 15 | Months = 1 Days = 15 |

## 3. Relational operators

| `<` | `<=` | `>` | `>=` | `==` | `!=` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| less than | less or equal | greater than | greater or equal | **equal to** | not equal to |

`ae-1 relational-operator ae-2` : le résultat vaut **1 (true)** ou **0
(false)**. Les **arithmetic operators ont priorité** sur les relational.

| Expression | Valeur |
|---|---|
| `4.5 <= 10` | TRUE |
| `4.5 < -10` | FALSE |
| `-35 >= 0` | FALSE |
| `10 < 7+5` | TRUE (7+5 calculé d'abord) |
| `a+b == c+d` | TRUE si les deux sommes sont égales |

**Complements** : chaque opérateur est le complément d'un autre, on simplifie
un `!` ainsi :

| `>` ↔ `<=` | `<` ↔ `>=` | `==` ↔ `!=` |
|---|---|---|

| Avec `!` | Simplifié |
|---|---|
| `!(x < y)` | `x >= y` |
| `!(x > y)` | `x <= y` |
| `!(x != y)` | `x == y` |
| `!(x <= y)` | `x > y` |
| `!(x >= y)` | `x < y` |
| `!(x == y)` | `x != y` |

## 4. Logical operators

`&&` (AND), `||` (OR), `!` (NOT) : pour tester **plusieurs conditions**.

| op-1 | op-2 | `op-1 && op-2` | `op-1 \|\| op-2` |
|---|---|---|---|
| non-zero | non-zero | **1** | 1 |
| non-zero | 0 | 0 | **1** |
| 0 | non-zero | 0 | **1** |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | **0** |

```c
if (age > 55 && salary < 1000)
if (number < 0 || number > 100)
```

Précédence relative : **`!`** (plus haut) → **`> >= < <=`** → **`== !=`** →
**`&&`** → **`||`** (plus bas).

Worked-out problem 4.5 : `a = 5 <= 8 && 6 != 5;` → `5 <= 8` vaut 1,
`6 != 5` vaut 1, `1 && 1` = **1**.

## 5. Assignment operators (shorthand)

`v op= exp;` équivaut à `v = v op (exp);` (**v évalué une seule fois**).

| Simple assignment | Shorthand |
|---|---|
| `a = a + 1` | `a += 1` |
| `a = a - 1` | `a -= 1` |
| `a = a * (n + 1)` | `a *= n + 1` |
| `a = a / (n + 1)` | `a /= n + 1` |
| `a = a % b` | `a %= b` |

> **Piège :** `x += y + 1;` vaut `x = x + (y + 1);` et `a *= n + 1` vaut
> `a = a * (n + 1)`, **pas** `a * n + 1`.

Worked-out problem 4.2 (carrés successifs) :

```c
#define N 100
#define A 2
a = A;
while (a < N) {
    printf("%d\n", a);
    a *= a;          /* a = a * a */
}
/* sortie : 2  4  16   (256 n'est plus < 100) */
```

## 6. Increment et decrement : prefix vs postfix

`++m` / `m++` ≡ `m = m + 1` ; `--m` / `m--` ≡ `m = m - 1`. **Identiques
seuls**, **différents dans une expression**.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Prefix : on incrémente d'abord. Postfix : on utilise l'ancienne valeur d'abord. Départ m = 5.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "h1", "x": 150, "y": 20, "shape": "text", "label": "y = ++m;  (prefix)", "bold": true },
    { "id": "a1", "x": 60, "y": 80, "w": 110, "label": "① m = m + 1\nm = 6", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "a2", "x": 240, "y": 80, "w": 110, "label": "② y = m\ny = 6", "tone": "sky", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "r1", "x": 150, "y": 150, "w": 150, "label": "y = 6, m = 6", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "bold": true },
    { "id": "h2", "x": 480, "y": 20, "shape": "text", "label": "y = m++;  (postfix)", "bold": true },
    { "id": "b1", "x": 390, "y": 80, "w": 110, "label": "① y = m\ny = 5", "tone": "sky", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "b2", "x": 570, "y": 80, "w": 110, "label": "② m = m + 1\nm = 6", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "r2", "x": 480, "y": 150, "w": 150, "label": "y = 5, m = 6", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "bold": true }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "a1", "to": "a2" }, { "from": "b1", "to": "b2" }
  ]
}
```

**Règles** :

- `++` et `--` sont **unary** et exigent une **variable** comme opérande
  (`++5` ou `(a+b)++` sont illégaux).
- Leur **precedence et associativity** sont celles du unary `+` et unary `-`
  (rang 2, **right to left**).
- **Ne pas** les utiliser sur des **floating point** variables (conseil des
  slides).

### Worked-out problem 4.3

```c
a = 15; b = 10;
c = ++a - b;     /* a = 16, c = 16 - 10 = 6            */
d = b++ + a;     /* d = 10 + 16 = 26, puis b = 11       */
a/b              /* 16 / 11 = 1                          */
a%b              /* 16 % 11 = 5                          */
a *= b           /* a = 16 * 11 = 176                    */
(c > d) ? 1 : 0  /* 6 > 26 faux → 0                      */
(c < d) ? 1 : 0  /* → 1                                  */
```

## 7. Conditional operator `?:` (ternary)

`exp1 ? exp2 : exp3` : on évalue **exp1** ; si **non nulle (true)**, la valeur
est **exp2**, sinon **exp3**.

```c
a = 10; b = 15;
x = (a > b) ? a : b;       /* x = 15 */

/* équivalent */
if (a > b)
    x = a;
else
    x = b;
```

## 8. Bitwise operators

Manipulent les données **au niveau du bit** ; **interdits sur `float` et
`double`**.

| `&` | `\|` | `^` | `<<` | `>>` | `~` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| bitwise AND | bitwise OR | bitwise **exclusive OR** | shift left | shift right | one's complement |

Exemple : `12 & 10` → `1100 & 1010 = 1000` = 8 ; `12 | 10` = 14 ;
`12 ^ 10` = 6 ; `3 << 2` = 12.

## 9. Special operators : comma et sizeof

**Comma operator** : évalue **de gauche à droite** et prend la valeur de
l'expression **la plus à droite**. C'est l'opérateur de **plus basse
précédence**, d'où les parenthèses :

```c
value = (x = 10, y = 5, x + y);              /* x = 10, y = 5, value = 15 */
for (n = 1, m = 10; n <= m; n++, m++)        /* dans un for */
while (c = getchar(), c != '10')             /* dans un while */
t = x, x = y, y = t;                         /* échange de valeurs */
```

**`sizeof`** : opérateur **compile time** qui renvoie le **nombre d'octets**
occupés par l'opérande.

```c
m = sizeof(sum);
n = sizeof(long int);
k = sizeof(235L);
```

Usage : connaître la taille des **arrays** et **structures**, et **allouer de
la mémoire dynamiquement**.

## 10. Évaluer une expression

`variable = expression;` : l'expression est **évaluée d'abord**, puis le
résultat **remplace** l'ancienne valeur. Toutes les variables doivent avoir
une valeur **avant**.

| Algébrique | En C |
|---|---|
| a × b − c | `a * b - c` |
| (m + n)(x + y) | `(m + n) * (x + y)` |
| ab / c | `a * b / c` |
| 3x² + 2x + 1 | `3 * x * x + 2 * x + 1` |
| x/y + c | `x / y + c` |

### Precedence des arithmetic operators

**High priority : `* / %`** — **Low priority : `+ -`**. Sans parenthèses :
**deux passes de gauche à droite** (d'abord les high, puis les low).

**Exemple** (Fig. 4.5) : `x = a - b / 3 + c * 2 - 1` avec **a = 9, b = 12,
c = 3**.

Avec parenthèses : `9 - 12 / (3 + 3) * (2 - 1)` → (3+3) = 6, (2−1) = 1 →

**Worked-out problem 4.4** (a = 9, b = 12, c = 3, en `float`) :

| Expression | Valeur |
|---|---|
| `x = a - b / 3 + c * 2 - 1` | **10.000000** |
| `y = a - b / (3 + c) * (2 - 1)` | **7.000000** |
| `z = a - (b / (3 + c) * 2) - 1` | **4.000000** |

**Règles d'évaluation** :

1. Les **sous-expressions parenthésées** d'abord, de gauche à droite ; si elles
   sont **imbriquées**, on commence par la **plus intérieure**.
2. La **precedence rule** fixe l'ordre des opérateurs dans une sous-expression.
3. L'**associativity rule** départage des opérateurs de **même** précédence.

### Some computational problems

- Les réels sont des **approximations** : `a = 1.0/3.0; b = a * 3.0;` ne donne
  **pas forcément 1**. Exemple 4.6 : sommer n fois 1/n donne 1.000001 (n = 99)
  ou 0.999999 (n = 143) : **round-off errors**.
- **Division par zéro** : arrêt anormal du programme.
- **Overflow / underflow** : à nous de garantir le bon **type** et la bonne
  **plage**.

## 11. Type conversions

### Implicit (automatic) conversion

Si les opérandes sont de types différents, le type **« lower » est converti
vers le « higher »** avant l'opération. `short` et `char` sont **toujours
d'abord convertis en `int`**.

### Explicit conversion : le cast

`(type-name) expression`

```c
ratio = female_number / male_number;          /* deux int : division entière, FAUX */
ratio = (float) female_number / male_number;  /* division réelle, CORRECT          */
```

Le cast ne change **ni la valeur ni le type** de `female_number` ailleurs dans
le programme.

| Exemple (Table 4.7) | Action |
|---|---|
| `x = (int) 7.5` | 7.5 tronqué → **7** |
| `a = (int) 21.3 / (int) 4.5` | évalué comme 21 / 4 → **5** |
| `b = (double) sum / n` | division en **floating point** |
| `y = (int) (a + b)` | le **résultat** de a + b converti en int |
| `z = (int) a + b` | **a** converti en int, puis ajouté à b |
| `p = cos((double) x)` | x converti en double avant l'appel |

**Arrondir** avec un cast : `x = (int) (y + 0.5);` → y = 27.6 → 28.1 → **28**.

Exemple 4.7 : `sum = sum + 1/(float)n;` pour n = 1…10 → 1.0000, 1.5000,
1.8333, … **2.9290**. Sans le cast, `1/n` vaudrait **0** dès n = 2.

| 9 | `^` bitwise XOR | left → right |
| 10 | `\|` bitwise OR | left → right |
| 11 | `&&` | left → right |
| 12 | `\|\|` | left → right |
| 13 | `?:` | **right → left** |
| 14 | `= += -= *= /= %=` … | **right → left** |
| 15 | `,` comma | left → right |

Les arguments **x et y sont des `double`**, les angles sont en **radians**,
toutes les fonctions **renvoient un `double`**. Compiler avec **`-lm`**.

| `fmod(x, y)` | **reste** de x/y (réels) | `cos`, `sin`, `tan` | trigo (radians) |

## Pièges d'exam

- `14 / 4 = 3`, `14 % 4 = 2` ; `%` **uniquement sur des entiers** ; signe du
  `%` = signe du **dividende** (`-14 % 3 = -2`).
- `15 / 10 = 1` mais `15 / 10.0 = 1.5`.
- `y = ++m` (m = 5) → y = 6, m = 6 ; `y = m++` → y = 5, m = 6.
- `a *= n + 1` ≡ `a = a * (n + 1)`.
- `9 - 12/3 + 3*2 - 1 = 10` ; `9 - 12/(3+3)*(2-1) = 7`.
- `(int) 21.3 / (int) 4.5 = 21 / 4 = 5`.
- `(float) a / b` : le cast s'applique à **a** seulement (unary, rang 2), la
  division devient réelle.
- Pas d'espace dans `==`, `<=`, `+=` ; ne pas inverser `!=`, `<=`, `>=` (`=!`
  est faux) ; ne pas confondre **`==`** (comparaison) et **`=`**
  (assignment).
- Comma operator : **plus faible précédence**, valeur = **dernière**
  expression.
- Bitwise : **pas** sur `float` / `double`.

## À retenir

- 8 catégories : arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, increment /
  decrement, conditional, bitwise, special.
- Integer / real / mixed-mode arithmetic ; division entière **tronque**.
- Relational → 1 ou 0 ; `&&` vrai si les deux, `||` vrai si l'un des deux.
- Precedence : `()` → unary → `* / %` → `+ -` → relational → `== !=` → `&&` →
  `||` → `?:` → assignment → `,`.
- Implicit conversion : lower → higher ; cast `(type) expr` pour forcer.
- `<math.h>` : arguments et résultats en `double`, angles en radians, `-lm`.

lesson:
# Computer Programming — Week 5 · Input / Output & Decision Making (if)

**Cours** : Chapter 5, *Managing Input and Output Operations* (slides 5_1) :
`getchar` / `putchar`, les **character test functions** de `<ctype.h>`, la
lecture formatée avec **`scanf`** et l'affichage formaté avec **`printf`**
(largeur, précision, flags). Puis Chapter 6 (1re partie), *Decision Making and
Branching* (slides 5_2) : **simple if**, **if…else**, **nested if…else**,
**else if ladder**, De Morgan et le **dangling else**.

> **En bref.** `getchar()` lit **un** caractère (y compris le `\n` qui reste
> dans le buffer !). Dans `scanf`, `%wd` lit **au plus w chiffres** et
> `%*d` **saute** un champ ; `scanf` renvoie le **nombre d'items lus**. Dans
> `printf`, `%wd` = largeur **minimale** (jamais de troncature d'un nombre),
> `-` aligne à gauche, `0` remplit de zéros, `%w.pf` = p décimales,
> `%w.ps` = les **p premiers caractères**. Pour décider : `if`, `if…else`,
> `if` imbriqués, ou une **else if ladder** ; un `else` s'associe **toujours
> au `if` sans `else` le plus proche**.

---

## 1. Lire et écrire un caractère

```c
char answer;
answer = getchar();          /* lit UN caractère sur stdin */
putchar(answer);             /* écrit UN caractère sur stdout */
putchar('\n');
```

Fig. 5.1 : `if (answer == 'Y' || answer == 'y')` → « My name is BUSY BEE »,
sinon « You are good for nothing ».

> **WARNING :** `getchar()` accepte **n'importe quel caractère**, y compris
> **RETURN** et **TAB**. Quand on tape `Y⏎`, le `\n` **reste dans la file
> d'entrée** et sera lu par le `getchar()` suivant. Solution : un **dummy
> `getchar()`** pour « manger » le `\n`, ou `fflush`.

```diagram

    { "id": "buf", "x": 200, "y": 40, "shape": "table", "size": 13, "label": "input queue après la frappe « Y⏎ »", "header": false, "rows": [["'Y'","'\\n'"]], "cols": [60,60] },
    { "id": "g1", "x": 80, "y": 140, "w": 170, "label": "1er getchar() → 'Y'", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "g2", "x": 320, "y": 140, "w": 190, "label": "2e getchar() → '\\n'  (!)", "tone": "rose", "filled": true, "size": 12 }
  ],

    { "from": "buf", "to": "g1" }, { "from": "buf", "to": "g2" }

```

### Character test functions (`<ctype.h>`)

| Fonction | Teste si c est… |
|---|---|
| `isalnum(c)` | **alphanumérique** (lettre ou chiffre) |
| `isalpha(c)` | une **lettre** |
| `isdigit(c)` | un **chiffre** |
| `islower(c)` | une **minuscule** |
| `isupper(c)` | une **majuscule** |
| `isprint(c)` | **imprimable** |
| `ispunct(c)` | un **signe de ponctuation** |
| `isspace(c)` | un **white space** |

Elles renvoient **non-zéro (true)** ou **0**. Conversions : `toupper(c)`,
`tolower(c)`.

Fig. 5.3 — inverser la casse :

```c
alphabet = getchar();
if (islower(alphabet))
    putchar(toupper(alphabet));   /* a → A */
else
    putchar(tolower(alphabet));   /* Z → z */
```

## 2. Formatted input : `scanf`

`scanf("control string", arg1, arg2, …, argn);`

- Le **control string** contient des **field specifications** (`%`, une
  **largeur** optionnelle, un **type specifier**) et éventuellement des
  blancs/tabs/newlines.
- Les **arguments** sont des **adresses** (`&a`).

### Lire des entiers : `%wd`

```c
scanf("%2d %5d", &num1, &num2);
```

```diagram
{
  "title": "La largeur w limite le nombre de caractères lus. Le reste est lu par le champ suivant.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t", "x": 320, "y": 30, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "label": "scanf(\"%2d %5d\", &num1, &num2)", "rows": [["Entrée tapée","num1","num2","Commentaire"],["50 31426","50","31426","OK"],["31426 50","31","426","%2d coupe : 50 reste dans le buffer"]], "mark": [2], "cols": [110,60,60,260] }
  ],
  "edges": []
}
```

- Solution : **ne pas mettre de largeur** (`"%d %d"`).
- **`%*d`** : le champ est **lu puis ignoré** (skipped).

```c
scanf("%d %*d %d", &a, &b);   /* entrée : 123 456 789 → a = 123, 456 sauté, b = 789 */
```

- Si on tape un **réel** pour un `%d`, la partie décimale peut être perdue et
  `scanf` peut **arrêter** de lire.

### Lire des réels : `%f`, `%lf`

- **Pas de largeur** pour les réels : `%f` lit les deux notations (décimale et
  exponentielle).
- **`%lf`** pour un **`double`** (`%Lf` pour long double).

```c
scanf("%f %f", &x, &y);       /* 12.3456 17.5e-2 → x = 12.345600, y = 0.175000 */
scanf("%lf %lf", &p, &q);
```

### Lire des strings : `%ws`, `%wc`, `%[…]`

| Spécification | Lit… |
|---|---|
| `%s` | un **mot** : s'arrête au **premier blanc** (« New York » → `New`) |
| `%ws` | au plus **w** caractères d'un mot |
| `%wc` | exactement **w** caractères, **blancs compris** |
| `%[characters]` | uniquement les caractères **listés** ; s'arrête au premier autre |
| `%[^characters]` | **l'inverse** : tout **sauf** les caractères listés |

```c
scanf("%[a-z]", address);     /* "new delhi 110002" → "new" (s'arrête à l'espace) */
scanf("%[^\n]", address);     /* lit toute la ligne jusqu'au ⏎ : "New Delhi 110 002" */
```

### Mixed data et détection d'erreurs

```c
scanf("%d %c %f %s", &count, &code, &ratio, name);   /* 15 P 1.575 coffee : OK */
```

Si un item ne correspond pas au type attendu, `scanf` **s'arrête** et
**renvoie le nombre d'items lus avec succès** :

```c
scanf("%d %f %s", &a, &b, name);
/* "20 150.25 motor" → renvoie 3
   "20 motor 150.25" → renvoie 1 (motor n'est pas un float) */
```

```flowchart

    { "id": "s", "kind": "start", "label": "START" },
    { "id": "r", "kind": "io", "label": "n = scanf(\"%d %f %c\", &a, &b, &c)" },
```

> Dans Fig. 5.8, l'entrée `15.75 23 X` donne **a = 15, b = 0.75, c = '2'** :
> `%d` s'arrête au point, `%f` lit `.75`, `%c` lit le `2`. `scanf` renvoie
> bien 3, mais les valeurs ne sont pas celles voulues.

### Format codes de `scanf` (Table 5.2)

| Code | Lit | Code | Lit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `%c` | un caractère | `%o` | un entier **octal** |
| `%d` | un entier décimal | `%s` | une string |
| `%e`, `%f`, `%g` | un réel | `%u` | un entier **unsigned** |
| `%h` | un **short** integer | `%x` | un entier **hexadécimal** |
| `%i` | un entier décimal, hexa ou octal | `%[..]` | une string de mot(s) |

Préfixes : **`h`** short, **`l`** long ou double, **`L`** long double.

### Règles de `scanf`

1. Tous les arguments sauf le control string sont des **pointeurs** (`&`).
2. Les spécifications sont dans le **même ordre** que les arguments.
3. Les données tapées sont séparées par des **espaces** et dans le même ordre.
4. La lecture s'arrête à un **mismatch** ou à un caractère invalide.
5. `scanf` **ignore les fins de ligne** quand il cherche une valeur.
6. Les données **non lues** d'une ligne servent au **`scanf` suivant**.
7. Une largeur w doit être **assez grande** pour la donnée.
8. Tout caractère **non-blanc** du format doit être **tapé tel quel**.
9. **Ne jamais finir le format par un blanc**, ni mettre de **virgules** ou
   de **précision** (`%5.2f` interdit en entrée).

## 3. Formatted output : `printf`

`printf("control string", arg1, …, argn);` — le control string contient :
**(1)** des caractères affichés tels quels, **(2)** des **format
specifications**, **(3)** des **escape sequences** (`\n`, `\t`, `\b`).

### Entiers : `%wd`

`w` = largeur **minimale** ; si le nombre est plus long, il est affiché **en
entier**.

```diagram
{
  "title": "printf d'un entier (Fig. 5.9) : chaque case = une colonne. · = espace.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t", "x": 300, "y": 30, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "label": "valeur 9876", "rows": [["Format","Sortie","Règle"],["%d","9876","largeur naturelle"],["%6d","··9876","aligné à DROITE sur 6"],["%2d","9876","w trop petit : affiché en entier"],["%-6d","9876··","- : aligné à GAUCHE"],["%06d","009876","0 : zéros devant"]], "cols": [80,100,230] }
  ],
  "edges": []
}
```

Fig. 5.9 avec m = 12345, n = 987654 : `%10d` → `·····12345`, `%010d` →
`0000012345`, `%-10d` → `12345·····`, `%10ld` → `····987654`.

### Réels : `%w.pf` et `%w.pe`

`w` = largeur **minimale totale** (point et signe compris), `p` = chiffres
**après la virgule** (6 par défaut). `%e` = notation exponentielle
`[-]m.nnnnnne[±]xx`.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Fig. 5.10 avec y = 98.7654 (float). La valeur est ARRONDIE à p décimales.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t", "x": 300, "y": 30, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "label": "float y = 98.7654", "rows": [["Format","Sortie","Remarque"],["%7.4f","98.7654","7 colonnes, 4 décimales"],["%f","98.765404","6 décimales par défaut (float imprécis)"],["%7.2f","··98.77","arrondi à 2 décimales"],["%-7.2f","98.77··","aligné à gauche"],["%07.2f","0098.77","zéros devant"],["%*.*f, 7, 2","··98.77","largeur et précision à l'exécution"],["%10.2e","··9.88e+01","exponentiel, 2 décimales"],["%12.4e (−y)","·-9.8765e+01","signe compris dans la largeur"],["%e","9.876540e+01","6 décimales"]], "cols": [100,120,250] }
  ],
  "edges": []
}
```

`printf("%*.*f", width, precision, number);` : la largeur et la précision
sont fournies **au moment de l'exécution** (format **dynamique**).

### Caractères et strings : `%wc`, `%w.ps`

- `%wc` : le caractère est **aligné à droite** dans w colonnes (`%-wc` à
  gauche).
- `%w.ps` : w = largeur, **p = nombre de caractères affichés** (les p
  premiers). Aligné **à droite** par défaut.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Fig. 5.11 sur la string \"NEW DELHI 110001\" (16 caractères). · = espace.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t", "x": 300, "y": 30, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "label": "char name[] = \"NEW DELHI 110001\"", "rows": [["Format","Sortie","Règle"],["%s","NEW DELHI 110001","toute la string"],["%20s","····NEW DELHI 110001","20 colonnes, à droite"],["%20.10s","··········NEW DELHI·","10 premiers car., à droite sur 20"],["%.5s","NEW D","5 premiers caractères"],["%-20.10s","NEW DELHI···········","10 premiers, à gauche sur 20"],["%5s","NEW DELHI 110001","w trop petit : tout est affiché"]], "cols": [90,200,230] }
  ],
  "edges": []
}
```

### Format codes et flags de `printf` (Tables 5.3 et 5.4)

| Code | Affiche | Code | Affiche |
|---|---|---|---|
| `%c` | un caractère | `%i` | un entier signé |
| `%d` | un entier décimal | `%o` | octal **sans** `0` devant |
| `%e` | réel en **exponentiel** | `%s` | une string |
| `%f` | réel **sans** exposant | `%u` | unsigned |
| `%g` | `%e` ou `%f`, **le plus court** | `%x` | hexa **sans** `0x` |

| Flag | Effet |
|---|---|
| `-` | **aligné à gauche** dans le champ |
| `+` | un **signe** `+` ou `−` devant tout nombre signé |
| `0` | **zéros** devant |
| `#` (avec `o` / `x`) | préfixe `0` / `0x` |
| `#` (avec `e`, `f`, `g`) | force le **point décimal** ; avec `g`, garde les zéros de fin |

### Les erreurs classiques d'I/O (Always remember)

- Inclure **`<stdio.h>`** (et **`<ctype.h>`** pour les fonctions de
  caractères).
- **`&`** devant les variables de base dans `scanf`, mais **jamais** dans
  `printf` (sinon on affiche une adresse : erreur).
- **Guillemets doubles** pour les strings et les formats, **apostrophes** pour
  un caractère.
- Mauvais code de conversion pour le type → **résultat faux / erreur à
  l'exécution**.
- Ne pas oublier la **virgule** après le format.

## 4. Decision making : les 4 formes de `if`

C dispose de **4 instructions de décision** : `if`, `switch`, le
**conditional operator** `?:` et `goto` (W6 pour les trois dernières).

```diagram

    { "id": "b", "x": 260, "y": 40, "w": 150, "h": 70, "label": "if…else\ndeux chemins\n(true / false)", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "c", "x": 430, "y": 40, "w": 150, "h": 70, "label": "Nested if…else\nun if dans\nun if", "tone": "violet", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "d", "x": 600, "y": 40, "w": 150, "h": 70, "label": "else if ladder\nn conditions\n+ un default", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "size": 12 }
  ],
  "edges": []

```

### Simple if

```c
if (test expression)
{
    statement-block;
}
statement-x;
```

Si le test est **vrai**, le bloc est exécuté ; sinon il est **sauté** et on
passe à `statement-x`.

```c
if (c - d != 0) {
```

Fig. 6.4 — compter les garçons avec `weight < 50 && height > 170` (10 saisies

### De Morgan's rule

On préfère une **logique positive**. Pour enlever un `!` devant une expression
composée : appliquer le NOT à **chaque** composant **et** inverser `&&` ↔ `||`
(et les relational operators par leur complément).

| Avant | Après |
|---|---|
| `x` | devient `!x` |
| `!x` | devient `x` |
| `&&` | devient `\|\|` |
| `\|\|` | devient `&&` |
| `!(x && y \|\| !z)` | `!x \|\| !y && z` |
| `!(x <= 0 \|\| !condition)` | `x > 0 && condition` |

### if…else

```c
if (test expression)
{
    true-block statement(s);
}
else
{
    false-block statement(s);
}
statement-x;
```

```flowchart

  "title": "if…else : exactement UN des deux blocs est exécuté.",

    { "id": "d", "kind": "decision", "label": "test expression ?" },
    { "id": "t", "kind": "process", "label": "True-block" },
    { "id": "f", "kind": "process", "label": "False-block" },
    { "id": "x", "kind": "process", "label": "statement-x" },

  ],

    { "from": "s", "to": "d" },
    { "from": "d", "to": "t", "branch": "yes" }, { "from": "d", "to": "f", "branch": "no" },
    { "from": "t", "to": "x" }, { "from": "f", "to": "x" }, { "from": "x", "to": "e" }
  ]
```

Fig. 6.6 — série de eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + … : chaque terme se calcule à
partir du précédent, **Tₙ = Tₙ₋₁ · x / n**. On s'arrête (`n = 999`) quand
`term < ACCURACY` (0.0001), sinon `n = n + 1`. x = 1 → **9 termes, sum =
2.718279** (≈ e).

### Nested if…else

```c
if (test condition-1) {
    if (test condition-2)
        statement-1;
    else
        statement-2;
} else {
    statement-3;
}
statement-x;
```

Condition-1 fausse → statement-3. Sinon on teste condition-2 : vraie →
statement-1, fausse → statement-2.

**Dangling else** : quand il manque un `else`, **« an else is always paired
with the most recent unpaired if »** (dans le bloc courant).

```c
/* Ce qu'on a écrit (l'indentation suggère le 1er if) */
if (n > 0)
    if (a > b)
        z = a;
else
    z = b;

/* Ce que le compilateur comprend : le else va au if le plus proche */
if (n > 0) {
    if (a > b)
        z = a;
    else
        z = b;
}
```

Pour associer le `else` au **premier** `if`, il faut des **accolades** :
`if (n > 0) { if (a > b) z = a; } else z = b;`.

### else if ladder

```c
if (condition 1)
    statement-1;
else if (condition 2)
    statement-2;
else if (condition 3)
    statement-3;
...
else
    default-statement;
statement-x;
```

Dès qu'une condition est **vraie**, son instruction est exécutée et on saute
à `statement-x`. Si **toutes** sont fausses → **default-statement**.

## 5. Rules for indentation

- Indenter les instructions dépendantes d'**au moins 3 espaces**.
- **Aligner** chaque `else` avec son `if`.
- Accolades sur des **lignes séparées**, alignées entre elles.
- **Une seule** instruction ou clause par ligne ; commentaires de début / fin
  de bloc.

### Exo 5 — année bissextile

Une année est **leap** si elle est **divisible par 4 mais pas par 100**, **ou**
**divisible par 400**.

```c
if ((n % 4 == 0 && n % 100 != 0) || (n % 400 == 0))
```

| Année | % 4 | % 100 | % 400 | Leap ? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | 0 | 24 | 424 | ✅ (÷ 4, pas ÷ 100) |
| 1900 | 0 | **0** | 300 | ❌ (÷ 100 mais pas ÷ 400) |
| 2000 | 0 | 0 | **0** | ✅ (÷ 400) |
| 2023 | 3 | 23 | 23 | ❌ |

### Exo 6 — le plus grand de trois (nested if, Fig. 6.8)

```c
if (a > b) {
    if (a > c) printf("%d", a);
    else       printf("%d", c);
} else {
    if (b > c) printf("%d", b);
    else       printf("%d", c);
}
```

### Exo 2 — les largeurs dans `scanf` (Fig. 5.4)

| Instruction | On tape | Résultat |
|---|---|---|
| `scanf("%d %*d %d", &a, &b, &c)` | `1 2 3` | a = 1, **2 sauté**, b = 3, **c non lu** (garbage) |
| `scanf("%2d %4d", &x, &y)` | `6789 4321` | x = **67**, y = **89** ; `4321` reste dans le buffer |
| `scanf("%d %d", &a, &x)` | `44 66` | a = **4321** (le reste précédent !), x = 44 |
| `scanf("%3d %4d %3d", &p, &q, &r)` | `123456789` | p = **66** (reste), q = **1234**, r = **567** ; `89` reste |
| `scanf("%d %d", &x, &y)` | `123 456` | x = **89** (reste), y = **123** |

> **Leçon :** les données non lues restent dans la file et faussent les
> lectures suivantes. Éviter les largeurs dans `scanf`.

### Exo 3 & 4 — `%[a-z]` et formats de strings

`scanf("%[a-z]", address)` s'arrête au premier caractère **hors** de `a-z` :
majuscule, chiffre… et aussi l'**espace**. La slide (Fig. 5.7) affiche
`new delhi`, mais avec gcc on obtient **`new`** : pour accepter les espaces il
faut `%[a-z ]`. Pour toute la ligne : **`%[^\n]`**.

---

## Pièges d'exam

- `getchar()` lit aussi le **`\n`** ; il faut le « manger ».
- `scanf` renvoie le **nombre d'items lus** ; `%*d` saute un champ ; `%2d`
  coupe `31426` en `31` + `426`.
- `%lf` pour lire un **double** ; **pas** de précision en entrée.
- `%s` s'arrête au premier **blanc** ; `%[^\n]` lit toute la ligne.
- `printf` : w est un **minimum** (`%2d` de 9876 → `9876`) ; `%.5s` = 5
  premiers caractères ; `%7.2f` de 98.7654 → `··98.77`.
- `&` dans un `printf` = **erreur** (adresse affichée).
- **Pas de `;`** après `if (…)` : `if (x > 0);` exécute un bloc vide.
- `else` ↔ **le `if` sans `else` le plus proche**.
- De Morgan : `!(a && b)` = `!a || !b`.
- Leap year : `(n%4==0 && n%100!=0) || n%400==0`.

## À retenir

- `getchar` / `putchar` ; `<ctype.h>` : `isalpha`, `isdigit`, `isalnum`,
  `islower`, `isupper`, `isspace`, `ispunct`, `isprint`, `toupper`,
  `tolower`.
- `scanf` : adresses, ordre, type ; `%wd`, `%*d`, `%f`/`%lf`, `%s`, `%wc`,
  `%[…]`, `%[^…]`.
- `printf` : `%wd`, `%w.pf`, `%w.pe`, `%wc`, `%w.ps` ; flags `- + 0 #`.
- `if`, `if…else`, nested `if`, `else if` ladder ; indentation et accolades.

lesson:
# Computer Programming — Week 6 · switch, ?: and goto

**Cours** : Chapter 6 (2e partie), *Decision Making and Branching* : le
**`switch`** (sélection multiple), le **conditional operator `?:`**
(exemple du prêt, GCD), les **guidelines** pour écrire une sélection
multiple, et le **`goto`** (sauts avant / arrière, sortie de boucles).

> **En bref.** `switch (expression)` compare une valeur **entière** à des
> **case labels constants et uniques** ; on exécute le bloc qui correspond
> **jusqu'au `break`** (sans `break`, on **continue dans le case suivant** :
> *fall through*). `default` est optionnel, au plus un. `x = cond ? a : b`
> remplace un `if…else` simple. `goto label;` saute **sans condition** vers
> `label:` ; à éviter, sauf pour sortir de boucles imbriquées.

---

## 1. Le `switch`

Quand il faut choisir **parmi beaucoup d'alternatives**, une longue `else if`
ladder devient illisible : C a un **multiway decision statement**, le
`switch`.

```c
switch (expression)
{
    case value-1:
        block-1
        break;
    case value-2:
        block-2
        break;
    ...
    default:
        default-block
        break;
}
statement-x;
```

- L'expression est **comparée successivement** à value-1, value-2, …
- Si une valeur **correspond**, on exécute le bloc qui suit ce `case`.
- **`break`** signale la **fin** du case et **sort** du `switch`.
- **`default`** est exécuté si **aucune** valeur ne correspond.
- Les case labels se terminent par un **deux-points `:`**.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Selection process of the switch statement (Fig. 6.11).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "in", "x": 330, "y": 20, "w": 150, "label": "Entry", "tone": "neutral", "filled": true },
    { "id": "sw", "x": 330, "y": 90, "w": 200, "label": "switch (expression)", "tone": "violet", "filled": true, "bold": true },
    { "id": "b1", "x": 100, "y": 190, "w": 130, "label": "block-1", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "b2", "x": 260, "y": 190, "w": 130, "label": "block-2", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "bn", "x": 420, "y": 190, "w": 130, "label": "…", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "df", "x": 580, "y": 190, "w": 130, "label": "default-block", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "x", "x": 330, "y": 290, "w": 200, "label": "statement-x", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "in", "to": "sw" },
    { "from": "sw", "to": "b1", "label": "= value-1" },
    { "from": "sw", "to": "b2", "label": "= value-2" },
    { "from": "sw", "to": "bn" },
    { "from": "sw", "to": "df", "label": "no match" },
    { "from": "b1", "to": "x", "label": "break" },
    { "from": "b2", "to": "x", "label": "break" },
    { "from": "bn", "to": "x" },
    { "from": "df", "to": "x" }
  ]
}
```

### Rules for switch statement

| Règle | Exemple / remarque |
|---|---|
| L'expression doit être de type **integral** (`int`, `char`) | `switch (x)` avec `float x` → **erreur** |
| Les case labels sont des **constantes** ou **constant expressions** | `case 'A':`, `case 2 + 1:` ✅ ; `case n:` ❌ |
| Les case labels sont **uniques** | deux `case 3:` → **erreur** |
| Chaque case label finit par **`:`** | (les slides écrivent « semicolon » par erreur : c'est un **colon**) |
| `break` fait **sortir** du switch | |
| `break` est **optionnel** → plusieurs labels peuvent partager les mêmes instructions | `case 'a': case 'A': …` |
| `default` est **optionnel**, **au plus un** | exécuté si rien ne correspond |
| `default` peut être **n'importe où**, en général **à la fin** | |
| On peut **imbriquer** des `switch` | |

### Le fall through (oubli de `break`)

```c
int x = 2;
switch (x) {
    case 1: printf("one ");
    case 2: printf("two ");
    case 3: printf("three ");
    default: printf("other");
}
/* sortie : two three other */
```

```diagram

  "title": "Sans break, l'exécution « tombe » dans les cases suivants jusqu'à la fin du switch.",

    { "id": "c1", "x": 100, "y": 40, "w": 150, "label": "case 1: \"one\"", "tone": "neutral", "filled": true },
    { "id": "c2", "x": 100, "y": 110, "w": 150, "label": "case 2: \"two\"", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "bold": true },
    { "id": "c3", "x": 100, "y": 180, "w": 150, "label": "case 3: \"three\"", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "d", "x": 100, "y": 250, "w": 150, "label": "default: \"other\"", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "x", "x": 330, "y": 110, "w": 120, "label": "x = 2", "tone": "violet", "filled": true },
    { "id": "n", "x": 400, "y": 215, "w": 200, "shape": "note", "tone": "rose", "label": "pas de break :\non continue !", "size": 12 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "x", "to": "c2", "label": "match" },
    { "from": "c2", "to": "c3", "tone": "rose" },
    { "from": "c3", "to": "d", "tone": "rose" }
  ]
}
```

### Worked-out problem 6.6 : le mois et le suivant

```c
char month[12][20] = {"January", "February", ..., "December"};
scanf("%d", &i);
if (i < 1 || i > 12) {
    printf("Incorrect value!!\n");
    exit(0);
}
if (i != 12)
    printf("%s followed by %s", month[i-1], month[i]);
else
    printf("%s followed by %s", month[i-1], month[0]);   /* December → January */
/* 6 → June followed by July */
```

> Les indices de tableau commencent à **0** : le mois `i` est `month[i-1]`.

## 2. Le conditional operator `?:`

`conditional expression ? expression1 : expression2`

- La condition est évaluée d'abord ; **non nulle** → valeur de
  **expression1**, sinon **expression2**.

```c
if (x < 0)
    flag = 0;
else
    flag = 1;

/* équivaut à */
flag = (x < 0) ? 0 : 1;
```

### Worked-out problem 6.7 : le prêt

Règles : **(1)** pas plus de **deux prêts** en même temps ; **(2)** total
**plafonné** à `MAXLOAN = 50000`.

```c
sancloan = (loan1 > 0) ? 0
         : ((sum23 > MAXLOAN) ? MAXLOAN - loan2 : loan3);
/* sum23 = loan2 + loan3 */
```

```flowchart
    { "from": "d1", "to": "z", "branch": "yes" }, { "from": "d1", "to": "d2", "branch": "no" },
    { "from": "d2", "to": "m", "branch": "yes" }, { "from": "d2", "to": "l", "branch": "no" },
```

| loan1 | loan2 | loan3 | sum23 | Sanctioned |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 20000 | 45000 | 65000 > 50000 | **30000** (= 50000 − 20000) |
| 1000 | 15000 | 25000 | — | **0** (déjà deux prêts en cours) |

### Worked-out problem 6.8 : le GCD

Le **plus grand commun diviseur** par l'**algorithme d'Euclide** :
GCD(a, b) = GCD(b, a % b) jusqu'à ce que b = 0.

```c
int GCD(int a, int b)
{
    if (b > a)
        return GCD(b, a);        /* on met le plus grand en premier */
    if (b == 0)
        return a;
    return GCD(b, a % b);
}
/* GCD of 18 and 12 is 6 */
```

```diagram
  ],
```

## 3. Guidelines for multiway selection

- **Éviter** les négations composées ; préférer les tests **positifs**.
- Expressions **simples** (**KISS** — Keep It Simple and Short), quitte à
  imbriquer des `if`.
- Coder **d'abord** le cas **normal / attendu**, et la condition **la plus
  probable** en premier (moins de tests inutiles).
- `if` imbriqués ou `switch` : affaire de goût ; règle pratique : **`switch`
  quand il y a de 3 à 10 alternatives**.
- Bonne **indentation**, **toujours** un `default`, **regrouper** les case
  labels qui font la même chose.

## 4. Le `goto`

Branchement **inconditionnel** d'un point à un autre du programme. Il faut un
**label** : un nom valide suivi de **`:`**, placé juste avant l'instruction
cible.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Forward jump (le label est après) et backward jump (le label est avant : risque de boucle infinie).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "f1", "x": 110, "y": 40, "w": 160, "label": "goto label;", "tone": "rose", "filled": true },
    { "id": "f2", "x": 110, "y": 100, "w": 160, "label": "…  (sauté)", "tone": "neutral" },
    { "id": "f3", "x": 110, "y": 160, "w": 160, "label": "label: statement;", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "h1", "x": 110, "y": 215, "shape": "text", "label": "Forward jump", "bold": true },
    { "id": "b1", "x": 420, "y": 40, "w": 160, "label": "label: statement;", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "b2", "x": 420, "y": 100, "w": 160, "label": "…", "tone": "neutral" },
    { "id": "b3", "x": 420, "y": 160, "w": 160, "label": "goto label;", "tone": "rose", "filled": true },
    { "id": "h2", "x": 420, "y": 215, "shape": "text", "label": "Backward jump (boucle)", "bold": true }
  ],

    { "from": "b3", "to": "b1", "via": [[540, 160], [540, 40]], "tone": "rose" }
  ]

```

- Le label peut être **avant ou après** le `goto`.
- Usage légitime : **sortir de boucles imbriquées** d'un coup quand une
  condition particulière survient (`goto end_of_program;`).
- **À éviter autant que possible** ; acceptable s'il améliore la
  **lisibilité** ou la **vitesse**.
- Attention aux **boucles infinies** avec un backward jump sans condition de
  sortie.

### Worked-out problem 6.9 : racines carrées avec `goto`

```c
count = 1;
read:
    scanf("%lf", &x);
    if (x < 0)
        printf("Value - %d is negative\n", count);
    else {
        y = sqrt(x);
        printf("%lf\t %lf\n", x, y);
    }
    count = count + 1;
    if (count <= 5)
        goto read;          /* backward jump : relit tant que count <= 5 */
printf("\nEnd of computation");
```

Entrée `50.75 40 -36 75 11.25` → 7.123903, 6.324555, « Value - 3 is negative »,
8.660254, 3.354102, puis « End of computation ».

**Key concept** : une **infinite loop** est un ensemble d'instructions
exécuté **indéfiniment** (par ex. `goto start;` sans condition, comme dans
les exercices 2 et 3 du TD : il faut `Ctrl+C` pour arrêter).

---

## 5. Exercices du TD, expliqués

### Exo 1 — note selon un code (switch sur un int)

```c
switch (exp) {
    case 1: printf("A+"); break;
    case 2: printf("B+"); break;
    case 3: printf("C+"); break;
    case 4: printf("D+"); break;
    default: printf("F"); break;
}
```

### Exo 2 — calculatrice (switch sur un char)

```diagram
{
  "title": "Exo 2 : le switch aiguille sur l'opérateur ; la division vérifie b != 0 ; goto start relance indéfiniment (infinite loop).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "st", "x": 330, "y": 20, "w": 120, "label": "start:", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "bold": true },
    { "id": "in", "x": 330, "y": 80, "w": 220, "label": "READ a, b   puis   op", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "sw", "x": 330, "y": 145, "w": 160, "label": "switch (op)", "tone": "violet", "filled": true, "bold": true },
    { "id": "p", "x": 70, "y": 230, "w": 100, "label": "a + b", "size": 12 },
    { "id": "m", "x": 190, "y": 230, "w": 100, "label": "a - b", "size": 12 },
    { "id": "t", "x": 310, "y": 230, "w": 100, "label": "a * b", "size": 12 },
    { "id": "d", "x": 450, "y": 230, "w": 140, "label": "b != 0 ? a / b\n: \"Division by zero\"", "size": 11 },
    { "id": "df", "x": 600, "y": 230, "w": 120, "label": "\"Invalid\"", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "g", "x": 330, "y": 320, "w": 140, "label": "goto start;", "tone": "rose", "filled": true, "bold": true }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "st", "to": "in" }, { "from": "in", "to": "sw" },
    { "from": "sw", "to": "p", "label": "'+'" }, { "from": "sw", "to": "m", "label": "'-'" }, { "from": "sw", "to": "t", "label": "'*'" },
    { "from": "sw", "to": "d", "label": "'/'" }, { "from": "sw", "to": "df", "label": "default" },
    { "from": "p", "to": "g" }, { "from": "m", "to": "g" }, { "from": "t", "to": "g" }, { "from": "d", "to": "g" }, { "from": "df", "to": "g" },
    { "from": "g", "to": "st", "via": [[700, 320], [700, 20]], "tone": "rose", "dashed": true }
  ]

```

- `scanf(" %c", &exp)` : l'**espace avant `%c`** saute le `\n` resté après
  la lecture des nombres (sinon `%c` lirait ce `\n`, comme `getchar`, W5).
- `case '+':` : un **caractère constant** est une constante entière (son code
  ASCII) → autorisé.

### Exo 3 — voyelle ou consonne

```c
if ((letter >= 'A' && letter <= 'Z') || (letter >= 'a' && letter <= 'z'))
    isVowel(letter) ? "vowel" : "consonant"
else
    "not a correct letter"
```

Version `switch` avec **cases regroupés** (fall through volontaire) :

```c
switch (letter) {
    case 'a': case 'e': case 'i': case 'o': case 'u':
    case 'A': case 'E': case 'I': case 'O': case 'U':
        printf("vowel");
        break;
    default:
        printf("consonant");
}
```

---

## Pièges d'exam

- Expression du `switch` : **integral** seulement (pas de `float`, pas de
  string).
- `case` : **constantes** uniques ; `case x:` avec une variable = **erreur**.
- Oublier `break` → **fall through** dans les cases suivants.
- `default` : optionnel, **au plus un**, placé n'importe où.
- `x = (a > b) ? a : b;` → le plus grand.
- `goto` : label = **nom + `:`** ; saut **inconditionnel** ; risque de
  **boucle infinie**.
- Always remember : pas de `;` après `if (…)`, `==` et non `=`, pas d'espace
  dans `<=` / `!=`, **ne pas comparer deux `float` avec `==`** (rarement
  exactement égaux), `&&` et `||` doublés, attention aux **side effects**
  (`x-- && ++y` : le 2e opérande peut ne **pas être évalué**).

## À retenir

- `switch` pour **3 à 10** alternatives sur une valeur entière ; `break` +
  `default`.
- `?:` = `if…else` en une expression ; s'imbrique pour 3 cas (max de trois).
- GCD : `GCD(a, b) = GCD(b, a % b)`, `GCD(a, 0) = a`.
- `goto` : forward / backward jump ; seul usage conseillé : sortir de boucles
  imbriquées.

lesson:
# Computer Programming — Week 7 · Programming Exercise 2 & révision midterm

**Cours** : la feuille *Programming Exercise – 2* (6 exercices sur les
opérateurs `/` et `%`, les casts, `scanf` et le conditional operator) et une
**fiche de révision** des semaines 1 à 6 avant le **midterm (semaine 8)**.

> **En bref.** Presque tous les exercices reposent sur **deux outils** :
> **`n / 10`** enlève le dernier chiffre, **`n % 10`** le garde. Pour
> découper une durée : **quotient** avec `/`, **reste** avec `%`, de la plus
> grande unité à la plus petite. Pour la partie entière d'un réel :
> **`(int) x`**. Pour max / min de trois : `?:` imbriqués.

---

## 1. Les deux briques : `/` et `%` sur les entiers

```diagram
{
  "title": "Sur un entier en base 10 : / 10 décale vers la droite, % 10 garde le chiffre des unités.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "n", "x": 300, "y": 30, "shape": "table", "size": 14, "label": "n = 7395", "header": false, "rows": [["7","3","9","5"]], "cols": [50,50,50,50] },
    { "id": "q", "x": 120, "y": 140, "shape": "table", "size": 14, "label": "n / 10 = 739", "header": false, "rows": [["7","3","9"]], "cols": [50,50,50] },
    { "id": "r", "x": 470, "y": 140, "shape": "table", "size": 14, "label": "n % 10 = 5", "header": false, "rows": [["5"]], "cols": [50] },
    { "id": "q2", "x": 120, "y": 240, "shape": "table", "size": 14, "label": "n / 100 = 73", "header": false, "rows": [["7","3"]], "cols": [50,50] },
    { "id": "r2", "x": 470, "y": 240, "shape": "table", "size": 14, "label": "n % 100 = 95", "header": false, "rows": [["9","5"]], "cols": [50,50] }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "n", "to": "q", "label": "/ 10" }, { "from": "n", "to": "r", "label": "% 10" }
  ]
}
```

| On veut… | Expression | 7395 |
|---|---|---|
| le chiffre des **unités** | `n % 10` | 5 |
| le chiffre des **dizaines** | `(n / 10) % 10` | 9 |
| le chiffre des **centaines** | `(n / 100) % 10` | 3 |
| le chiffre des **milliers** | `n / 1000` | 7 |
| les **deux derniers** chiffres | `n % 100` | 95 |
| tout **sauf le premier** | `n % 1000` | 395 |

## 2. Q1 — jours → années, semaines, jours

```diagram
{
  "title": "On part de la plus grande unité. Exemple : 800 jours (1 an = 365 jours).",
  "nodes": [

    { "id": "y", "x": 250, "y": 30, "w": 150, "label": "years = 800 / 365\n= 2", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "r", "x": 250, "y": 115, "w": 150, "label": "days = 800 % 365\n= 70", "tone": "neutral", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "w", "x": 470, "y": 70, "w": 150, "label": "weeks = 70 / 7\n= 10", "tone": "sky", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "dd", "x": 470, "y": 155, "w": 150, "label": "days = 70 % 7\n= 0", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "o", "x": 650, "y": 110, "w": 120, "label": "2 ans\n10 semaines\n0 jour", "tone": "violet", "filled": true, "bold": true }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "d", "to": "y", "label": "/ 365" }, { "from": "d", "to": "r", "label": "% 365" },
    { "from": "r", "to": "w", "label": "/ 7" }, { "from": "r", "to": "dd", "label": "% 7" },
    { "from": "w", "to": "o" }, { "from": "dd", "to": "o" }
  ]

```

```c
years = days / 365;      days = days % 365;
weeks = days / 7;        days = days % 7;
```

> L'ordre compte : il faut **réutiliser le reste** (`days % 365`) pour
> calculer les semaines, sinon on recompte les années.

## 3. Q2 & Q3 — chiffres de la partie entière d'un réel

```flowchart
{
  "title": "On convertit d'abord le réel en entier avec un cast (troncature), puis on applique % 10.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "s", "kind": "start", "label": "START" },
    { "id": "in", "kind": "io", "label": "READ value  (ex. 1234.567)" },
    { "id": "c", "kind": "process", "label": "integral = (int) value  → 1234" },
    { "id": "u", "kind": "process", "label": "units = integral % 10  → 4" },
    { "id": "t", "kind": "process", "label": "tens = (integral % 100) / 10  → 3" },
    { "id": "o", "kind": "io", "label": "DISPLAY tens, units  → 3 4" },
    { "id": "e", "kind": "end", "label": "END" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "s", "to": "in" }, { "from": "in", "to": "c" }, { "from": "c", "to": "u" },
    { "from": "u", "to": "t" }, { "from": "t", "to": "o" }, { "from": "o", "to": "e" }
  ]
}
```

- `%` est **interdit sur un `float`** : `value % 10` ne compile pas → il faut
  le cast `(int)`.
- Nombre **négatif** : `-1234 % 10` vaut **−4** (signe du dividende) ; on
  prend la valeur absolue si on veut le chiffre.
- Q3 en une seule expression : `integral % 100` → **34**.

## 4. Q4 — afficher un nombre à 4 chiffres « en escalier »

Pour 7395 :

```
7395      ← n
395       ← n % 1000
95        ← n % 100
5         ← n % 10
```

```c
printf("%d\n%d\n%d\n%d\n", n, n % 1000, n % 100, n % 10);
```

> Piège : avec n = 7005, `n % 1000` vaut **5** (pas « 005 »). Pour garder
> les zéros, afficher avec `%03d`, `%02d` : `printf("%03d", n % 1000)` →
> `005`.

## 5. Q5 — somme des chiffres

```c
sum = n / 1000 + (n / 100) % 10 + (n / 10) % 10 + n % 10;
/* 7395 → 7 + 3 + 9 + 5 = 24 */
```

## 6. Q6 — somme, moyenne, plus grand, plus petit

```c
float sum = a + b + c;
float average = sum / 3.0;
float largest  = (a > b) ? ((a > c) ? a : c) : ((b > c) ? b : c);
float smallest = (a < b) ? ((a < c) ? a : c) : ((b < c) ? b : c);
```

```diagram
{
  "title": "Le ?: imbriqué du plus grand de trois, avec a = 4, b = 9, c = 7.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "r", "x": 300, "y": 30, "w": 120, "label": "a > b ?\n4 > 9 : faux", "tone": "violet", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "l", "x": 140, "y": 120, "w": 140, "label": "a > c ? a : c", "tone": "neutral", "size": 12 },
    { "id": "rr", "x": 460, "y": 120, "w": 140, "label": "b > c ?\n9 > 7 : vrai", "tone": "sky", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "b", "x": 400, "y": 210, "w": 80, "label": "b = 9", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "bold": true },
    { "id": "c", "x": 520, "y": 210, "w": 80, "label": "c", "tone": "neutral" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "r", "to": "l", "label": "vrai", "dashed": true }, { "from": "r", "to": "rr", "label": "faux", "bold": true },
    { "from": "rr", "to": "b", "label": "vrai", "bold": true }, { "from": "rr", "to": "c", "label": "faux", "dashed": true }
  ]
}
```

> `sum / 3.0` (et pas `/ 3`) : si `sum` était un `int`, `/ 3` tronquerait la
> moyenne.

---

## 7. Fiche de révision midterm (W1 → W6)

| Semaine | Thème | Ce qui tombe |
|---|---|---|
| **W1** | problem solving, algorithmes, flowcharts | symboles (terminal, I/O parallélogramme, process rectangle, decision losange), compilation → `a.out` |
| **W2** | overview of C, character set, tokens, constants | structure en 6 sections, 1 seul `main`, identifiers valides, octal `0…` / hexa `0x…`, `'5'` vs `5` vs `"5"`, escape sequences |
| **W3** | data types, storage classes, `scanf`, `#define` | tailles (`int` 32 bits, `float` 32 / 6 chiffres, `double` 64 / 14), littéral réel = `double`, `auto` / `static` / `extern` / `register`, `#define` sans `=` ni `;`, 3 types d'erreurs |
| **W4** | operators & expressions | `14/4 = 3`, `14%4 = 2`, `++m` vs `m++`, precedence (`* / %` avant `+ -`), cast `(float)`, conversion hierarchy, `<math.h>` |
| **W5** | I/O formatée, `if` | `getchar` + `\n`, `%2d`, `%*d`, `%[^\n]`, `printf` `%7.2f` / `%-6d` / `%.5s`, `if…else`, dangling else, else if ladder, leap year |
| **W6** | `switch`, `?:`, `goto` | case constants et uniques, `break` / fall through, `default`, `?:`, GCD, `goto label;` |

### Les 12 réflexes du midterm

1. `int / int` **tronque** ; un seul opérande réel suffit pour une division
   réelle.
2. `%` **seulement** entre entiers ; signe = signe du **dividende**.
3. `++x` : incrémente **puis** utilise ; `x++` : utilise **puis** incrémente.
4. `* / %` avant `+ -`, **gauche → droite** ; assignment et `?:` **droite →
   gauche**.
5. Littéral entier → `int` ; littéral réel → `double`.
6. `scanf` : `&`, pas de texte, `%lf` pour `double`, renvoie un **compte**.
7. `printf` : largeur = **minimum** ; précision = décimales (`f`) ou
   caractères (`s`).
8. `static` local garde sa valeur ; `auto` = garbage ; `static`/`extern` = 0.
9. `else` → `if` le plus proche ; pas de `;` après `if (…)`.
10. `switch` : expression **entière**, `case` **constants**, penser au
    `break`.
11. `==` compare, `=` affecte ; ne jamais comparer deux `float` avec `==`.
12. Erreur de **syntaxe** (compilation) / **run-time** (÷ 0) / **logique**
    (aucun message).

int a = 17, b = 5; What is a / b?

exercises.prompt: What is the value of 10 - 6 / 2 + 3 * 2 (int arithmetic)?
int a = 7, b = 2; float r = (float) a / b; What is r?
exercises.explanation: W4 : le cast s'applique à a avant la division, qui devient réelle.

exercises.prompt: In an expression mixing a long int and a double, the result type is:
exercises.explanation: W4 : lower → higher dans la conversion hierarchy.

exercises.prompt: Which operator has the lowest precedence?

exercises.prompt: Which <math.h> function rounds x UP to the nearest integer?
exercises.explanation: W4 : floor arrondit vers le bas.

exercises.prompt: After reading a character with getchar(), why can the next getchar() return immediately?
choices: The newline typed after the character is still in the input queue
exercises.explanation: W5 : un dummy getchar() ou fflush supprime le \n.

exercises.explanation: W5 : %3d lit 3 caractères ; le reste du nombre va au champ suivant.

The most recent unpaired if in the same block
The if with the same indentation

exercises.explanation: W5 : on complémente chaque relation et && devient ||.

exercises.explanation: W5 : divisible par 400 ; 1900 et 2100 sont divisibles par 100 mais pas par 400.

exercises.prompt: Electricity bill: 0–200 units at 0.50, 201–400 units cost 100 + 0.65 × (units − 200). How much for 300 units?
Which type of expression may a switch test?

exercises.prompt: int n = 1; switch (n) { case 1: printf("A"); case 2: printf("B"); break; case 3: printf("C"); } prints:

exercises.explanation: W6 : constantes ou constant expressions uniquement.

exercises.explanation: W6 : backward jump.

What is the sum of the digits of 4321?

lesson:
# Computer Programming — Mid Term (W1–W7) · Plan de révision

Le **midterm** (semaine 8 du syllabus) couvre **tout le cours depuis la
semaine 1**. Cette catégorie mélange des questions de **toutes les leçons** de
Computer Programming dans le style d'un QCM d'examen : chaque réponse se
trouve dans une leçon Week 1 à Week 7.

**Méthode conseillée :**

1. Faire ce quiz une première fois à froid : **Toutes** puis **Aléatoire**.
2. Pour chaque semaine où tu rates des questions, relire la **leçon** (sections
   *Pièges d'exam* et *À retenir*) puis refaire son quiz.
3. **Dérouler à la main** les petits programmes : opérateurs, `printf`,
   `switch` sans `break`.
4. Relire la **fiche midterm de Week 7** (les 12 réflexes) la veille.

---

## La checklist par semaine

| Semaine | Ce qu'il faut savoir sans hésiter |
|---|---|
| **W1** · Problem solving | machine code → assembly → **HLL** (portabilité) ; **edit → compile → link → run** ; CPU = **ALU + CU + registers** ; RAM volatile / ROM non volatile ; system software (OS, **loader**, **linker**, **translator**) ; **algorithm** = fini, non ambigu, indépendant du langage ; constructs **imperative / conditional / iterative** ; symboles de **flowchart** (terminal ovale, **I/O parallélogramme**, **process rectangle**, **decision losange à 2 sorties**, connector cercle) |
| **W2** · Overview & constants | 6 sections, **une seule `main()`** ; `cc` → **`a.out`**, `-o`, **`-lm`** ; character set (4 catégories) ; **tokens** ; 32 **keywords** en minuscules ; **identifiers** (lettre ou `_` d'abord, pas de `-` `$` espace keyword) ; **octal `0…`**, **hexa `0x…`**, suffixes `U L UL` ; exposant **entier** ; `'5'` (53) ≠ `5` ≠ `"5"` ; **escape sequences** |
| **W3** · Types & storage | `int` **32 bits** (16 sur machine 16 bits), `float` 32 / **6** chiffres, `double` 64 / **14** ; littéral réel = **`double`** ; `typedef`, `enum` (0, 1, 2…) ; **`auto`** (garbage) / **`static`** (garde sa valeur, 0) / **`extern`** (global, 0) / **`register`** ; `scanf("%d", &x)` ; `#define` **sans `=` ni `;`** ; `const` / `volatile` ; erreurs **syntax / run-time / logic** |
| **W4** · Operators | `14/4 = 3`, `14%4 = 2`, `%` entiers seulement, signe du **dividende** ; mixed-mode ; **`++m` vs `m++`** ; `v op= exp` ; `?:` ; bitwise (pas sur float) ; comma (plus faible) ; `sizeof` ; precedence `* / %` avant `+ -` ; **conversion hierarchy** ; cast `(float) a / b` ; `<math.h>` (double, radians, `-lm`) |
| **W5** · I/O & if | `getchar` / `putchar`, le **`\n`** qui reste ; `<ctype.h>` ; `scanf` **`%2d`**, **`%*d`**, `%lf`, `%s`, **`%[^\n]`**, **valeur de retour** ; `printf` **`%6d`**, `%-6d`, `%06d`, **`%7.2f`**, **`%.5s`** ; 4 formes de `if` ; **dangling else** ; **De Morgan** ; leap year ; else if ladder (facture) |
| **W6** · switch, ?:, goto | expression **integral**, case **constants uniques**, **`break`** (sinon **fall through**), **un seul `default`** ; switch pour **3 à 10** alternatives ; `?:` (prêt, max de trois) ; **GCD(a, b) = GCD(b, a % b)** ; `goto label;` forward / backward, **boucle infinie** |
| **W7** · Exercise 2 | `/` et `%` pour découper (jours → années / semaines / jours, chiffres d'un nombre) ; `(int)` avant `%` sur un réel ; somme des chiffres ; moyenne `/ 3.0` ; min / max avec `?:` |

## Les sorties à savoir prédire

| Code | Sortie |
|---|---|
| `m = 5; y = ++m;` | y = 6, m = 6 |
| `m = 5; y = m++;` | y = 5, m = 6 |
| `9 - 12/3 + 3*2 - 1` | 10 |
| `(int) 21.3 / (int) 4.5` | 5 |
| `printf("%6d", 9876)` | `··9876` |
| `printf("%7.2f", 98.7654)` | `··98.77` |
| `printf("%.5s", "NEW DELHI 110001")` | `NEW D` |
| `scanf("%2d %5d")` sur `31426 50` | 31 et 426 |
| `switch (2)` sans `break` : cases 1, 2, 3, default | `two three other` |
| `static int d = 10; d = d + 10;` appelée 3 fois | 20, 30, 40 |

name: Week 3
lesson:
# Database Design — Week 3

Lecture 05 — *E-R Diagrams – 2*. Roles, recursive relationship sets, mapping
cardinality, participation constraints, weak entity sets, superclass /
subclass, generalization vs specialization, and a full worked example (the NHL
database).

Lecture 06 — *E-R Diagrams – 3* (sections 9–14). Aggregation, the Hospital
Management System diagram, reducing an E-R diagram to a database schema, the
full symbol summary (arrow cardinalities, total / partial and disjoint /
overlapping specialization), integrity constraints, and ERD exercise 2 (a
university).

---

## 0. The symbols, all in one place

```er
{
  "title": "E-R diagram symbols (Chen notation, as used in the course).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "e", "kind": "entity", "label": "Strong entity set", "x": 130, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "w", "kind": "weak_entity", "label": "Weak entity set", "x": 130, "y": 115 },
    { "id": "r", "kind": "relationship", "label": "Strong relationship", "x": 130, "y": 205 },
    { "id": "ir", "kind": "identifying_relationship", "label": "Weak relationship", "x": 130, "y": 300 },
    { "id": "isa", "kind": "isa", "label": "ISA", "x": 130, "y": 385 },
    { "id": "a", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Simple attribute", "x": 450, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "k", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "Key attribute", "x": 450, "y": 105 },
    { "id": "pk", "kind": "partial_key_attribute", "label": "Partial key (discriminator)", "x": 450, "y": 170 },
    { "id": "m", "kind": "multi_attribute", "label": "Multivalued attribute", "x": 450, "y": 240 },
    { "id": "d", "kind": "derived_attribute", "label": "Derived attribute", "x": 450, "y": 310 },
    { "id": "c", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Composite attribute", "x": 450, "y": 375 },
    { "id": "c1", "kind": "attribute", "label": "part 1", "x": 380, "y": 440 },
    { "id": "c2", "kind": "attribute", "label": "part 2", "x": 520, "y": 440 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "c", "to": "c1" }, { "from": "c", "to": "c2" }
  ]
}
```

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| rectangle | strong entity set (has its own primary key) |
| **double** rectangle | **weak** entity set (no primary key of its own) |
| diamond | relationship set |
| **double** diamond | **identifying** (weak) relationship, tying a weak entity to its strong entity |
| oval | attribute; **underlined** = key attribute; **dashed underline** = discriminator; **double** oval = multivalued; **dashed** oval = derived; oval with sub-ovals = composite |
| triangle "ISA" | superclass / subclass link (generalization, specialization) |
| single line | (partial) participation of an entity set in a relationship |
| **double** line | **total** participation |
| `1` / `N` on a line | mapping cardinality |

## 1. Role names

**Roles** are indicated by **labelling the lines** that connect a diamond
(relationship) to a rectangle (entity). Role labels are **optional**; they are
used to clarify the **semantics** (meaning) of the relationship — especially
when the same entity set appears twice.

```er
{
  "title": "Faculty takes part in Reports_To twice, once as Coordinator and once as Head: the two labels are roles.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "f", "kind": "entity", "label": "Faculty", "x": 200, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "id", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "EmpID", "x": 100, "y": 60 },
    { "id": "nm", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Name", "x": 270, "y": 50 },
    { "id": "br", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Branch", "x": 100, "y": 270 },
    { "id": "ex", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Experience", "x": 280, "y": 280 },
    { "id": "r", "kind": "relationship", "label": "Reports_To", "x": 520, "y": 160 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "f", "to": "id" }, { "from": "f", "to": "nm" }, { "from": "f", "to": "br" }, { "from": "f", "to": "ex" },
    { "from": "f", "to": "r", "role": "Coordinator" },
    { "from": "f", "to": "r", "role": "Head" }
  ]
}
```

The labels *Coordinator* and *Head* specify **which Faculty entities interact
with which** via the `Reports_To` relationship set.

## 2. Recursive relationship set

When **the same entity set participates in a relationship set more than
once**, the relationship set is **recursive**. `Reports_To` above is recursive:
both of its ends are `Faculty`.

```er
{
  "title": "Faculty works in a Department (ordinary binary relationship) and Faculty reports to Faculty (recursive relationship set).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "f", "kind": "entity", "label": "Faculty", "x": 160, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "fi", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "FacID", "x": 60, "y": 60 },
    { "id": "fn", "kind": "attribute", "label": "FName", "x": 220, "y": 50 },
    { "id": "po", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Post", "x": 40, "y": 260 },
    { "id": "w", "kind": "relationship", "label": "Works", "x": 380, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "d", "kind": "entity", "label": "Department", "x": 590, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "di", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "DeptID", "x": 520, "y": 60 },
    { "id": "dn", "kind": "attribute", "label": "DName", "x": 660, "y": 60 },
    { "id": "rr", "kind": "relationship", "label": "Reports_To", "x": 160, "y": 330 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "f", "to": "fi" }, { "from": "f", "to": "fn" }, { "from": "f", "to": "po" },
    { "from": "f", "to": "w" }, { "from": "w", "to": "d" },
    { "from": "d", "to": "di" }, { "from": "d", "to": "dn" },
    { "from": "f", "to": "rr", "role": "HOD" },
    { "from": "f", "to": "rr", "role": "Prof." }
  ]
}
```

With data, the recursion is obvious: a professor's *head* is another row of the
same `Faculty` table.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Instances: Lee and Kim (professors) report to David (HOD) — all three are Faculty rows.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "f", "x": 160, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Faculty", "rows": [["FName","Post"],["Lee","Professor"],["Kim","Professor"],["David","HOD"]], "mark": [3] },
    { "id": "d", "x": 500, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Department", "rows": [["DName"],["Computer"],["Civil"],["Mechanical"]] },
    { "id": "n", "x": 160, "y": 175, "w": 260, "h": 34, "shape": "note", "size": 12, "label": "Reports_To: Lee → David, Kim → David", "tone": "amber" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "n", "to": "f", "tone": "amber", "dashed": true }
  ]
}
```

## 3. Mapping cardinality (cardinality constraints)

The mapping cardinality represents **the number of entities of another entity
set that can be connected to one entity through a relationship set**. It is
most useful for describing **binary** relationship sets, where it must be one
of four types. The examples use `customer` —`borrow`— `loan`.

### One-to-one (1 – 1)

An entity in A is associated with **only one** entity in B, and an entity in B
is associated with **only one** entity in A.

```diagram
{
  "title": "1 – 1: each customer holds one loan and each loan belongs to one customer.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "ha", "x": 80, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "customer", "bold": true },
    { "id": "hb", "x": 240, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "loan", "bold": true },
    { "id": "sa", "x": 80, "y": 110, "w": 64, "h": 150, "shape": "ellipse" },
    { "id": "sb", "x": 240, "y": 110, "w": 64, "h": 150, "shape": "ellipse" },
    { "id": "c1", "x": 80, "y": 70, "shape": "text", "label": "C1" }, { "id": "c2", "x": 80, "y": 110, "shape": "text", "label": "C2" }, { "id": "c3", "x": 80, "y": 150, "shape": "text", "label": "C3" },
    { "id": "l1", "x": 240, "y": 70, "shape": "text", "label": "L1" }, { "id": "l2", "x": 240, "y": 110, "shape": "text", "label": "L2" }, { "id": "l3", "x": 240, "y": 150, "shape": "text", "label": "L3" },
    { "id": "e1", "x": 400, "y": 110, "w": 100, "label": "customer", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "r", "x": 540, "y": 110, "shape": "diamond", "label": "borrow", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "e2", "x": 680, "y": 110, "w": 100, "label": "loan", "tone": "sky" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "c1", "to": "l1", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "c2", "to": "l2", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "c3", "to": "l3", "arrow": "none" },
    { "from": "e1", "to": "r", "arrow": "none", "label": "1", "bold": true },
    { "from": "r", "to": "e2", "arrow": "none", "label": "1", "bold": true }
  ]
}
```

### One-to-many (1 – N)

An entity in A is associated with **more than one** entity in B, and an entity
in B is associated with **only one** entity in A. *A loan is connected with only
one customer, but a customer may hold several loans.*

```diagram
{
  "title": "1 – N: a customer may hold several loans; each loan has a single customer.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "ha", "x": 80, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "customer", "bold": true },
    { "id": "hb", "x": 240, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "loan", "bold": true },
    { "id": "sa", "x": 80, "y": 120, "w": 64, "h": 150, "shape": "ellipse" },
    { "id": "sb", "x": 240, "y": 120, "w": 64, "h": 180, "shape": "ellipse" },
    { "id": "c1", "x": 80, "y": 80, "shape": "text", "label": "C1" }, { "id": "c2", "x": 80, "y": 120, "shape": "text", "label": "C2" }, { "id": "c3", "x": 80, "y": 160, "shape": "text", "label": "C3" },
    { "id": "l1", "x": 240, "y": 66, "shape": "text", "label": "L1" }, { "id": "l2", "x": 240, "y": 102, "shape": "text", "label": "L2" }, { "id": "l3", "x": 240, "y": 138, "shape": "text", "label": "L3" }, { "id": "l4", "x": 240, "y": 174, "shape": "text", "label": "L4" },
    { "id": "e1", "x": 400, "y": 120, "w": 100, "label": "customer", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "r", "x": 540, "y": 120, "shape": "diamond", "label": "borrow", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "e2", "x": 680, "y": 120, "w": 100, "label": "loan", "tone": "sky" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "c1", "to": "l1", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "c1", "to": "l2", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "c2", "to": "l3", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "c3", "to": "l4", "arrow": "none" },
    { "from": "e1", "to": "r", "arrow": "none", "label": "1", "bold": true },
    { "from": "r", "to": "e2", "arrow": "none", "label": "N", "bold": true }
  ]
}
```

### Many-to-one (N – 1)

An entity in A is associated with **only one** entity in B, and an entity in B
is associated with **more than one** entity in A. *A loan is connected with
more than one customer (a joint loan), but a customer holds only one loan.*

```diagram
{
  "title": "N – 1: several customers can share one loan; each customer holds a single loan.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "ha", "x": 80, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "customer", "bold": true },
    { "id": "hb", "x": 240, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "loan", "bold": true },
    { "id": "sa", "x": 80, "y": 120, "w": 64, "h": 180, "shape": "ellipse" },
    { "id": "sb", "x": 240, "y": 120, "w": 64, "h": 150, "shape": "ellipse" },
    { "id": "c1", "x": 80, "y": 66, "shape": "text", "label": "C1" }, { "id": "c2", "x": 80, "y": 102, "shape": "text", "label": "C2" }, { "id": "c3", "x": 80, "y": 138, "shape": "text", "label": "C3" }, { "id": "c4", "x": 80, "y": 174, "shape": "text", "label": "C4" },
    { "id": "l1", "x": 240, "y": 80, "shape": "text", "label": "L1" }, { "id": "l2", "x": 240, "y": 120, "shape": "text", "label": "L2" }, { "id": "l3", "x": 240, "y": 160, "shape": "text", "label": "L3" },
    { "id": "e1", "x": 400, "y": 120, "w": 100, "label": "customer", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "r", "x": 540, "y": 120, "shape": "diamond", "label": "borrow", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "e2", "x": 680, "y": 120, "w": 100, "label": "loan", "tone": "sky" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "c1", "to": "l1", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "c2", "to": "l1", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "c3", "to": "l2", "arrow": "none" }, { "from": "c4", "to": "l3", "arrow": "none" },
    { "from": "e1", "to": "r", "arrow": "none", "label": "N", "bold": true },
    { "from": "r", "to": "e2", "arrow": "none", "label": "1", "bold": true }
  ]
}
```

### Many-to-many (N – N)

An entity in A is associated with **more than one** entity in B, and an entity
in B is associated with **more than one** entity in A. *A customer holds
several loans and a loan can be shared by several customers.*

```diagram
{
  "title": "N – N: customers hold several loans and loans are shared by several customers.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "ha", "x": 80, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "customer", "bold": true },
    { "id": "hb", "x": 240, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "loan", "bold": true },
    { "id": "sa", "x": 80, "y": 120, "w": 64, "h": 180, "shape": "ellipse" },
    { "id": "sb", "x": 240, "y": 120, "w": 64, "h": 180, "shape": "ellipse" },
    { "id": "c1", "x": 80, "y": 66, "shape": "text", "label": "C1" }, { "id": "c2", "x": 80, "y": 102, "shape": "text", "label": "C2" }, { "id": "c3", "x": 80, "y": 138, "shape": "text", "label": "C3" }, { "id": "c4", "x": 80, "y": 174, "shape": "text", "label": "C4" },
    { "id": "l1", "x": 240, "y": 66, "shape": "text", "label": "L1" }, { "id": "l2", "x": 240, "y": 102, "shape": "text", "label": "L2" }, { "id": "l3", "x": 240, "y": 138, "shape": "text", "label": "L3" }, { "id": "l4", "x": 240, "y": 174, "shape": "text", "label": "L4" },
    { "id": "e1", "x": 400, "y": 120, "w": 100, "label": "customer", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "r", "x": 540, "y": 120, "shape": "diamond", "label": "borrow", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "e2", "x": 680, "y": 120, "w": 100, "label": "loan", "tone": "sky" }
```

## 4. Participation constraints

A participation constraint specifies **the participation of an entity set in a
relationship set**. Two kinds:

| Kind | Meaning | Drawn as |
|---|---|---|
| **Partial participation** | **some** entities of the set may **not participate** in any relationship of the set | **single line** |
| **Total participation** | **every** entity of the set participates in **at least one** relationship of the set | **double line** |

## 5. Weak entity sets

An entity set that **does not have a primary key** is called a **weak entity
set**. Its existence **depends on the existence of a strong entity set**.

```er
{
  "title": "loan (strong entity set) — L_P (weak / identifying relationship, double diamond) — payment (weak entity set, double rectangle). payment-no is the discriminator (dashed underline).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "l", "kind": "entity", "label": "loan", "x": 150, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "ln", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "loan-no", "x": 70, "y": 50 },
    { "id": "am", "kind": "attribute", "label": "amount", "x": 210, "y": 50 },
    { "id": "lp", "kind": "identifying_relationship", "label": "L_P", "x": 350, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "p", "kind": "weak_entity", "label": "payment", "x": 560, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "pn", "kind": "partial_key_attribute", "label": "payment-no", "x": 450, "y": 50 },
    { "id": "pd", "kind": "attribute", "label": "payment-date", "x": 600, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "pa", "kind": "attribute", "label": "payment-amount", "x": 620, "y": 270 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "l", "to": "ln" }, { "from": "l", "to": "am" },
    { "from": "l", "to": "lp", "card": "1" },
    { "from": "lp", "to": "p", "card": "N", "total": true },
    { "from": "p", "to": "pn" }, { "from": "p", "to": "pd" }, { "from": "p", "to": "pa" }
  ]
}
```

- Drawn as a **double rectangle**; the relationship that ties it to its strong
  entity (the **weak entity relationship**, or identifying relationship) is a
  **double diamond**.
- The **discriminator** (**partial key**) of a weak entity set is the set of
  attributes that distinguishes all the entities of the weak entity set *among
  those attached to the same strong entity*. It is underlined with a **dashed
  line**.
- The **primary key** of a weak entity set = **primary key of the strong entity
  set** it depends on **+ its own discriminator**.
- Example: `payment` has `payment-no` as discriminator; `loan` has `loan-no` as
  primary key; so the primary key of `payment` is **(loan-no, payment-no)**.
  Payment n° 1 of loan 17 and payment n° 1 of loan 42 are two different
  payments — `payment-no` alone cannot tell them apart.
- A weak entity always participates **totally** in its identifying relationship
  (a payment cannot exist without its loan), hence the double line on the
  `payment` side.

## 6. Superclass vs subclass

| Super class | Sub class |
|---|---|
| an entity from which **other entities can be derived** | an entity that is **derived from another entity** |
| `Account` has two subsets, `Saving_Account` and `Current_Account`, so `Account` is a superclass | `Saving_Account` and `Current_Account` are derived from `Account`, so they are subclasses |

```er
{
  "title": "Account is the superclass; Saving_Account and Current_Account are its subclasses, linked through the ISA triangle.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "a", "kind": "entity", "label": "Account", "x": 330, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "isa", "kind": "isa", "label": "ISA", "x": 330, "y": 130 },
    { "id": "s", "kind": "entity", "label": "Saving_Account", "x": 180, "y": 230 },
    { "id": "c", "kind": "entity", "label": "Current_Account", "x": 480, "y": 230 }

  ]
}
```

A subclass **inherits** all the attributes of its superclass and adds its own.

## 7. Generalization vs specialization

Both produce the **same picture** — a superclass above an ISA triangle,
subclasses below — but they are built in **opposite directions**.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Generalization builds the superclass bottom-up from common features; specialization splits a superclass top-down into subsets.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "h1", "x": 160, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "Generalization — bottom-up", "bold": true },
    { "id": "h2", "x": 500, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "Specialization — top-down", "bold": true },
    { "id": "g1", "x": 160, "y": 60, "w": 200, "h": 40, "label": "Person\n(Name, Address)", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "g2", "x": 80, "y": 200, "w": 130, "h": 40, "label": "Student\n(Name, Address, SPI)", "tone": "sky", "size": 11 },
    { "id": "g3", "x": 240, "y": 200, "w": 140, "h": 40, "label": "Faculty\n(Name, Address, Salary)", "tone": "sky", "size": 11 },
    { "id": "gn", "x": 160, "y": 245, "shape": "text", "label": "↑ extract the common features", "size": 11 },
    { "id": "s1", "x": 500, "y": 60, "w": 200, "h": 40, "label": "Person\n(Name, Address)", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "s2", "x": 420, "y": 200, "w": 130, "h": 40, "label": "Student\n(+ SPI)", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "size": 11 },
    { "id": "s3", "x": 580, "y": 200, "w": 130, "h": 40, "label": "Faculty\n(+ Salary)", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "size": 11 },
    { "id": "sn", "x": 500, "y": 245, "shape": "text", "label": "↓ split by distinguishing features", "size": 11 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "g2", "to": "g1", "tone": "emerald" }, { "from": "g3", "to": "g1", "tone": "emerald" },
    { "from": "s1", "to": "s2", "tone": "emerald" }, { "from": "s1", "to": "s3", "tone": "emerald" }
  ]
}
```

| | Generalization | Specialization |
|---|---|---|
| definition | **extracts the common features of multiple entities to form a new entity** | **splits an entity to form multiple new entities that inherit some feature of the splitting entity** |
| process | creation of a **group** from various entities | creation of **sub-groups** within an entity |
| approach | **bottom-up** | **top-down** |
| set operation | takes the **union** of two or more **lower-level** entity sets to produce a **higher-level** entity set | takes a **subset** of a **higher-level** entity set to form a **lower-level** entity set |
| starting point | starts from **several** entity sets and creates a high-level entity set using their **common** features | starts from a **single** entity set and creates different low-level entity sets using **different** features |

Example from the slides: `Student(Name, Address, SPI)` and `Faculty(Name,
Address, Salary)` share `Name` and `Address` → generalize into `Person(Name,
Address)`; conversely, `Person` specializes into `Student` (adds `SPI`) and
`Faculty` (adds `Salary`).

## 8. Worked example — the NHL database

> The NHL has many **teams**; each team has a name, a city, a coach, a captain
> and a set of players. Each **player** belongs to only one team; a player has a
> name, a position (left wing, goalie…), a skill level and a set of **injury
> records**. A team captain is also a player. A **game** is played between two
> teams (host team and guest team) and has a date and a score. Construct a
> clean and concise E-R diagram.

Method — the same five steps for any description:

1. **Entities** (nouns that have their own data): team, player, game, injury
   record → rectangles.
2. **Attributes** for each, and the **primary key** underlined. An injury
   record has no key of its own — it only makes sense for a given player →
   **weak entity** with a discriminator.
3. **Relationships** (verbs): a player *belongs to* a team; a team *has a
   captain*; a game is *hosted by* a team and *visited by* a team; a player
   *logs* injury records.
4. **Roles** where one entity plays two parts in one relationship (a team is
   `host` in one game and `guest` in another).
5. **Cardinality and participation** on every line.
