## 9. Aggregation

**Limitation of the E-R model:** a relationship connects **entities**, never
other relationships. *In the E-R model we cannot express relationships between
two relationships.*

```diagram
{
  "title": "The problem: Borrow would have to connect to the Works relationship itself — not allowed.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "comp", "x": 330, "y": 40, "w": 120, "label": "Company", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "emp", "x": 110, "y": 130, "w": 120, "label": "Employee", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "works", "x": 330, "y": 130, "shape": "diamond", "label": "Works", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "dept", "x": 550, "y": 130, "w": 120, "label": "Department", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "borrow", "x": 330, "y": 250, "shape": "diamond", "label": "Borrow", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "loan", "x": 330, "y": 340, "w": 120, "label": "Loan", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "n", "x": 560, "y": 200, "w": 250, "h": 34, "shape": "note", "size": 12, "label": "✗ cannot connect two relationships", "tone": "rose" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "comp", "to": "works", "arrow": "none" },
    { "from": "emp", "to": "works", "arrow": "none" },
```

The fix is **aggregation**: treat the whole `Employee — Works — Company —

and connect `Borrow` to that box.

> **Aggregation** = the process of creating an entity by **combining various
> components of an E-R diagram** (entities + a relationship) into one
> abstract entity, so that it can take part in another relationship.

## 11. Reducing an E-R diagram to a database schema

Turning the diagram into **tables** follows five steps.

| Step | E-R element | Becomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Entity** + simple attributes | **one table**; each attribute (except multivalued) is a column; the key attribute is the **primary key** (underlined) |
| 2 | **Multivalued** attribute | a **new table** with its own PK + the parent's PK as **foreign key**; 1:N between the two tables |
| 3 | **1 : 1** relationship | both entities → tables; put the PK of **either** table into the other as FK |
| 4 | **1 : N** relationship | both entities → tables; the PK of the **"1" side** goes as FK into the **"N" side** |
| 5 | **N : N** relationship | both entities → tables **+ a separate table for the relationship**, holding the PKs of both as FKs |

Convention from the slides: every table should **start with its primary key**,
named `TablenameID`.

### Steps 1 and 2 — entity and multivalued attribute

`Person` has `PersonID` (key), `Name`, `Address`, `City` and a **multivalued**
`PhoneNo` (one person, several phones).

```diagram
{
  "title": "PhoneNo cannot be a column of Person (several values) → its own table, linked by the foreign key PersonID.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "p", "x": 150, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Person", "rows": [["PersonID","Name","Address","City"],["1","Lee","12 Inha-ro","Incheon"],["2","Kim","5 Gangnam","Seoul"]], "cols": [70, 50, 80, 60] },
    { "id": "ph", "x": 520, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "emerald", "label": "PhoneNo", "rows": [["PhoneID","PersonID","PhoneNo"],["1","1","010-1111"],["2","1","010-2222"],["3","2","010-3333"]], "cols": [60, 70, 80] }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "ph", "to": "p", "label": "FK PersonID (N : 1)", "tone": "emerald" }
  ]
}
```

Schema: `Person (PersonID, Name, Address, City)` and
`PhoneNo (PhoneID, PersonID, PhoneNo)`.

### Step 3 — 1 : 1

`Person —Having— Wife`, one-to-one. Either choice is correct:

- `Person (PersonID, PName)` and `Wife (WifeID, WName, PersonID)` — **or**
- `Wife (WifeID, WName)` and `Person (PersonID, PName, WifeID)`.

### Step 4 — 1 : N

`Person —Having— House`: a person owns many houses, a house has one owner. The
FK goes on the **many** side:

`Person (PersonID, PName)` and `House (HouseID, HName, PersonID)`.

(Putting `HouseID` in `Person` would need several values in one cell — that is
why the FK always goes to the "N" side.)

### Step 5 — N : N

`Customer —Has_Acct— Account`, many-to-many: a **third table** is created for
the relationship.

```diagram
{
  "title": "N : N → the relationship becomes its own table, holding the primary keys of both entities as foreign keys.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "c", "x": 110, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Customer", "rows": [["CID","CName"],["C1","Lee"],["C2","Kim"]] },
    { "id": "h", "x": 340, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "amber", "label": "Has_Acct", "rows": [["HasAcctID","CID","ActNo"],["1","C1","A1"],["2","C1","A2"],["3","C2","A2"]] },
    { "id": "a", "x": 570, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Account", "rows": [["ActNo","Balance"],["A1","500"],["A2","1200"]] }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "h", "to": "c", "label": "FK CID", "tone": "amber" },
    { "from": "h", "to": "a", "label": "FK ActNo", "tone": "amber" }
  ]
}
```

Schema: `Customer (CID, CName)`, `Account (ActNo, Balance)`,
`Has_Acct (HasAcctID, CID, ActNo)`. Account A2 is shared by Lee and Kim; Lee
holds A1 and A2 — exactly what N : N needs.

## 12. Summary of the E-R symbols (Lecture 06 additions)

Section 0 lists the shapes. Lecture 06 adds two notations.

**Cardinality with arrows** — an **arrow points towards the "one" side**:

| Drawing | Cardinality |
|---|---|
| `E ←— R —→ E` (arrows on both sides) | **one to one** |
| `E ←— R ——— E` (arrow on the left only) | **one to many** (left = one) |
| `E ——— R —→ E` (arrow on the right only) | **many to one** (right = one) |
| `E ——— R ——— E` (no arrow) | **many to many** |

**Constraints on an ISA (specialization / generalization):**

| Mark | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **double line** above ISA | **total** specialization | every superclass entity belongs to **at least one** subclass |
| single line above ISA | **partial** specialization | a superclass entity may belong to **no** subclass |
| label **Disjoint** | **disjoint** | an entity belongs to **at most one** subclass |
| label **Overlapping** | **overlapping** | an entity can belong to **several** subclasses at once |

Examples: `Patient` → `Indoor` / `Outdoor` is disjoint (a stay is one or the
other). `Person` → `Student` / `Employee` is overlapping (a working student is
both). `Account` → `Saving` / `Current` is total if every account must be one
of the two.

## 13. Integrity constraints

**Integrity constraints** are a **set of rules** used to **maintain the quality
of information**: inserts, updates and other operations must not break data
integrity. They **guard against accidental damage** to the database.

| Constraint | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Check** | a **business rule** on a column: every row must satisfy it; limits values to a set, a **range** or a list; on one or several columns | `SPI` must be between 0 and 10 |
| **Not null** | every row must have a **definite value**; NULL is not allowed | `name` must have a value |
| **Unique** | values are **distinct** in each row; **NULL is allowed**, duplicates are not | `enrollmentno` must be unique |
| **Primary key** | column(s) that **uniquely identify each row**; **Primary key = Unique + Not null** | `enrollmentno` unique and never null |
| **Foreign key** (**referential integrity**) | between two tables: every FK value in table 1 must be **NULL or present in the PK column** of table 2 | `Student.DeptID` must exist in `Department.DeptID` |

```diagram
{
  "title": "Referential integrity: each DeptID in Student must be NULL or exist in Department.DeptID. Inserting a student with DeptID = 3 would be rejected.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "d", "x": 140, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Department", "rows": [["DeptID","Dept_Name","HOD"],["1","Computer","Lee"],["2","IT","Kim"]] },
    { "id": "s", "x": 490, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "emerald", "label": "Student", "rows": [["RollNo","Student_Name","DeptID"],["101","Jacob","1"],["102","Alex","2"]] }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "s", "to": "d", "label": "Foreign key DeptID", "tone": "emerald" }
  ]
}
```

The key difference to remember: **Unique accepts NULL, Primary key does not.**

| `Enrols (sid, courseno, secno, year, semester, grade)` | N : N → own table, carries the relationship attribute `grade` |
| `Teaches (iid, courseno, secno, year, semester)` | N : N → own table |
| `Requires (maincourse, prerequisite)` | recursive N : N on Course → two FKs to `Course.courseno` |

## To remember

- **Role** = label on a line, needed when the same entity set takes part twice
  in one relationship (**recursive** relationship set).
- **Mapping cardinality** of a binary relationship: **1:1, 1:N, N:1, N:N** —
  the `1`/`N` on one side says how many of *that* side one entity of the other
  side can have.
- **Participation**: single line = **partial** (some entities may not take
  part), double line = **total** (every entity takes part).
- **Weak entity set** = no primary key of its own; **double rectangle**, tied
  by a **double diamond** (identifying relationship); **discriminator** with a
  **dashed underline**; primary key = strong key + discriminator.
- **Superclass / subclass** linked through the **ISA** triangle; the subclass
  inherits the superclass's attributes.
- **Generalization = bottom-up** (union of lower-level sets into one
  higher-level set, from common features); **specialization = top-down**
  (subsets of a higher-level set, from distinguishing features).
- Method for any statement: entities → attributes & keys → relationships →
  roles → cardinality & participation.
- **Aggregation** = wrapping entities + their relationship into one abstract
  entity, because a relationship **cannot connect to another relationship**.
- **E-R → schema**: entity → table; multivalued attribute → new table with an
  FK; **1:1** → PK of either side as FK in the other; **1:N** → PK of the
  **one** side as FK in the **many** side; **N:N** → a **separate
  relationship table** holding both PKs.
- **Arrow notation**: the arrow points to the **one** side; no arrow = many.
- **ISA constraints**: double line = **total**, single = **partial**;
  **disjoint** = at most one subclass, **overlapping** = several.
- **Integrity constraints**: Check, Not null, Unique, Primary key (**= Unique +
  Not null**), Foreign key (**referential integrity**: FK value is NULL or
  exists in the referenced PK).

questions.question_text: What is a role, in an E-R diagram?
questions.choice_a: The primary key of an entity
questions.choice_b: A label on the line connecting a relationship to an entity, clarifying how that entity participates
questions.choice_c: A synonym for the relationship's name
questions.choice_d: The cardinality written on a line
questions.explanation: Roles are indicated by labeling the lines that connect diamonds (relationship) to rectangles (entity); they clarify semantics and are optional.

questions.question_text: In the Faculty — Reports_To example, 'Coordinator' and 'Head' are examples of what?
questions.choice_a: Two different entity sets
questions.choice_b: Role names on the same recursive relationship
questions.choice_c: Two separate primary keys
questions.choice_d: Weak entity discriminators
questions.explanation: Coordinator and Head are role labels: they specify which Faculty entities interact with whom via the Reports_To relationship set.

questions.question_text: What makes a relationship set 'recursive'?
questions.choice_a: It has more than one attribute
questions.choice_b: The same entity set participates in the relationship set more than once
questions.choice_c: It connects three or more different entity sets
questions.choice_d: It has no cardinality constraint
questions.explanation: A recursive relationship set is one where the same entity participates in the relationship more than once, e.g. Faculty reporting to another Faculty.

questions.question_text: What does mapping cardinality describe?
questions.choice_a: The number of attributes an entity has
questions.choice_b: The number of entities of another set connected to an entity via a relationship set
questions.choice_c: Whether an entity set is weak or strong
questions.choice_d: The physical storage size of a table
questions.explanation: Mapping cardinality is most useful for describing binary relationship sets, and comes in four types: 1:1, 1:N, N:1, N:N.

questions.question_text: A customer holds exactly one loan, and that loan belongs to exactly one customer. What mapping cardinality is this?
questions.choice_a: One-to-many
questions.choice_b: Many-to-one
questions.choice_c: One-to-one
questions.choice_d: Many-to-many
questions.explanation: Both sides are restricted to exactly one: an entity in A is associated with only one entity in B and vice versa, which is 1:1.

questions.question_text: A loan is connected with more than one customer, and a customer is connected with only one loan. What mapping cardinality is this (from loan's perspective toward customer)?
questions.choice_a: One-to-one
questions.choice_b: Many-to-one
questions.choice_c: Many-to-many
questions.choice_d: One-to-many
questions.explanation: An entity in A (loan) is associated with more than one entity in B (customer), and each B is associated with only one A: that is one-to-many for loan-to-customer.

questions.question_text: In a many-to-many (N-N) relationship between customer and loan, what holds?
questions.choice_a: A customer can have only one loan and a loan only one customer
questions.choice_b: A customer can be connected with more than one loan, and a loan can be connected with more than one customer
questions.choice_c: Only customers can have multiple connections, loans cannot
questions.choice_d: N-N relationships are not allowed between binary entity sets
questions.explanation: Many-to-many means both sides can connect to more than one entity of the other set.

questions.question_text: What do participation constraints specify?
questions.choice_a: The maximum number of attributes an entity can have
questions.choice_b: The participation of an entity set in a relationship set: whether every entity must take part
questions.choice_c: The order in which relationships are drawn
questions.choice_d: Which entity set is the primary key holder
questions.explanation: Participation constraints describe whether every entity in a set participates in at least one relationship (total) or not (partial).

questions.question_text: How is total participation represented on an E-R diagram?
questions.choice_a: A dashed line
questions.choice_b: A single line
questions.choice_c: A double line
questions.choice_d: An arrow
questions.explanation: Total participation, where every entity in the set participates in at least one relationship, is drawn with a double line.

questions.question_text: How is partial participation represented on an E-R diagram?
questions.choice_a: A double line
questions.choice_b: A single line
questions.choice_c: A dotted oval
questions.choice_d: A double diamond
questions.explanation: Partial participation, where some entities may not participate in any relationship, is drawn with a single line.

questions.question_text: What is a weak entity set?
questions.choice_a: An entity set with fewer than three attributes
questions.choice_b: An entity set that does not have a primary key of its own
questions.choice_c: An entity set that only appears in recursive relationships
questions.choice_d: An entity set with no relationships at all
questions.explanation: A weak entity set is defined as an entity set that does not have a primary key; its identity depends on a strong entity set.

questions.question_text: What is a weak entity set's discriminator?
questions.choice_a: Its full primary key
questions.choice_b: The set of attributes that distinguishes all the entities of the weak entity set
questions.choice_c: A foreign key pointing at the strong entity
questions.choice_d: The relationship diamond connecting it to the strong entity
questions.explanation: The discriminator (partial key) is the attribute set that distinguishes the weak entity's own entities; it is not, by itself, a full primary key.

questions.question_text: How do you form the actual primary key of a weak entity set?
questions.choice_a: Use the discriminator alone
questions.choice_b: Combine the primary key of the identifying strong entity set with the weak entity's discriminator
questions.choice_c: Use the relationship's name as the key
questions.choice_d: Weak entity sets never have a usable primary key
questions.explanation: The primary key of a weak entity set is created by combining the identifying strong entity set's primary key with the weak entity's own discriminator, e.g. (loan-no, payment-no).

questions.question_text: How is the discriminator attribute of a weak entity set underlined?
questions.choice_a: With a solid line, exactly like an ordinary primary key
questions.choice_b: With a dashed line
questions.choice_c: It is never underlined
questions.choice_d: With a double line
questions.explanation: The discriminator (partial key) is underlined with a dashed line, distinguishing it visually from a full, solid-underlined primary key.

questions.question_text: How is a weak entity set itself drawn on the diagram?
questions.choice_a: As a diamond
questions.choice_b: As a single rectangle
questions.choice_c: As a double rectangle
questions.choice_d: As a dashed oval
questions.explanation: A weak entity set is indicated by a double rectangle; the identifying relationship that ties it to its strong entity is a double diamond.

questions.question_text: If `account` is an entity with two subsets `saving_account` and `current_account`, which is the superclass?
questions.choice_a: saving_account
questions.choice_b: current_account
questions.choice_c: account
questions.choice_d: None of them, superclasses do not apply here
questions.explanation: account is the superclass: another entity (saving_account, current_account) can be derived from it. Those two are the subclasses.

questions.question_text: What is the process of extracting the common features of multiple entities to form one new, higher-level entity called?
questions.choice_a: Specialization
questions.choice_b: Generalization
questions.choice_c: Normalization
questions.choice_d: Weak entity resolution
questions.explanation: Generalization extracts the common features of multiple entities to form a new (higher-level) entity, using a bottom-up approach.

questions.question_text: What is the process of splitting one entity into multiple new entities that each inherit some of its features called?
questions.choice_a: Generalization
questions.choice_b: Specialization
questions.choice_c: Weak entity discrimination
questions.choice_d: Recursive relationship resolution
questions.explanation: Specialization splits an entity to form new entities that inherit some of its features, using a top-down approach.

questions.question_text: Generalization takes the union of two or more lower-level entity sets to produce a higher-level entity set. What approach is this?
questions.choice_a: Top-down
questions.choice_b: Bottom-up
questions.choice_c: Left-to-right
questions.choice_d: Depth-first
questions.explanation: Generalization starts from a number of entity sets and builds a high-level entity set using common features: a bottom-up approach.

questions.question_text: Specialization takes a subset of a higher-level entity set to form a lower-level entity set. What approach is this?
questions.choice_a: Bottom-up
questions.choice_b: Top-down
questions.choice_c: Breadth-first
questions.choice_d: Recursive
questions.explanation: Specialization starts from a single entity set and creates different low-level entity sets using distinguishing features: a top-down approach.

questions.question_text: In an ISA hierarchy such as Person — ISA — {Student, Faculty}, what does the ISA triangle represent?
questions.choice_a: A weak entity relationship
questions.choice_b: A generalization/specialization link between a superclass and its subclasses
questions.choice_c: A cardinality constraint of many-to-many
questions.choice_d: A recursive relationship set
questions.explanation: The ISA triangle is the notation for a generalization/specialization hierarchy: Student and Faculty are subclasses derived from the Person superclass.

exercises.explanation: Total participation (every entity of the set must appear in the relationship) is drawn with a double line; partial participation uses a single line.

exercises.prompt: What kind of entity set has no primary key of its own and depends on a strong entity set for its identity?
exercises.explanation: A weak entity set has no primary key; its real primary key combines its own discriminator with the identifying strong entity set's key.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps to build an E-R diagram from a written description (e.g. the NHL database).
steps: Identify the entities and draw a rectangle for each
Attach each entity's attributes as ovals and underline the primary key
Identify the relationships between entities and draw a diamond for each
Add role names on the lines where an entity plays more than one part (recursive or ambiguous relationships)
Label each relationship's cardinality (1:1, 1:N, N:1, N:N)
Mark each relationship's participation constraints (single line = partial, double line = total)
exercises.explanation: Entities and their attributes come first, then the relationships between them, then the refinements — roles, cardinality, participation — that make the diagram precise.

exercises.prompt: Order the four mapping cardinalities from the most restrictive to the least restrictive (fewest possible connections to most).
steps: One-to-one (1:1) — each side connects to at most one entity of the other
One-to-many (1:N) or many-to-one (N:1) — one side connects to many, the other to only one
Many-to-many (N:N) — both sides can connect to many entities of the other set
exercises.explanation: 1:1 is the tightest constraint (one on both sides), N:N the loosest (many on both sides); 1:N/N:1 sit in between, restricting exactly one side.

exercises.prompt: Draw the customer–loan relationship 'borrow' as a many-to-many (N:N) relationship, with total participation on the loan side (every loan must have a customer) and partial participation on the customer side.
exercises.hint: Two entities (customer, loan) and a relationship diamond (borrow) between them. Click the loan–borrow line twice to cycle its cardinality to N, and the customer–borrow line to N as well.
exercises.explanation: A customer may hold several loans and a loan may be shared by several customers, so both sides of borrow carry an N cardinality: many-to-many.

exercises.prompt: Draw the weak entity set 'payment', identified through the strong entity 'loan' by the weak (double) relationship 'L_P', each with one key attribute.
exercises.hint: loan is a plain (single) rectangle with its key attribute loan-no. payment is a weak entity (double rectangle) with its discriminator payment-no (use the “Discriminator (partial key)” shape: dashed underline), joined to loan through the weak relationship L_P (double diamond).
exercises.explanation: loan is strong (single rectangle, own primary key loan-no); payment has no primary key of its own so it is weak (double rectangle), tied to loan through the identifying (double-diamond) relationship L_P. Its real primary key is (loan-no, payment-no).

exercises.prompt: Draw the generalization/specialization hierarchy: Person is the superclass; Student and Faculty are its subclasses (one ISA link).
exercises.hint: One entity Person, an ISA node, and two entities Student and Faculty below it. The ISA node sits between Person (above) and the two subclasses (below).
exercises.explanation: The ISA triangle links the superclass Person to its subclasses Student and Faculty, each inheriting Person's shared attributes while adding their own.

exercises.prompt: Which pair correctly matches the total/partial participation marks used in an E-R diagram?
choices: Total = double line, Partial = single line
Total = single line, Partial = double line
Total = dashed line, Partial = solid line
Total and Partial use the same mark; only the cardinality label differs
exercises.explanation: Total participation (every entity of the set is involved) is drawn with a double line; partial participation is a single line.

exercises.prompt: What is the mapping cardinality of this relationship?
exercises.explanation: 1 on the customer side, N on the loan side: one customer may hold many loans, each loan belongs to one customer.

exercises.prompt: What is the mapping cardinality of this relationship?
exercises.explanation: N on the customer side, 1 on the loan side: several customers can share one loan (a joint loan), each customer holds a single loan.

exercises.prompt: What is the mapping cardinality of this relationship?
exercises.explanation: N on both sides: many customers, many loans.

exercises.prompt: What is the mapping cardinality of this relationship?
exercises.explanation: 1 on both sides.

exercises.prompt: What does the double line on the loan side mean?
choices: Total participation: every loan takes part in borrow
Partial participation: some loans have no customer
exercises.explanation: A double line is total participation — every entity of the set participates in at least one relationship. Cardinality is the 1/N mark, and a weak entity would be a double rectangle.

exercises.prompt: What does the single line on the customer side mean?
choices: Partial participation: a customer may have no loan
Total participation: every customer has a loan
exercises.explanation: A single line is partial participation: some customers may not take part in any borrow relationship.

exercises.prompt: What is the primary key of the entity set payment?
exercises.explanation: payment is weak (double rectangle): payment-no is only a discriminator (dashed underline). Its primary key combines the strong entity's key with the discriminator.

exercises.prompt: What kind of entity set is payment on this diagram?
exercises.explanation: Double rectangle = weak entity set, tied to loan by the double diamond (identifying relationship).

exercises.prompt: What are Coordinator and Head on this diagram?
choices: Role names on a recursive relationship
exercises.explanation: The same entity set Faculty takes part twice in Reports_To; the labels on the two lines are roles, which clarify the meaning of each participation.

exercises.prompt: On this diagram, which entity set is the superclass?
exercises.explanation: Account sits above the ISA triangle: Saving_Account and Current_Account are derived from it and inherit its attributes.

exercises.prompt: What limitation of the E-R model does aggregation solve?
choices: A weak entity cannot have attributes
An entity cannot have more than one key attribute
A relationship cannot be connected to another relationship
exercises.explanation: En E-R, une relationship relie des entités, jamais une autre relationship. L'agrégation regroupe des entités et leur relationship en une seule « entité » abstraite, qui peut alors participer à une autre relationship.

exercises.prompt: What is aggregation in an E-R diagram?
choices: Creating an entity by combining various components of the E-R diagram (entities and their relationship)
Splitting an entity into several subclasses
Merging two attributes into a composite attribute
Turning a multivalued attribute into a separate table
exercises.explanation: Définition du cours : « Process of creating an entity by combining various components of E-R diagram is called aggregation. » Ne pas confondre avec la generalization (fusion d'entités qui partagent des attributs, avec ISA).

exercises.prompt: What does the dashed box labelled Customer represent in this diagram?
choices: An aggregation: Employee–Works–Company–Department treated as one entity
exercises.explanation: Le cadre regroupe Works et ses entités : c'est une agrégation. Borrow peut ainsi se relier au cadre comme à une entité, ce qui serait interdit directement sur le losange Works.

exercises.prompt: In the Hospital Management System diagram, an arrow goes from Admitted to Hospital (Patient —Admitted→ Hospital). What does it mean?
choices: One patient is admitted to many hospitals (1 : N)
Many patients are admitted to one hospital (N : 1)
exercises.explanation: Dans la notation à flèches, la flèche pointe vers le côté « one ». Donc plusieurs patients pour un seul hôpital : N : 1.

exercises.prompt: In the hospital diagram, Patient —Treats— Doctor has no arrow on either side. What is its cardinality?
exercises.explanation: Pas de flèche = « many » des deux côtés : un médecin soigne plusieurs patients, un patient voit plusieurs médecins (many-to-many).

exercises.prompt: In the hospital diagram, Indoor and Outdoor hang under Patient through an ISA triangle. What is this?
exercises.explanation: ISA = superclass / subclass. Patient se spécialise en Indoor (ajoute RoomNo) et Outdoor (ajoute Charge).

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of reducing an E-R diagram to a database schema in the order of the lecture.
exercises.explanation: Step 1 entités, step 2 attributs multivalués, puis les relationships par cardinalité : 1:1, 1:N, N:N.

exercises.prompt: Person has a multi-valued attribute PhoneNo. How is it reduced to tables?
choices: A column PhoneNo in Person holding a comma-separated list
Three columns Phone1, Phone2, Phone3 in Person
A new table PhoneNo(PhoneID, PersonID, PhoneNo) with PersonID as a foreign key
It is dropped: multi-valued attributes are not stored
exercises.explanation: Step 2 : un attribut multivalué devient une nouvelle table, avec sa propre PK et la PK du parent en foreign key. Les deux tables sont en 1:N.

exercises.prompt: Person —Having— House is 1 : N (one person owns many houses, a house has one owner). Where does the foreign key go?
choices: A separate table Having(PersonID, HouseID) is mandatory
Both tables receive a foreign key
exercises.explanation: Step 4 : la PK du côté « 1 » va en foreign key dans la table du côté « N ». House(HouseID, HName, PersonID).

exercises.prompt: Customer —Has_Acct— Account is N : N. Which schema is correct?
choices: One table Customer_Account(CID, CName, ActNo, Balance)
Customer(CID, CName), Account(ActNo, Balance), Has_Acct(HasAcctID, CID, ActNo)
exercises.explanation: Step 5 : une N:N devient une table séparée qui contient les PK des deux entités en foreign keys. Une FK simple ne suffit pas (il faudrait plusieurs valeurs dans une case).

exercises.prompt: Person —Having— Wife is 1 : 1. Which statement is true?
choices: The foreign key must go in Person
The foreign key must go in Wife
The primary key of either table can be placed in the other as a foreign key
exercises.explanation: Step 3 : en 1:1, on met la PK de n'importe laquelle des deux tables dans l'autre. Wife(WifeID, WName, PersonID) ou Person(PersonID, PName, WifeID), les deux sont corrects.

exercises.prompt: Match each E-R element with what it becomes in the database schema.
pairs: A new table with a foreign key to the parent
PK of either side as FK in the other
PK of the one side as FK in the many side
A separate table holding both primary keys
exercises.explanation: Les 5 steps de la réduction E-R → schéma.

exercises.prompt: In arrow notation, what does E ←— R ——— E (an arrow on the left side only) mean?
choices: One to many (the left entity is the one side)
exercises.explanation: La flèche pointe vers le côté « one ». Flèche à gauche seulement : un E de gauche pour plusieurs E de droite, donc one to many. Deux flèches = 1:1, aucune = M:N.

exercises.prompt: What does a double line between the superclass and the ISA triangle mean?
choices: Total specialization: every superclass entity belongs to at least one subclass
exercises.explanation: Double ligne = total (chaque entité de la superclass est dans au moins une subclass). Ligne simple = partial.

exercises.prompt: A Person can be a Student and an Employee at the same time. This specialization is:
exercises.explanation: Overlapping = une entité peut appartenir à plusieurs subclasses à la fois. Disjoint = au plus une.

exercises.prompt: True or false? In a disjoint specialization, an entity can belong to several subclasses at once.
exercises.explanation: Faux : disjoint = au plus une subclass. Plusieurs à la fois, c'est overlapping.

exercises.prompt: Match each integrity constraint with its rule.
pairs: A business rule on a column, e.g. SPI between 0 and 10
Every row must have a value
No duplicates, but NULL is allowed
Value is NULL or exists in the referenced primary key
exercises.explanation: Les 5 integrity constraints du cours.

exercises.prompt: Which formula is correct?
choices: Primary key = Not null + Foreign key
exercises.explanation: Primary key = Unique key + Not null. C'est la seule différence avec Unique, qui accepte NULL.

exercises.prompt: Which constraint allows NULL values but forbids duplicates?
exercises.explanation: Unique : valeurs distinctes, mais une colonne Unique peut contenir NULL. La primary key, elle, interdit NULL.

exercises.prompt: Student.DeptID references Department.DeptID. Which insertion into Student is rejected?
exercises.explanation: Referential integrity : chaque valeur de la FK doit être NULL ou exister dans la PK référencée. DeptID 3 n'existe pas dans Department ⇒ rejeté. NULL est accepté.

exercises.prompt: What are integrity constraints mainly used for?
choices: Maintaining the quality of information and guarding against accidental damage to the database
exercises.explanation: Cours : « Integrity constraints are a set of rules used to maintain the quality of information… to guard against accidental damage to the database. »

exercises.prompt: In this university diagram, course-offerings is a double rectangle linked to course by a double diamond. What does that mean?
choices: course-offerings is a multivalued attribute of course
course-offerings is a weak entity: it only exists for a course and is identified through 'is offered'
course-offerings has total participation in teaches
exercises.explanation: Double rectangle = weak entity, double losange = identifying relationship, double ligne = participation totale. Sa clé = courseno + discriminator (secno, year, semester).

exercises.prompt: In the university diagram, 'requires' links course to itself with the roles prerequisite and maincourse. It is:
exercises.explanation: Le même entity set (course) participe deux fois, avec deux rôles : relationship récursive. En table : Requires(maincourse, prerequisite), deux FK vers Course.

exercises.prompt: In the university diagram, 'grade' is attached to the 'enrols' diamond. Why?
choices: It is a mistake in the diagram
It is the key of enrols
It is a descriptive attribute of the relationship: a grade belongs to one student in one offering
exercises.explanation: Une note ne dépend ni de l'étudiant seul, ni de l'offering seule, mais du couple : c'est un attribut de la relationship (descriptive attribute).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Primary key = Unique + ______
exercises.explanation: Primary key = Unique key + Not null.

flashcards.back: Label sur la ligne entre un losange et un rectangle ; sert quand le même entity set participe deux fois (Coordinator / Head).
Le même entity set participe plusieurs fois à la relationship (Faculty Reports_To Faculty).
Nombre d'entités de l'autre côté qu'une entité peut avoir via la relationship : 1:1, 1:N, N:1, N:N.
Partial = ligne simple (certaines entités ne participent pas). Total = double ligne (toutes participent).
Pas de primary key propre ; double rectangle, relié par un double losange (identifying relationship). PK = PK du strong entity + discriminator.
Attributs qui distinguent les weak entities d'un même strong entity ; souligné en pointillés.
Generalization = bottom-up (union, attributs communs). Specialization = top-down (subsets, attributs distinctifs).
Regrouper des entités et leur relationship en une seule entité abstraite, car une relationship ne peut pas se relier à une autre relationship.
La flèche pointe vers le côté « one ». Deux flèches = 1:1, une = 1:N ou N:1, aucune = M:N.
Double ligne au-dessus de l'ISA = total (chaque entité est dans au moins une subclass) ; simple = partial.
Disjoint = au plus une subclass. Overlapping = plusieurs subclasses à la fois.
Une table ; chaque attribut simple = une colonne ; l'attribut clé = primary key (TablenameID).
Nouvelle table (sa PK + la PK du parent en FK), en 1:N avec le parent.
PK de n'importe quelle des deux tables mise en FK dans l'autre.
PK du côté « 1 » en FK dans la table du côté « N ».
Table séparée pour la relationship, avec les PK des deux entités en FK (Has_Acct(HasAcctID, CID, ActNo)).
Règles qui maintiennent la qualité des données : Check, Not null, Unique, Primary key, Foreign key.
Unique accepte NULL ; Primary key = Unique + Not null.
Chaque valeur de la FK est NULL ou existe dans la PK de la table référencée.
Règle métier sur une colonne (plage, liste, ensemble de valeurs) : SPI entre 0 et 10.

name: Week 4

exercises.prompt: Match each relational term with its synonym or meaning.
pairs: Set of all possible values of a column
exercises.explanation: Relation = table, attribute = colonne, tuple = ligne. Degree = nombre de colonnes, cardinality = nombre de lignes, domain = valeurs possibles d'une colonne.

exercises.prompt: A Student table has 5 columns and 7 rows. What is its degree?
exercises.explanation: Degree = nombre de colonnes (5). La cardinality serait 7 (les lignes).

exercises.prompt: A Student table has 5 columns and 7 rows. What is its cardinality?
exercises.explanation: Cardinality d'une table = nombre de tuples (lignes) = 7.

exercises.prompt: The Branch column only ever holds CE, CI, ME or EE. What is {CE, CI, ME, EE} called?
exercises.explanation: Le domain est l'ensemble de toutes les valeurs possibles d'une colonne.

exercises.prompt: What is the horizontal component of a table, holding one value for each column?
exercises.explanation: Le tuple (record, row) est horizontal ; l'attribute (column) est vertical.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about a column (attribute) is correct?
choices: Its number gives the cardinality of the table
It must always be part of the primary key
It is the horizontal component of a table
It has a name and a particular data type such as varchar, decimal, integer or datetime
exercises.explanation: Une colonne a un nom et un type ; le nombre de colonnes donne le degree.

exercises.prompt: What is a super key?
choices: An attribute that refers to the primary key of another table
The key chosen by the database designer
The smallest set of attributes that identifies a record
A set of one or more attributes whose values uniquely identify each record of a table
exercises.explanation: Super key = n'importe quel ensemble qui identifie chaque ligne, attributs en trop compris.

exercises.prompt: What is a candidate key?
choices: A minimal super key: no attribute can be removed without losing uniqueness
A candidate key that was not chosen
Any super key of the table
A key that may contain NULL values
exercises.explanation: La candidate key est la super key minimale.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is TRUE?
choices: A super key and a candidate key are always the same set
Every super key is a candidate key
A candidate key always has exactly one attribute
Every candidate key is a super key, but not every super key is a candidate key
exercises.explanation: Candidate ⊂ super keys : une candidate key est une super key minimale, l'inverse est faux.

exercises.prompt: What is the primary key?
choices: The first column of the table
The key with the most attributes
The candidate key chosen by the database designer to identify tuples
Every candidate key of the table
exercises.explanation: Primary key = la candidate key choisie par le concepteur.

exercises.prompt: What is an alternate key?
choices: A super key with extra attributes
A primary key made of several attributes
A foreign key that refers to another table
A candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key
exercises.explanation: Les candidate keys non choisies deviennent les alternate keys.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is NOT a rule of the primary key?
choices: A primary key attribute value cannot be NULL
A primary key may have one or more attributes
A table may have several primary keys
Generally, the value of a primary key does not change
exercises.explanation: Il n'y a qu'UNE primary key par table (elle peut avoir plusieurs attributs).

exercises.prompt: In this Student table, which attribute set is a candidate key?
exercises.explanation: RollNo vaut 101 partout ; (RollNo, Branch) se répète (101 CE deux fois). EnrollNo est unique et minimal ; {Name, EnrollNo} est une super key mais pas minimale.

exercises.prompt: In the same Student table, is {EnrollNo, Name} a candidate key?
choices: No: it is not even a super key
Yes: it uniquely identifies every row
Yes: because it has two attributes
No: it is a super key, but Name is extra (not minimal)
exercises.explanation: EnrollNo suffit déjà : {EnrollNo, Name} est une super key non minimale.

exercises.prompt: Student has two candidate keys, EnrollNo and (RollNo, Branch, Sem). The designer picks EnrollNo. What is (RollNo, Branch, Sem)?
exercises.explanation: Candidate key non choisie = alternate key.

exercises.prompt: A relation R(A, B, C) has A as its only candidate key. How many super keys does R have?
exercises.explanation: A, AB, AC, ABC : A plus n'importe quel sous-ensemble de {B, C}, soit 2² = 4.

exercises.prompt: A relation R(A, B, C, D) has A as its only candidate key. How many super keys does R have?
exercises.explanation: A plus n'importe quel sous-ensemble de {B, C, D} : 2³ = 8.

exercises.prompt: What is a foreign key?
choices: An attribute (or set of attributes) in one table that refers to the primary key of another table
The primary key of the child table
A key imported from another database
A candidate key that was not chosen
exercises.explanation: La foreign key relie deux tables en référençant la primary key de l'autre.

exercises.prompt: Employee.DeptID refers to Department.DeptID. Which table is the child table?
choices: Employee, because it contains the foreign key
Department, because it contains the primary key
Neither: child tables only exist with weak entities
exercises.explanation: La table qui contient la FK est la child ; celle qui contient la PK référencée est la parent.

exercises.prompt: In the same figure, D1 appears twice in Employee.DeptID. Is that allowed?
choices: No: a foreign key must be unique
Yes: a foreign key value may repeat in the child table
No: a foreign key must be the primary key of its table
exercises.explanation: Plusieurs employés peuvent être dans le même département : la FK se répète.

exercises.prompt: Match each key with its definition.
pairs: Any attribute set that uniquely identifies each record
Candidate key chosen by the designer
Refers to the primary key of another table
exercises.explanation: Super ⊃ candidate ⊃ {primary, alternate} ; la foreign key relie deux tables.

exercises.prompt: Order the key concepts from the broadest set to the single chosen key.
exercises.explanation: On réduit les super keys aux minimales (candidate), puis on en choisit une (primary).

exercises.prompt: Which value can a primary key attribute NEVER take?
exercises.explanation: Règle de la primary key : jamais NULL.

exercises.prompt: In the car-insurance E-R diagram, how many entity sets does 'participated' connect?
choices: Three: person, car and accident (a ternary relationship)
exercises.explanation: participated relie person (rôle driver), car et accident : c'est une relationship ternaire.

exercises.prompt: Why is damage-amount attached to 'participated' and not to accident?
choices: Because attributes can never be placed on entities
It depends on the combination driver + car + accident, not on the accident alone
exercises.explanation: Un même accident peut impliquer plusieurs voitures avec des dégâts différents : le montant appartient à la participation.

exercises.prompt: In the car-insurance diagram, what is 'driver' written on the person–participated line?
exercises.explanation: Une étiquette sur la ligne entre losange et rectangle est un rôle.

exercises.prompt: What is the primary key of the table participated(driver-id, license, report-number, damage-amount)?
exercises.explanation: La table d'une relationship prend comme PK les primary keys des entity sets reliés ; chacune est aussi une FK.

exercises.prompt: Which table did the professor's car-insurance solution leave out?
exercises.explanation: La relationship owns n'a pas de table dans les slides ; il faut une table owns (si M:N) ou une FK driver-id dans car (si 1:N).

exercises.prompt: Match each car-insurance table with its primary key.
exercises.explanation: Les entités ont leur propre clé ; la relationship combine les trois.

exercises.prompt: Draw the core of the car-insurance diagram: entities person and car linked by the relationship owns, where one person owns many cars (1:N).
exercises.hint: Two rectangles (person, car) and a diamond (owns). Put 1 on the person side and N on the car side.
exercises.explanation: Une personne possède une ou plusieurs voitures : 1 côté person, N côté car.

exercises.prompt: Customer —Owns— Car is 1:N. How is it turned into tables?
choices: Put CustomerID as a foreign key in the Car table (the N side)
Merge Customer and Car into one table
Put LicenseNo as a foreign key in the Customer table
Always create a separate Owns table with no keys
exercises.explanation: Une relationship 1:N devient une FK du côté N ; une M:N devient sa propre table.

exercises.prompt: If accident is modelled as a weak entity of car (identifying relationship Involved), what is the primary key of the Accident table?
choices: (LicenseNo, ReportNo): the owner's key plus the discriminator
exercises.explanation: PK d'une weak entity = PK de l'entité forte + partial key ; LicenseNo est à la fois PK et FK.

exercises.prompt: Match each Crow's Foot symbol with its meaning.
exercises.explanation: Barre = 1, patte = many, cercle = 0. Le symbole le plus près de l'entité donne le maximum.

exercises.prompt: In Crow's Foot notation, what does the circle mean?
exercises.explanation: Le cercle = zéro : la participation est optionnelle.

exercises.prompt: In Crow's Foot notation, how is a relationship drawn?
choices: As a line between the two entity boxes, labelled with a verb
exercises.explanation: Le losange, c'est la notation Chen ; en Crow's Foot la relationship est une ligne.

exercises.prompt: Which slide example uses 'zero or one'?
exercises.explanation: Un étudiant a zéro ou un numéro de sécurité sociale. Instructor–Class = one or many, Classroom–Chair = zero or many, Student–Chair = one and only one.

exercises.prompt: Match each slide example with its Crow's Foot cardinality (on the right-hand entity).
exercises.explanation: Ce sont les exemples du tableau des slides.

exercises.prompt: In the slides' Crow's Foot example, Professor —teaches— Term ends with a circle and a crow's foot on the Term side. What does it mean?
choices: A professor teaches zero or many terms
A professor teaches exactly one term
A term has zero or many professors
A professor teaches one or many terms
exercises.explanation: Cercle + patte côté Term : un professeur enseigne 0..N terms ; côté Professor, deux barres : un term a un seul professeur.

exercises.prompt: Student —has— ID Card has two bars on both ends. What kind of relationship is it?
exercises.explanation: Deux barres = un et un seul, des deux côtés : 1:1 obligatoire.

exercises.prompt: In Crow's Foot, which symbol gives the MAXIMUM cardinality?
choices: The symbol furthest from the entity
The symbol closest to the entity (bar = 1, crow's foot = many)
The verb written on the line
exercises.explanation: Extérieur (près de l'entité) = maximum ; intérieur = minimum (cercle 0, barre 1).

exercises.prompt: Match each element with how Chen notation draws it.
exercises.explanation: En Crow's Foot : entité = boîte avec ses attributs, relationship = ligne, participation = cercle (0) ou barre (1).

exercises.prompt: Library system: a member can borrow many books and a book can be borrowed by many members. Where do IssueDate and DueDate go?
choices: On the Borrows relationship (its own table)
exercises.explanation: Les dates décrivent un emprunt précis (membre + livre) : ce sont des attributs de la relationship M:N, qui devient sa propre table.

exercises.prompt: How is a many-to-many (M:N) relationship turned into tables?
choices: It becomes its own table whose key combines the keys of both entities
A foreign key on either side
exercises.explanation: M:N → table propre ; 1:N → FK du côté N.

exercises.prompt: A member can have several phone numbers. How is Phone drawn in Chen notation?
exercises.explanation: Plusieurs valeurs pour un même membre = multivalued, double ovale ; il deviendra une table MemberPhone.

flashcards.back: Table / colonne / ligne (record).
Nombre de colonnes.
Nombre de lignes (tuples).
Ensemble de toutes les valeurs possibles d'une colonne. Ex : Branch ∈ {CE, CI, ME, EE}.
Ensemble d'un ou plusieurs attributs qui identifie de façon unique chaque record (attributs en trop autorisés).
Super key minimale. Toute candidate key est une super key, pas l'inverse.
Candidate key choisie par le concepteur. Une seule par table, jamais NULL, ne change pas, peut avoir plusieurs attributs.
Candidate key non choisie comme primary key.
Attribut(s) qui référence(nt) la primary key d'une autre table. Child = table avec la FK, parent = table avec la PK.

flashcards.front: Nombre de super keys de R(A, B, C) si A est la seule candidate key

lesson:
# Database Design — Week 4 · Keys & ERD notations

**Cours** : Lecture 07, *Key and ERD Notations*. Le vocabulaire d'une table
(relation, attribute, tuple, degree, cardinality, domain), les **clés** (super
key, candidate key, primary key, alternate key, foreign key), un exercice
complet (E-R diagram d'une assurance auto, puis ses tables) et la notation
**Crow's Foot**.

> **En bref.** Une **super key** identifie chaque ligne ; une **candidate key**
> est une super key **minimale** ; la **primary key** est la candidate key
> **choisie** par le concepteur ; les autres candidate keys sont des
> **alternate keys**. Une **foreign key** dans la table **child** pointe vers
> la primary key de la table **parent**. Au quiz, sache **reconnaître chaque
> clé dans une table** et **lire les symboles Crow's Foot**.

Les termes en **gras anglais** sont ceux qui tombent au quiz : apprends-les
tels quels.

---

## 1. La structure d'une base relationnelle

Une **database** est une collection de **tables** (relations), chacune avec un
**nom unique**.

| Terme | Synonymes | Définition |
|---|---|---|
| **Table** | **Relation** | objet qui contient les données d'un **sujet précis** ; faite de lignes et de colonnes |
| **Column** | **Attribute**, field | composant **vertical** ; a un **nom** et un **type** (`varchar`, `decimal`, `integer`, `datetime`…) |
| **Record** | **Tuple**, **row** | composant **horizontal** : une valeur pour chaque colonne |
| **Degree** | — | **nombre de colonnes** |
| **Cardinality** | — | **nombre de lignes** (tuples) |
| **Domain** | — | ensemble de **toutes les valeurs possibles** d'une colonne |

```diagram
{
  "title": "Student : degree = 5 (colonnes), cardinality = 7 (lignes). Le domain de Branch est {CE, CI, ME, EE}.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t", "x": 300, "y": 130, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Student",
      "rows": [["RollNo","Name","Branch","Semester","SPI"],["101","Raju","CE","3","8"],["102","Mitesh","CI","3","7"],["103","Mayur","CE","3","6"],["104","Nilesh","EE","3","9"],["105","Hitesh","CI","3","7"],["106","Tarun","ME","3","8"],["107","Suresh","CE","3","9"]],
      "cols": [70, 70, 70, 80, 50] },
    { "id": "a", "x": 300, "y": -20, "shape": "note", "tone": "amber", "size": 12, "label": "Attributes = titres des colonnes · Degree = 5" },
    { "id": "r", "x": 600, "y": 130, "shape": "note", "tone": "emerald", "size": 12, "label": "Rows = tuples = records\nCardinality = 7" },
    { "id": "ra", "x": 470, "y": 130, "shape": "text" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "a", "to": "t", "dashed": true, "tone": "amber" },
    { "from": "r", "to": "ra", "dashed": true, "tone": "emerald" }
  ]
}
```

> **Piège :** en base de données, **cardinality d'une table = nombre de
> lignes** et **degree = nombre de colonnes**. Ne confonds pas avec la
> *mapping cardinality* d'une relationship (1:1, 1:N…) vue en semaine 3.

## 2. Les clés

Tous les exemples utilisent la même table `Student` : plusieurs étudiants ont
le même `RollNo` (dans des branches ou semestres différents), mais
l'`EnrollNo` est unique.

```diagram
{
  "title": "La table Student des slides. EnrollNo seul identifie une ligne ; (RollNo, Branch, Sem) aussi.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t", "x": 320, "y": 110, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Student",
      "rows": [["EnrollNo","RollNo","Branch","Sem","SPI","Name","BL"],["190540107001","101","CE","3","8","Raju","0"],["190540107002","102","CE","3","7","Mitesh","1"],["190540106001","101","CI","3","6","Mayur","2"],["190540106002","102","CI","3","9","Nilesh","0"],["180540107001","101","CE","5","7","Hitesh","1"],["180540106001","101","CI","5","8","Tarun","0"],["180540106002","102","CI","5","9","Suresh","0"]],
      "cols": [110, 60, 60, 40, 40, 70, 40] }
  ]
}
```

### Super key

Une **super key** est un **ensemble d'un ou plusieurs attributs** dont les
valeurs **identifient de façon unique chaque record** de la table.

Dans `Student` : `{EnrollNo}`, `{RollNo, Branch, Sem}`, et sur ces données
`{SPI, Name, BL}` sont des super keys. Tout **sur-ensemble** d'une super key
est aussi une super key : `{EnrollNo, Name}`, `{EnrollNo, RollNo, SPI}`…

### Candidate key

- Une **candidate key** est un **sous-ensemble d'une super key**.
- C'est **un seul attribut** ou la **plus petite combinaison** d'attributs
  qui identifie chaque record.
- **La super key minimale est la candidate key** : on ne peut retirer aucun
  attribut sans perdre l'unicité.
- **Toute candidate key est une super key, mais toute super key n'est pas une
  candidate key.**

Dans `Student` : `EnrollNo` et `(RollNo, Branch, Sem)` sont des candidate
keys. `{EnrollNo, Name}` est une super key mais **pas** une candidate key
(`Name` est en trop).

### Primary key

La **primary key** est **la candidate key choisie par le concepteur** pour
identifier les tuples. Ici : `EnrollNo`.

**Règles de la primary key** :

1. elle peut avoir **un ou plusieurs attributs** ;
2. il n'y a **qu'une seule** primary key par table ;
3. sa valeur ne peut **pas être NULL** ;
4. en général, sa valeur **ne change pas** ;
5. **deux lignes ne peuvent pas avoir la même valeur** de primary key.

### Alternate key

Une **alternate key** est une **candidate key qui n'a pas été choisie** comme
primary key. Ici : `(RollNo, Branch, Sem)`.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Les clés s'emboîtent : primary key et alternate keys sont des candidate keys, elles-mêmes des super keys.",
  "groups": [
    { "x": 330, "y": 145, "w": 640, "h": 270, "label": "Super keys (toute combinaison qui identifie une ligne)", "tone": "neutral" },
    { "x": 330, "y": 135, "w": 460, "h": 130, "label": "Candidate keys (super keys minimales)", "tone": "sky" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "pk", "x": 220, "y": 150, "w": 180, "label": "Primary key\nEnrollNo", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "ak", "x": 440, "y": 150, "w": 180, "label": "Alternate key\n(RollNo, Branch, Sem)", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "sk", "x": 330, "y": 245, "w": 360, "shape": "text", "label": "{EnrollNo, Name}, {EnrollNo, SPI, BL}, {RollNo, Branch, Sem, SPI}…" }
  ]
}
```

| Clé | Une phrase |
|---|---|
| **Super key** | identifie chaque ligne, attributs en trop autorisés |
| **Candidate key** | super key **minimale** |
| **Primary key** | candidate key **choisie** ; unique, **jamais NULL** |
| **Alternate key** | candidate key **non choisie** |
| **Foreign key** | attribut(s) qui **référence(nt) la primary key d'une autre table** |

> **Astuce de calcul :** si une table a les attributs A, B, C et que **A est la
> seule candidate key**, les super keys sont A, AB, AC, ABC : **4** (A plus
> n'importe quel sous-ensemble des 2 autres = 2² = 4).

### Foreign key

- Une **foreign key** sert à **relier deux tables**.
- C'est un attribut (ou un groupe d'attributs) d'une table qui **référence la
  primary key d'une autre table**.
- La table qui **contient la foreign key** est la **child table** ; celle qui
  contient la **primary key** est la **parent table**.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Project.EnrollNo est une foreign key vers Student.EnrollNo : Student est la parent table, Project la child table.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "s", "x": 150, "y": 70, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Student (parent)",
      "rows": [["EnrollNo (PK)","Name","Branch","Sem"],["190540107001","Raju","CE","3"],["190540107002","Mitesh","CE","3"],["190540107003","Nilesh","CE","3"],["190540107004","Meet","CE","3"]],
      "cols": [110, 60, 55, 40] },
    { "id": "p", "x": 520, "y": 70, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "violet", "label": "Project (child)",
      "rows": [["ProjectID (PK)","Title","EnrollNo (FK)"],["101","Bank","190540107001"],["102","College","190540107002"],["103","School","190540107003"],["104","Hospital","190540107001"]],
      "cols": [95, 70, 110] }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "p", "to": "s", "label": "references", "tone": "violet" }
  ]
}
```

> **Piège :** une foreign key **peut se répéter** dans la child table (Raju a
> deux projets, 101 et 104) et elle n'est pas forcément la primary key de la
> child table.

## 3. Exercice ERD 3 : l'assurance auto

**(a)** *Construct an E-R diagram for a car-insurance company whose customers
own one or more cars each. Each car has associated with it zero to any number
of recorded accidents.*

```er
{
  "title": "Solution du professeur : person possède des cars (owns) ; participated relie une person (rôle driver), une car et un accident, avec le damage-amount.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "p", "kind": "entity", "label": "person", "x": 120, "y": 200 },
    { "id": "pi", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "driver-id", "x": 40, "y": 100 },
    { "id": "pa", "kind": "attribute", "label": "address", "x": 140, "y": 60 },
    { "id": "pn", "kind": "attribute", "label": "name", "x": 230, "y": 110 },
    { "id": "o", "kind": "relationship", "label": "owns", "x": 300, "y": 200 },
    { "id": "c", "kind": "entity", "label": "car", "x": 470, "y": 200 },
    { "id": "cl", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "license", "x": 390, "y": 100 },
    { "id": "cm", "kind": "attribute", "label": "model", "x": 480, "y": 60 },
    { "id": "cy", "kind": "attribute", "label": "year", "x": 570, "y": 110 },
    { "id": "pt", "kind": "relationship", "label": "participated", "x": 470, "y": 360 },
    { "id": "pd", "kind": "attribute", "label": "damage-amount", "x": 470, "y": 460 },
    { "id": "a", "kind": "entity", "label": "accident", "x": 690, "y": 360 },
    { "id": "ar", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "report-number", "x": 640, "y": 250 },
    { "id": "al", "kind": "attribute", "label": "location", "x": 780, "y": 260 },
    { "id": "ad", "kind": "attribute", "label": "date", "x": 790, "y": 440 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "p", "to": "pi" }, { "from": "p", "to": "pa" }, { "from": "p", "to": "pn" },
    { "from": "p", "to": "o" }, { "from": "o", "to": "c" },
    { "from": "c", "to": "cl" }, { "from": "c", "to": "cm" }, { "from": "c", "to": "cy" },
    { "from": "p", "to": "pt", "role": "driver" }, { "from": "c", "to": "pt" }, { "from": "pt", "to": "a" },
    { "from": "pt", "to": "pd" },
    { "from": "a", "to": "ar" }, { "from": "a", "to": "al" }, { "from": "a", "to": "ad" }
  ]
}
```

À remarquer :

- `participated` est une relationship **ternaire** (3 entity sets : person,
  car, accident) ;
- `damage-amount` est un **attribut de la relationship** : le montant dépend
  du conducteur, de la voiture **et** de l'accident, il n'appartient à aucun
  des trois seuls ;
- `driver` est un **rôle** : la person qui participe à l'accident y joue le
  rôle de conducteur.

**(b)** *Construct appropriate tables for the above ER diagram.*

```diagram
{
  "title": "Les tables de la solution. La table d'une relationship reprend les primary keys des entity sets qu'elle relie, plus ses propres attributs.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "p", "x": 110, "y": 40, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "person", "rows": [["driver-id (PK)","name","address"]], "cols": [105, 60, 70] },
    { "id": "c", "x": 370, "y": 40, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "car", "rows": [["license (PK)","year","model"]], "cols": [90, 50, 60] },
    { "id": "a", "x": 640, "y": 40, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "accident", "rows": [["report-number (PK)","date","location"]], "cols": [140, 50, 70] },
    { "id": "pt", "x": 370, "y": 220, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "violet", "label": "participated", "rows": [["driver-id (PK, FK)","license (PK, FK)","report-number (PK, FK)","damage-amount"]], "cols": [135, 120, 170, 115] }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "pt", "to": "p", "tone": "violet", "dashed": true },
    { "from": "pt", "to": "c", "tone": "violet", "dashed": true },
    { "from": "pt", "to": "a", "tone": "violet", "dashed": true }
  ]
}
```

- person (<u>driver-id</u>, name, address)
- car (<u>license</u>, year, model)
- accident (<u>report-number</u>, date, location)
- participated (<u>driver-id</u>, <u>license</u>, <u>report-number</u>, damage-amount)

> **Attention :** la solution des slides **oublie `owns`**. Si une voiture peut
> avoir plusieurs propriétaires, il faut une table
> `owns (driver-id, license)` ; si elle n'en a qu'un, on ajoute `driver-id`
> comme **foreign key** dans `car`.

**Variante.** On peut aussi modéliser `accident` comme une **weak entity** de
`car` (relation identifiante `Involved`, `ReportNo` en partial key) : la table
`Accident` a alors pour primary key `(LicenseNo, ReportNo)`, avec `LicenseNo`
qui est **à la fois PK et FK**. `Customer —Owns— Car` en 1:N met
`CustomerID` comme FK `NOT NULL` dans `Car` (participation totale).

## 4. La notation Crow's Foot

La notation **Crow's Foot** (« patte de corbeau ») est une autre façon de
dessiner un ERD : les entités sont des **boîtes** avec leurs attributs, et la
cardinalité est dessinée **au bout de chaque ligne**. Le symbole se lit **du
côté de l'entité qu'il touche**.

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="560" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2">
<g><line x1="20" y1="20" x2="150" y2="20"/><text x="190" y="25" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Relationship (une simple ligne)</text></g>
<g><line x1="20" y1="60" x2="150" y2="60"/><line x1="130" y1="50" x2="130" y2="70"/><text x="190" y="65" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">One (une barre)</text></g>
<g><line x1="20" y1="100" x2="150" y2="100"/><line x1="130" y1="100" x2="150" y2="90"/><line x1="130" y1="100" x2="150" y2="110"/><text x="190" y="105" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Many (la patte de corbeau)</text></g>
<g><line x1="20" y1="140" x2="150" y2="140"/><line x1="125" y1="130" x2="125" y2="150"/><line x1="135" y1="130" x2="135" y2="150"/><text x="190" y="145" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">One and ONLY one (deux barres)</text></g>
<g><line x1="20" y1="180" x2="112" y2="180"/><circle cx="120" cy="180" r="8"/><line x1="128" y1="180" x2="150" y2="180"/><line x1="140" y1="170" x2="140" y2="190"/><text x="190" y="185" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Zero or one (cercle + barre)</text></g>
<g><line x1="20" y1="220" x2="150" y2="220"/><line x1="122" y1="210" x2="122" y2="230"/><line x1="132" y1="220" x2="150" y2="210"/><line x1="132" y1="220" x2="150" y2="230"/><text x="190" y="225" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">One or many (barre + patte)</text></g>
<g><line x1="20" y1="260" x2="104" y2="260"/><circle cx="112" cy="260" r="8"/><line x1="120" y1="260" x2="150" y2="260"/><line x1="132" y1="260" x2="150" y2="250"/><line x1="132" y1="260" x2="150" y2="270"/><text x="190" y="265" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Zero or many (cercle + patte)</text></g>
</svg>

| Notation | Meaning | Exemple des slides |
|---|---|---|
| ligne simple | **Relationship** | Student — *Enrolls* — University |
| une barre `┼` | **One** | Student *Has* Student ID Number |
| patte `<` | **Many** | Student *Attends* Class |
| deux barres `╫` | **One and ONLY one** | Student *Uses* Chair |
| cercle + barre `o┼` | **Zero or one** | Student *Has* Social Security Number |
| barre + patte `┼<` | **One or many** | Instructor *Teaches* Class |
| cercle + patte `o<` | **Zero or many** | Classroom *Has* Chair |

**Comment lire :** le symbole le plus **près de l'entité** donne le **maximum**
(barre = 1, patte = many) ; le symbole **intérieur** donne le **minimum**
(cercle = 0, barre = 1).

> **Piège :** le **cercle** veut dire **zéro** (participation optionnelle), pas
> « un ». La **patte** veut dire **plusieurs**.

### L'exemple Crow's Foot des slides

```diagram
{
  "title": "Le schéma Crow's Foot des slides (les * marquent les clés). Les étiquettes donnent la cardinalité de chaque côté.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "s", "x": 90, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Student", "rows": [["*StudentID"],["FName"],["LName"]], "header": false, "cols": [110] },
    { "id": "i", "x": 560, "y": 60, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "ID Card", "rows": [["*StudentID"],["Name"]], "header": false, "cols": [110] },
    { "id": "c", "x": 90, "y": 260, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Course", "rows": [["*CourseID"],["*CourseName"],["CourseNum"]], "header": false, "cols": [110] },
    { "id": "ct", "x": 560, "y": 260, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "CourseTerm", "rows": [["*CourseID"],["*TermID"],["StartDate"],["EndDate"]], "header": false, "cols": [110] },
    { "id": "t", "x": 560, "y": 460, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Term", "rows": [["*TermID"],["SectionNumber"]], "header": false, "cols": [110] },
    { "id": "p", "x": 90, "y": 460, "shape": "table", "size": 12, "tone": "sky", "label": "Professor", "rows": [["*ProfID"],["Name"],["Status"]], "header": false, "cols": [110] }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "s", "to": "i", "arrow": "none", "label": "has : one and only one ↔ one and only one" },
    { "from": "s", "to": "c", "arrow": "none", "label": "takes : one or many ↔ one or many" },
    { "from": "c", "to": "ct", "arrow": "none", "label": "has : 1 seul ↔ 1..N" },
    { "from": "ct", "to": "t", "arrow": "none", "label": "has : 1..N ↔ 1 seul" },
    { "from": "p", "to": "t", "arrow": "none", "label": "teaches : 1 seul ↔ 0..N" }
  ]
}
```

- **Student has ID Card** : chaque étudiant a **exactement une** carte, chaque
  carte appartient à **exactement un** étudiant (1:1 obligatoire des deux
  côtés).
- **Student takes Course** : un étudiant suit **un ou plusieurs** cours, un
  cours est suivi par **un ou plusieurs** étudiants (M:N).
- **Course has CourseTerm** : un cours a **une ou plusieurs** sessions, une
  session concerne **un seul** cours.
- **Term has CourseTerm** : un term a une ou plusieurs CourseTerm, une
  CourseTerm est dans **un seul** term.
- **Professor teaches Term** : un professeur enseigne **zéro ou plusieurs**
  terms (il peut ne rien enseigner), un term a **un seul** professeur.

### Chen vs Crow's Foot

| | **Chen** (semaines 2–3) | **Crow's Foot** |
|---|---|---|
| Entité | rectangle | boîte avec la liste des attributs |
| Attribut | ovale | ligne dans la boîte |
| Relationship | **losange** | **ligne** avec un verbe |
| Cardinalité | `1`, `N`, `M` écrits sur la ligne | **symboles** au bout de la ligne |
| Participation | ligne simple / double | **cercle** (0) ou **barre** (1) en minimum |

```er
    { "from": "k", "to": "ki" }, { "from": "k", "to": "kt" },
    { "from": "k", "to": "w", "card": "M" }, { "from": "w", "to": "a", "card": "N" },
    { "from": "k", "to": "pb", "card": "N", "total": true }, { "from": "pb", "to": "p", "card": "1" }
  ]
}
```

Tables correspondantes : `Member(MemberID, Name)`, `MemberPhone(MemberID,
Phone)`, `Book(ISBN, Title, PublisherID)`, `Publisher(PublisherID, …)`,
`Author(AuthorID, …)`, `Written_by(ISBN, AuthorID)`,
`Borrows(MemberID, ISBN, IssueDate, DueDate)`. Une relationship **M:N**
devient **sa propre table** ; une **1:N** devient une **foreign key** du côté
N.

---

## À retenir

- Table = **relation**, colonne = **attribute**, ligne = **tuple / record**.
  **Degree = colonnes**, **cardinality = lignes**, **domain = valeurs
  possibles** d'une colonne.
- **Super key** : identifie chaque ligne. **Candidate key** : super key
  **minimale**. **Primary key** : candidate key **choisie** (une seule, **pas
  NULL**, ne change pas). **Alternate key** : candidate key non choisie.
- Toute candidate key est une super key, **l'inverse est faux**.
- **Foreign key** : référence la PK d'une autre table ; **child** = table qui
  contient la FK, **parent** = table qui contient la PK.
- Assurance auto : `participated` est **ternaire**, `damage-amount` est un
  attribut **de la relationship**, sa table a pour PK les 3 clés.
- **Crow's Foot** : barre = 1, patte = many, cercle = 0, deux barres = un et un
  seul.

## Pièges classiques du quiz

| Affirmation | Vrai / Faux |
|---|---|
| La cardinality d'une table est son nombre de colonnes | **Faux** : de lignes (le degree = colonnes) |
| Toute super key est une candidate key | **Faux** : seulement les minimales |
| Toute candidate key est une super key | **Vrai** |
| Une table peut avoir plusieurs primary keys | **Faux** : une seule (mais elle peut avoir plusieurs attributs) |
| Une primary key peut être NULL | **Faux** |
| Une alternate key est une candidate key non choisie | **Vrai** |
| La table qui contient la foreign key est la parent table | **Faux** : c'est la child table |
| Une foreign key doit être unique dans sa table | **Faux** : elle peut se répéter |
| En Crow's Foot, le cercle signifie « un » | **Faux** : zéro |
| En Crow's Foot, la relationship est un losange | **Faux** : une ligne (le losange, c'est Chen) |
