questions.choice_d: The final, unchangeable feature list
questions.explanation: A product vision identifies the proposed product, its users, and the value it provides; detailed features develop as the team learns more.

questions.question_text: In plan-driven development, when is planning mostly done?
questions.choice_a: Substantial requirements and design detail are defined before implementation
questions.choice_b: Only near-term detail is planned, revised as knowledge grows
questions.choice_c: Planning never happens, only coding
questions.choice_d: Planning happens exclusively during the Sprint Retrospective
questions.explanation: Plan-driven development defines substantial requirements and design detail up front, unlike agile which plans near-term detail and revises later work.

questions.question_text: What best describes agile development's approach to change?
questions.choice_a: Change is avoided entirely once planning is finished
questions.choice_b: Frequent increments are used to evaluate results and redirect work
questions.choice_c: Only the customer may request changes, and only once
questions.choice_d: Changes are batched and applied only at project end
questions.explanation: Agile development uses frequent increments to evaluate results and redirect work, embracing change as understanding grows.

questions.question_text: What is incremental development, as distinct from iterative development?
questions.choice_a: Revisiting and improving an existing result after evaluation
questions.choice_b: Extending the product with additional usable functionality that works with what already exists
questions.choice_c: Writing all requirements before any code
questions.choice_d: A synonym for the Sprint Retrospective
questions.explanation: Incremental development extends the product with additional usable functionality (Feature A -> A+B -> A+B+C); iterative development instead revisits and improves an existing result.

questions.question_text: According to the Agile Manifesto, which of these is valued MORE, without discarding the other side entirely?
questions.choice_a: Comprehensive documentation over working software
questions.choice_b: Working software over comprehensive documentation
questions.choice_c: Following a plan over responding to change
questions.choice_d: Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
questions.explanation: The manifesto values working software over comprehensive documentation, while still recognizing documentation's value.

questions.question_text: Which of the five agile development principles is 'reduce unnecessary complexity in the software and in the development process'?
questions.choice_a: Embrace change
questions.choice_b: Focus on people
questions.choice_c: Maintain simplicity
questions.choice_d: Involve the customer
questions.explanation: Maintain simplicity means reducing unnecessary complexity in both the software and the process used to build it.

questions.question_text: Which Extreme Programming practice means writing a test for required behaviour before coding it?
questions.choice_a: Continuous integration
questions.choice_b: Refactoring
questions.choice_c: Small releases
questions.choice_d: Test-driven development
questions.explanation: Test-driven development writes a test for the required behaviour before coding, then reruns the tests after changes.

questions.question_text: Which XP practice improves code structure while preserving its externally observable behaviour?
questions.choice_a: Refactoring
questions.choice_b: Incremental planning
questions.choice_c: Continuous integration
questions.choice_d: Test-driven development
questions.explanation: Refactoring improves the internal structure of code without changing its externally observable behaviour.

questions.question_text: What does Scrum organize complex product development around?
questions.choice_a: A single long planning phase followed by one release
questions.choice_b: Short Sprints and regular inspection
questions.choice_c: Unlimited-length iterations with no fixed events
questions.choice_d: A fixed contract signed before any work begins
questions.explanation: Scrum organizes complex product development around short Sprints and regular inspection, with defined responsibilities, events, and artifacts.

questions.question_text: What are Scrum's three pillars of empiricism, and in what relationship?
questions.choice_a: Transparency, Inspection, Adaptation — each supports the next
questions.choice_b: Planning, Coding, Testing — done in sequence once
questions.choice_c: Product Owner, Developers, Scrum Master — a command hierarchy
questions.choice_d: Backlog, Sprint, Increment — three separate teams
questions.explanation: Empiricism rests on Transparency (visible work), Inspection (examine progress), and Adaptation (adjust when inspection reveals a problem); each pillar supports the next.

questions.question_text: Which of these is one of the five Scrum values?
questions.choice_a: Documentation
questions.choice_b: Courage
questions.choice_c: Contract negotiation
questions.choice_d: Hierarchy
questions.explanation: The five Scrum values are Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, and Courage.

questions.question_text: Which Scrum accountability is responsible for maximizing product value and keeping the Product Backlog ordered and understandable?
questions.choice_a: Scrum Master
questions.choice_b: Developers
questions.choice_c: Product Owner
questions.choice_d: Stakeholders
questions.explanation: The Product Owner maximizes product value, communicates product direction, and keeps the Product Backlog ordered and understandable.

questions.question_text: Which Scrum accountability creates a usable Increment and plans the Sprint's work?
questions.choice_a: Developers
questions.choice_b: Product Owner
questions.choice_c: Scrum Master
questions.choice_d: Project manager
questions.explanation: Developers create a usable Increment, plan the Sprint's work, uphold quality, and adapt the plan as development progresses.

questions.question_text: What does 'self-managing', as applied to a Scrum Team, mean?
questions.choice_a: The team follows strict orders from the Scrum Master
questions.choice_b: The team decides who does what, when, and how; the accountabilities do not form a command hierarchy
questions.choice_c: Only the Product Owner can assign tasks
questions.choice_d: Each Developer works entirely alone with no coordination
questions.explanation: Self-managing means the team itself determines who does what, when, and how, with no command hierarchy among Product Owner, Developers, and Scrum Master.

questions.question_text: Which commitment gives the Product Backlog a shared basis for understanding its longer-term direction?
questions.choice_a: Sprint Goal
questions.choice_b: Definition of Done
questions.choice_c: Product Goal
questions.choice_d: Sprint Backlog
questions.explanation: The Product Goal is the commitment attached to the Product Backlog, describing a future state the product should reach.

questions.question_text: Which commitment states the quality conditions completed product work must satisfy?
questions.choice_a: Sprint Goal
questions.choice_b: Definition of Done
questions.choice_c: Product Goal
questions.choice_d: Sprint Backlog
questions.explanation: The Definition of Done states the quality conditions completed work must meet before it contributes to an Increment.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum length of a Sprint?
questions.choice_a: One week
questions.choice_b: One month or less
questions.choice_c: Three months
questions.choice_d: There is no maximum
questions.explanation: A Sprint is a fixed period of one month or less, containing planning, development, inspection, and improvement.

questions.question_text: What three questions does Sprint Planning address?
questions.choice_a: Who, When, Where
questions.choice_b: Why (Sprint Goal), What (selected items), How (the plan)
questions.choice_c: What, When, Budget
questions.choice_d: How much, How long, Who pays
questions.explanation: Sprint Planning addresses Why (the Sprint Goal), What (Product Backlog items selected), and How (the Developers' actionable delivery plan).

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum?
questions.choice_a: A 15-minute daily event to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan
questions.choice_b: A monthly status report to management
questions.choice_c: The event where the Product Backlog is created from scratch
questions.choice_d: A one-time kickoff meeting at the start of the whole project
questions.explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for Developers on every working day of the Sprint, inspecting progress and adjusting the plan for the day.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes the Sprint Review from the Sprint Retrospective in main focus?
questions.choice_a: Review focuses on the product outcome; Retrospective focuses on the development process
questions.choice_b: Review focuses on the process; Retrospective focuses on the product
questions.choice_c: They have exactly the same focus and participants
questions.choice_d: Review is for the Scrum Master only; Retrospective is for stakeholders only
questions.explanation: The Sprint Review inspects the product outcome and progress toward the Product Goal, with stakeholders present; the Retrospective examines the team's own process, with only the Scrum Team.

questions.question_text: Who participates in the Sprint Retrospective?
questions.choice_a: The Scrum Team and relevant stakeholders
questions.choice_b: Stakeholders only
questions.choice_c: The Scrum Team only
questions.choice_d: The Product Owner alone
questions.explanation: Unlike the Sprint Review, which includes stakeholders, the Sprint Retrospective involves only the Scrum Team, examining its own collaboration, tools, and quality.

exercises.prompt: Which Scrum accountability is responsible for coaching the team, establishing Scrum, and helping remove impediments to progress?
exercises.explanation: The Scrum Master helps establish Scrum, improves team effectiveness, coaches the team, and helps remove impediments to progress.

exercises.prompt: What is the name of the commitment attached to the Sprint Backlog, expressing one Sprint's shared objective?
exercises.explanation: The Sprint Goal is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog: the shared outcome the team seeks for that Sprint.

exercises.prompt: Order the events that occur within a single Sprint.
steps: Sprint Planning — the team defines the Sprint Goal, selects Product Backlog items, and plans the work
Development and Daily Scrum, repeated on every working day — inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the day's plan
Sprint Review — the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome and discuss what to do next
Sprint Retrospective — the Scrum Team examines its own process and chooses useful changes to how it works
exercises.explanation: A Sprint always opens with Planning, is filled with Development punctuated by the Daily Scrum, and closes with the Review (product-focused) followed by the Retrospective (process-focused).

exercises.prompt: Order the stages of the integrated Scrum cycle, from the Product Backlog to the next Sprint's Planning.
steps: Product Backlog / Product Goal — the ordered, evolving list of work and its longer-term direction
Sprint Planning — selects items and defines the Sprint Backlog / Sprint Goal
Development and Daily Scrum — Developers build toward an Increment that meets the Definition of Done
Sprint Review — inspects the product and informs the Product Backlog for the next cycle
Sprint Retrospective — inspects the development process and produces improvements for the next Sprint
exercises.explanation: Product decisions shape the Sprint; the Sprint produces an Increment; the Review feeds insights back into the Product Backlog, while the Retrospective's process improvements carry into the next Sprint's Planning.

exercises.prompt: Build the flowchart of one increment of incremental development: select features, refine them, implement and test, integrate and test the system, then deliver and evaluate, with feedback looping back to the next selection.
exercises.hint: Linear process chain of five steps, then loop back from the last step to the first (no decision node needed  it always loops).
exercises.explanation: Each increment selects a manageable set of features, refines and implements them, integrates and tests the whole, then delivers and evaluates — feedback from evaluation informs the next selection, so the cycle loops rather than ending.

exercises.prompt: Which pair of artifact and commitment is correctly matched?
exercises.explanation: Each artifact has one commitment: Product Backlog ↔ Product Goal, Sprint Backlog ↔ Sprint Goal, Increment ↔ Definition of Done.

name: Week 4

exercises.prompt: Match each representation with what it describes.
pairs: Use of the product in a situation
exercises.explanation: Persona → scenario → story → feature (un scenario suggère aussi directement des features).

exercises.prompt: What is a persona?
choices: An imagined character representing a type of potential product user
A narrative of a user using the product
A real user interviewed by the team
exercises.explanation: Une persona est imaginée et représente un type d'utilisateur ; le récit, c'est le scenario.

exercises.prompt: What does a persona add compared with a simple role such as 'teacher'?
choices: The list of features to build
The context needed to reason about how a particular type of teacher may use the system
exercises.explanation: Le rôle est une catégorie ; la persona ajoute contexte, activité, compétences, pertinence.

exercises.prompt: Match each persona aspect with the information it gives.
pairs: A name and circumstances make the user concrete
Responsibilities explain the tasks to support
What the user can understand and operate
Why the product may matter to this user
exercises.explanation: Les quatre aspects d'une persona (Sommerville, tableau 3.2).

exercises.prompt: What is a proto-persona?
choices: A persona representing one specific real person
A persona built from the team's limited current knowledge, whose assumptions still need investigation
A persona grounded in extensive interviews and observations
The first prototype of the product
exercises.explanation: Proto-persona : base de preuves plus faible, elle rend explicite la vision de l'équipe.

exercises.prompt: A persona description is very convincing. What does that establish?
choices: That user research is no longer needed
Nothing about evidence: its claims still depend on what is known about users
exercises.explanation: « A convincing description does not establish evidence. »

exercises.prompt: Match each iLearn persona with their profile.
pairs: Primary teacher and former web developer
History teacher who wants less administration
exercises.explanation: Jack : projets collaboratifs ; Emma : groupes et matériel ; Elena : configure les environnements.

exercises.prompt: What is a scenario?
choices: A one-sentence statement of a single need
A narrative of a user using a product in a particular situation
A complete specification of the product
exercises.explanation: Le scenario est un récit ; la story est une phrase courte sur un besoin.

exercises.prompt: Order the elements a scenario connects.
exercises.explanation: Le récit va de la situation au problème, puis à la façon dont le produit pourrait aider.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about early scenarios is TRUE?
choices: They are usually incomplete and do not constitute a full specification
They describe every interaction and every outcome
They must be written in Gherkin
exercises.explanation: Les premiers scenarios stimulent la compréhension, ils ne spécifient pas tout.

exercises.prompt: In Jack's scenario, pupils share photos but Jack must check them before publication. What does this reveal?
choices: A need for a new login system
A need for a moderated photo service
exercises.explanation: Besoin : partager ; contrainte : vérification avant publication ; réponse : service photo modéré (KidsTakePics).

exercises.prompt: Emma logs in with her Google credentials in the scenario. How should a designer read this detail?
choices: It means iLearn must be built by Google
Her real need may be to avoid another login and password; other mechanisms may satisfy it
It is irrelevant and should be ignored
Google login is a hard requirement that cannot change
exercises.explanation: Un mécanisme cité peut n'être qu'une solution parmi d'autres ; la revue sépare vraies contraintes et choix négociables.

exercises.prompt: Teachers specifically want WordPress blogs. Why not simply rewrite it as 'any blog'?
choices: It may be an actual requirement, and generalizing would lose relevant information
exercises.explanation: Certains détails sont de vraies exigences ; les remplacer perd de l'information.

exercises.prompt: Scenario or user story? Match each characteristic.
pairs: A person doing an activity in a situation
A role needing a particular capability
exercises.explanation: Le scenario garde le contexte et le déroulement ; la story isole un besoin.

exercises.prompt: What is the common structure of a user story?
choices: As a [role], I want [action], so that [rationale]
exercises.explanation: Role + action (+ rationale). Given/When/Then est le format des acceptance criteria.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of 'As a teacher, I need to report attendance for a class trip, so that the school can maintain its health and safety records.'
pairs: I need to report attendance for a class trip
so that the school can maintain its health and safety records
exercises.explanation: Le role (de qui ?), l'action (quoi ?), la rationale (pourquoi ?).

exercises.prompt: According to Sommerville, is the rationale ('so that…') mandatory in every user story?
choices: No: it is useful when it adds understanding
exercises.explanation: Elle est particulièrement utile quand les développeurs connaissent mal le travail de l'utilisateur.

exercises.prompt: What is an epic?
choices: A broad story that spans several Sprints
A story completed in one day
exercises.explanation: Une story trop large pour un Sprint ; on la découpe avant de la planifier.

exercises.prompt: 'A system manager needs backup and restoration of applications, files, directories and the entire system.' How should it be handled for Sprint planning?
choices: Implement it as one story in one Sprint
Separate the aspects into smaller stories and clarify each one
exercises.explanation: C'est un epic : on découpe en stories qui tiennent dans un Sprint.

exercises.prompt: Emma's scenario opening produces three stories. Which concerns do they separate?
choices: Authentication, account selection, and access to applications
exercises.explanation: Identifiants Google, choix du compte teacher/parent, accès aux applis de gestion.

exercises.prompt: What is a feature?
choices: A completion standard for the product
A fragment of functionality that supports a user or system need
exercises.explanation: Définition de Sommerville.

exercises.prompt: Jack's pupils contact a teachers' group by email. What should the designer conclude?
choices: A separate feature must be built for exactly that action
The action is a clue to a capability (email groups); discussion may combine or generalize it
exercises.explanation: Une action est un indice, pas un ordre automatique de construire une feature.

exercises.prompt: Match each action in Jack's scenario with the derived feature.
pairs: Contact a teachers' group by email
Configure the tools of a learning environment
exercises.explanation: Dérivation des features (tableau 3.10).

exercises.prompt: Emma's stories give the Groups feature: create a group, email all members, share information. What else must the team do?
choices: Nothing: the stories fully specify Groups
Review for omissions, such as changing or deleting a group and restricting access
exercises.explanation: Une dérivation depuis un seul scenario laisse des trous.

exercises.prompt: Match the parts of the New Group feature description.
pairs: A group name chosen by the user
Create a container with that name
An empty container and an updated document list
The New Group menu option or keyboard shortcut
exercises.explanation: Input, action, output et activation exposent chacun une partie du comportement.

exercises.prompt: Match each desirable feature property with its meaning.
pairs: Does not rely on another feature's internal implementation
Supports one connected item of functionality without unrelated side effects
exercises.explanation: Les trois propriétés recommandées par Sommerville.

exercises.prompt: Match each knowledge source for feature design with its contribution.
pairs: Needs and how a capability fits their work
exercises.explanation: Leur poids varie selon le produit.

exercises.prompt: Adding more capabilities supports more needs but makes the product harder to use. Which trade-off is this?
exercises.explanation: Plus de fonctions = moins de simplicité.

exercises.prompt: Automation reduces manual work, but some users want to configure what the software does. Which trade-off is this?
exercises.explanation: Automatiser retire du contrôle à l'utilisateur.

exercises.prompt: What is feature creep?
choices: The gradual expansion of a product's feature set as more uses and requests are proposed
A bug that spreads between features
exercises.explanation: Plus de features = interface plus complexe et plus d'occasions de bugs.

exercises.prompt: Which question is NOT one of the checks before accepting a new feature request?
choices: Does it add useful general capability?
Is the idea attractive on its own?
Could an existing feature be extended instead?
exercises.explanation: On compare à l'ensemble des features accepté, pas à l'attrait de l'idée seule.

exercises.prompt: What are acceptance criteria?
choices: The shared quality standard for every Increment
Conditions a story or feature must satisfy, turning intended value into checkable outcomes
exercises.explanation: Ce sont des spécifications, pas des résultats de test.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best acceptance criterion for New Group?
choices: The newly created group initially contains no documents or subgroups
exercises.explanation: Un bon critère est observable ; « well », « fast », « user-friendly » sont flous.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'The search page loads fast' a weak acceptance criterion?
choices: 'Fast' is ambiguous; a quantity or explicit condition should replace it
exercises.explanation: Remplacer par une quantité, ex : « results appear within 2 seconds for … ».

exercises.prompt: Order the three parts of a Gherkin behavior example.
exercises.explanation: Given / When / Then.

exercises.prompt: 'Given Emma is authenticated and offered her teacher and parent accounts, When she chooses her teacher account, Then…' What belongs in the Then part?
choices: Her welcome screen shows her selected applications and teacher management tools
exercises.explanation: Then = résultat observable.

exercises.prompt: Match each concept with its purpose.
pairs: State required outcomes for one story or feature
Shared quality conditions for every Increment
exercises.explanation: Criteria = spec ; tests = vérification ; DoD = standard commun.

exercises.prompt: What does executable Gherkin need in addition to its Given/When/Then text?
exercises.explanation: Les step definitions relient chaque étape à du code.

exercises.prompt: The New Group description does not say what happens when the name already exists. What should the team do?
choices: Clarify the rule before it becomes an expected result
exercises.explanation: Une règle non spécifiée doit être clarifiée, sans inventer de comportement.

exercises.prompt: Does Scrum prescribe the user-story sentence format?
choices: No; the Product Backlog includes product improvements in any form
Yes, always 'As a… I want… so that…'
exercises.explanation: Les user stories sont courantes mais pas imposées par le Scrum Guide.

exercises.prompt: What does Product Backlog refinement do?
choices: Adds detail to items and divides them as understanding grows
exercises.explanation: Le détail d'une story se développe à l'approche de l'implémentation.

exercises.prompt: Lab example: availability 10:00–11:00 and 10:30–11:30 on the same date and time zone. Which common interval is displayed?
exercises.explanation: L'intersection des deux intervalles : 10:30–11:00.

exercises.prompt: In the Week 4 lab, which minimum does M2_story_slice.md contain?
choices: Two core user stories with at least two acceptance criteria each
exercises.explanation: Deux stories, deux critères par story, et le lien vers l'utilisateur et le scenario.

exercises.prompt: A team writes a criterion and labels it 'passed' although no test was executed. What is wrong?
choices: Criteria describe expected future behavior; 'passed' must only follow an actual execution
exercises.explanation: Règle du lab : ne jamais inventer de résultat de test.

flashcards.back: Personnage imaginé représentant un type d'utilisateur : personal context, work/activity, skills, product relevance.
Persona construite avec les connaissances limitées de l'équipe ; hypothèses à vérifier.
Jack (instit, ex-web developer), Emma (prof d'histoire, moins d'admin), Elena (technicienne IT).
Récit d'un user dans une situation : situation → objectif → difficulté → usage possible du produit. Incomplet, pas une spec.
Scenario : une personne dans une activité, avec le contexte. Story : un rôle qui a besoin d'une capacité précise.
As a [role], I want [action], so that [rationale]. Rationale utile, pas obligatoire.
Story trop large, qui s'étale sur plusieurs Sprints ; à découper.
Fragment de fonctionnalité qui répond à un besoin user ou système. Description : input, action, output, activation.
Independence, coherence, relevance.

flashcards.front: Sources de connaissance du feature design
flashcards.back: Users, existing products, domain, technology.
Simplicity/functionality, familiarity/novelty, automation/control.
Expansion progressive des features ; plus de complexité et de bugs. Vérifier : utile, assez d'users, étendre l'existant ?
Conditions vérifiables d'une story/feature : claires, testables, observables, sans « good » ni « fast ».
État de départ / action ou événement / résultat observable (Gherkin).
Criteria = résultats attendus d'une story ; tests = comparaison observé/attendu ; Definition of Done = standard qualité commun à chaque Increment.
2 user stories, ≥ 2 acceptance criteria chacune, lien vers user et scenario ; un cas invalide traité ou une règle ouverte notée.

lesson:
# Software Engineering — Week 4 · Features, Scenarios & User Stories

**Cours** : *Understanding users and specifying outcomes* (Sommerville 2021,
chapitre 3). Les **personas**, les **scenarios**, les **user stories** (et les
**epics**), les **features** (dérivation, description, propriétés,
trade-offs, **feature creep**), les **acceptance criteria** au format
**Given / When / Then**, et la différence avec les **acceptance tests** et la
**Definition of Done**.
**Lab** : *Two stories, checkable outcomes* (M2_story_slice.md).

> **En bref.** Une **persona** = un **type d'utilisateur** imaginé. Un
> **scenario** = un **récit** de cette personne qui utilise le produit dans
> une situation. Une **user story** = **un besoin précis** : *As a [role], I
> want [action], so that [reason]*. Une **feature** = une **capacité du
> produit**. Les **acceptance criteria** rendent le besoin **vérifiable**
> (*Given / When / Then*). Au quiz, sache **distinguer ces représentations**
> et **reconnaître un bon critère** (observable, sans « good » ni « fast »).

---

# Partie 1 — Cours

## 1. Pourquoi ces représentations ?

La **product vision** donne la direction (*users and value*). Le développement
incrémental doit aussi décider **quelles capacités** les utilisateurs
trouveront utiles et **comment** chacune doit se comporter.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Les nouvelles informations issues de l'évaluation font évoluer le choix des features.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "v", "x": 70, "y": 50, "w": 120, "label": "Product vision\nusers and value", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "u", "x": 240, "y": 50, "w": 150, "label": "Understand use\nand refine features", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "d", "x": 420, "y": 50, "w": 140, "label": "Develop a usable\nincrement", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "e", "x": 590, "y": 50, "w": 120, "label": "Evaluate\nwith users", "tone": "violet", "filled": true }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "v", "to": "u" }, { "from": "u", "to": "d" }, { "from": "d", "to": "e" },
    { "from": "e", "to": "u", "dashed": true, "label": "new information", "via": [[590, 120], [240, 120]] }
  ]
}
```

**Personas, scenarios et stories** aident l'équipe à raisonner sur ces choix :
ils rendent **visibles les hypothèses** sur les utilisateurs et servent de
support de discussion.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Persona → scenario → user story → feature. Un scenario suggère aussi directement des features.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "p", "x": 70, "y": 50, "w": 120, "label": "Persona\na type of user", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "s", "x": 240, "y": 50, "w": 130, "label": "Scenario\nuse in a situation", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "u", "x": 410, "y": 50, "w": 130, "label": "User story\na specific need", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "f", "x": 580, "y": 50, "w": 130, "label": "Feature\nproduct capability", "tone": "violet", "filled": true }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "p", "to": "s" }, { "from": "s", "to": "u" }, { "from": "u", "to": "f" },
    { "from": "s", "to": "f", "dashed": true, "via": [[240, 120], [580, 120]] }
  ]
}
```

- **Un** scenario peut suggérer **plusieurs** stories.
- **Plusieurs** stories peuvent décrire différents aspects d'**une** feature.
- Une **feature** est un **fragment de fonctionnalité** qui répond à un besoin
  de l'utilisateur ou du système.

## 2. Personas

Une **persona** est un **personnage imaginé** qui représente **un type
d'utilisateur potentiel**. Elle aide les développeurs à partager une
compréhension de la **situation**, des **capacités** et des **raisons** de cet
utilisateur.

| Aspect | Ce qu'il apporte au design |
|---|---|
| **Personal context** | un nom et une situation rendent l'utilisateur concret |
| **Work or activity** | ses responsabilités expliquent les tâches à supporter |
| **Skills and experience** | son niveau technique dit ce qu'il peut comprendre et utiliser |
| **Product relevance** | pourquoi le produit compte pour lui |

> **Piège :** un **rôle** (« teacher ») est une **catégorie** ; une
> **persona** ajoute le **contexte** pour raisonner sur un **type** précis de
> teacher.

### Evidence et proto-personas

| **Personas grounded in user research** | **Proto-personas** |
|---|---|
| tirées d'**interviews, observations**, données utilisateurs ; on abstrait les **traits récurrents** puis on compare | construites avec les **connaissances limitées** de l'équipe pour **rendre explicite** sa vision des users |
| représentent un **type** d'utilisateur, pas la retranscription d'un individu | **base de preuves plus faible** : les hypothèses importantes restent **à vérifier** |

> **À retenir :** une description **convaincante** n'est **pas une preuve**.

### Les personas d'iLearn

**iLearn** permet aux écoles de configurer des outils d'apprentissage.

| Persona | Profil | Usage |
|---|---|---|
| **Jack** | instituteur, **ancien web developer**, croit au digital learning | projets de classe collaboratifs |
| **Emma** | prof d'**histoire**, veut **moins d'administratif**, préfère enseigner en classe | organiser des groupes, accéder à du matériel |
| **Elena** | **technicienne IT** compétente, se forme au digital learning | configurer et maintenir les environnements |

Même pour un seul produit, **compétences techniques et enthousiasme
varient**.

## 3. Scenarios

Un **scenario** est un **récit** (*narrative*) d'un utilisateur qui utilise le
produit **dans une situation particulière**. Il relie :

`user and situation` → `objective and current activity` → `difficulty or
unmet need` → `possible use of the product`.

- Il donne quelque chose de **concret** à discuter, révèle des **capacités
  manquantes** et des **contraintes**.
- Les premiers scenarios sont **généralement incomplets** : ils **ne sont pas
  une spécification complète**.

### Le scenario de Jack

Les élèves de Jack étudient l'**industrie de la pêche locale** : souvenirs de
famille, archives, **photos**, avec un **wiki iLearn** et l'archive **SCRAN**.

| Besoin | Contrainte | Réponse |
|---|---|---|
| partager et commenter des photos | Jack **vérifie les photos avant publication** | ajouter un service photo **modéré** |

Des collègues recommandent **KidsTakePics** ; comme il **n'utilise pas
l'authentification iLearn**, Jack crée des comptes prof et classe séparés puis
ajoute le service à l'environnement de la classe. Le récit révèle trois
besoins : **modération**, **accès à un service externe**, **configuration**.

### Contrainte réelle ou simple solution ?

Un détail concret peut être une **vraie contrainte** ou **une solution parmi
d'autres** :

| Détail du scenario | Sens pour le design |
|---|---|
| Emma se connecte avec ses **identifiants Google** | le vrai besoin est sans doute **d'éviter un login de plus** : d'autres mécanismes conviennent |
| les profs veulent des blogs **WordPress** | peut être une **vraie exigence** : la remplacer par « any blog » perdrait de l'information |

## 4. User stories

| | **Scenario** | **User story** |
|---|---|---|
| Focus | une **personne** dans une **activité** | un **rôle** qui a besoin d'**une capacité** |
| Contexte | relie actions, difficultés, travail autour | se concentre sur **un besoin** (et parfois sa raison) |
| Usage | communiquer avec les users, explorer | **affiner les features** et, assez détaillée, **planifier** |

Les deux sont **complémentaires** : des stories isolées peuvent perdre la
**situation** qui explique pourquoi elles vont ensemble.

### La structure

```diagram
{
  "title": "As a [role], I need/want [action], so that [rationale]. La rationale est utile, pas obligatoire.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "r", "x": 100, "y": 40, "w": 170, "label": "As a teacher,", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "a", "x": 330, "y": 40, "w": 260, "label": "I need to report attendance\nfor a class trip,", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "w", "x": 590, "y": 40, "w": 230, "label": "so that the school can maintain\nits health and safety records.", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "rl", "x": 100, "y": 110, "shape": "text", "label": "Role : whose need?" },
    { "id": "al", "x": 330, "y": 110, "shape": "text", "label": "Action : what capability?" },
    { "id": "wl", "x": 590, "y": 110, "shape": "text", "label": "Rationale : why useful?" }
  ]
}
```

- **Role** : le besoin de qui ?
- **Action** : quelle capacité ?
- **Rationale** : pourquoi c'est utile ? Sommerville la juge utile **quand elle
  apporte de la compréhension**, pas **obligatoire** à chaque story.
- La phrase est un **point de départ** pour clarifier, pas toute la
  connaissance nécessaire.

### Stories tirées du scenario d'Emma

Emma travaille de chez elle et a un compte **teacher** et un compte
**parent**. Trois besoins distincts :

| Détail | Story |
|---|---|
| identifiants existants | *As a teacher, I want to use my Google credentials from home so that I do not need another login and password.* |
| choisir un compte | *As a teacher and parent, I want to choose the appropriate iLearn account while using one set of credentials.* |
| atteindre ses outils | *As a teacher, I want access to the applications I use for class management and administration.* |

Elles séparent **authentification**, **choix du compte** et **accès aux
applis**.

### Taille des stories et epics

- Pour le **Sprint planning**, une story doit tenir **dans un Sprint**.
- Une story trop large, qui **s'étale sur plusieurs Sprints**, s'appelle un
  **epic**. Ex : un administrateur veut **sauvegarder et restaurer** applis,
  fichiers, dossiers et tout le système → à **découper**.
- En **découverte**, une story large peut rester utile : le niveau de détail
  dépend de la décision à prendre.

## 5. Features

### Dériver des features d'un scenario

On regarde **ce que font les users**, les **capacités** qui le permettent, et
si une capacité **plus générale** est nécessaire.

| Action dans le scenario de Jack | Feature |
|---|---|
| rassembler des histoires dans un **wiki** | **collaborative writing** |
| accéder à l'archive **SCRAN** | **accès à des ressources externes** (et à d'autres archives ?) |
| contacter un groupe de profs par **email** | **email groups** |
| ajouter **KidsTakePics** à la classe | **configurer les outils** d'un environnement |

> **Piège :** une action est un **indice**, pas un **ordre** de construire une
> feature séparée : on peut **regrouper** des actions ou trouver un besoin
> plus large.

### Une feature, plusieurs stories

La feature **Groups** d'iLearn regroupe : **créer un groupe** et choisir ses
membres, **envoyer un email** à tous via une adresse, **partager** des
fichiers. Ces stories **ne spécifient pas tout** : il manque **modifier /
supprimer** un groupe, **restreindre l'accès**… Après dérivation, il faut
**relire pour trouver les oublis**.

### Décrire une feature : New Group

```diagram
{
  "title": "New Group : input, action, output, et une activation (menu ou raccourci clavier).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "i", "x": 90, "y": 50, "w": 160, "label": "Input\na group name\nchosen by the user", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "a", "x": 320, "y": 50, "w": 170, "label": "Action\ncreate a container\nwith that name", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "o", "x": 560, "y": 50, "w": 180, "label": "Output\nan empty container +\nan updated document list", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "t", "x": 320, "y": 150, "w": 440, "shape": "note", "label": "Activation : New Group menu option or keyboard shortcut", "tone": "violet" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "i", "to": "a" }, { "from": "a", "to": "o" }, { "from": "t", "to": "a", "dashed": true }
  ]
}
```

Une utilité **familière** a besoin d'une description **courte** ; une
capacité **inhabituelle** demande plus d'explications avant
l'implémentation.

### Propriétés souhaitables d'une feature

| Propriété | Sens |
|---|---|
| **Independence** | ne dépend pas de l'**implémentation interne** d'une autre feature ni d'un **ordre d'activation** de features sans rapport |
| **Coherence** | supporte **un seul** élément de fonctionnalité cohérent, **sans effets de bord** sans rapport |
| **Relevance** | supporte des tâches que les users **font normalement**, pas des possibilités obscures |

### Les sources de connaissance

| Source | Apport |
|---|---|
| **Users** | leurs besoins, comment la capacité s'intègre à leur travail |
| **Existing products** | les capacités **familières** que les users attendent |
| **Domain** | les pratiques et contraintes du métier ; de nouvelles approches |
| **Technology** | des opportunités que les anciens produits n'ont pas |

Leur poids varie : un logiciel métier spécialisé demande plus de
connaissance du **domaine** qu'un utilitaire grand public.

### Les trade-offs

| Trade-off | Conséquence |
|---|---|
| **Simplicity / functionality** | plus de capacités = plus de besoins couverts, mais produit **plus dur** à comprendre |
| **Familiarity / novelty** | le familier facilite l'adoption ; la nouveauté donne une **raison de changer** |
| **Automation / control** | l'automatisation réduit le travail manuel, mais certains users veulent **contrôler** |

Aucun ensemble de features ne **maximise tout** : on choisit
**délibérément** (ex : favoriser la simplicité).

### Feature creep

Le **feature creep** est l'**expansion progressive** de l'ensemble des
features au fil des demandes. `user requests and competitive pressure` →
`more overlapping capabilities` → `more complexity in use and
implementation` (et plus de **bugs**).

Avant d'accepter une proposition, se demander :

1. ajoute-t-elle une **capacité générale utile** ?
2. **assez d'utilisateurs** en ont-ils besoin ?
3. peut-on plutôt **étendre une feature existante** ?

On la compare à l'**ensemble de features accepté**, pas à l'attrait de l'idée
seule.

## 6. Acceptance criteria

Les **acceptance criteria** énoncent les **conditions** qu'une story ou une
feature doit remplir : ils transforment la valeur visée en **résultats
convenus et vérifiables**.

Un bon critère est **clair**, **testable** et centré sur des **résultats
observables**. Des **quantités** ou des **conditions explicites** remplacent
les mots flous comme « **good** » ou « **fast** ». Il décrit **ce qui est
attendu**, pas **comment** l'implémenter.

**Critères tirés de New Group :**

- après création, le groupe porte **le nom fourni** par l'utilisateur ;
- le groupe est **initialement vide** (ni documents ni sous-groupes) ;
- la **liste des documents** contient le nouveau groupe.

> **Piège :** « *Group creation works well* » n'est **pas** un critère : on ne
> sait pas quel nom, quel contenu, quelle visibilité vérifier.

### Given, When, Then (Gherkin)

```diagram
{
  "title": "Gherkin : un état de départ, un événement, un résultat observable.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "g", "x": 100, "y": 40, "w": 170, "label": "Given\nthe starting state", "tone": "sky", "filled": true },
    { "id": "w", "x": 330, "y": 40, "w": 170, "label": "When\nan action or event", "tone": "amber", "filled": true },
    { "id": "t", "x": 560, "y": 40, "w": 170, "label": "Then\nan observable outcome", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true }
  ],
  "edges": [ { "from": "g", "to": "w" }, { "from": "w", "to": "t" } ]
}
```

Exemple iLearn :

> **Given** Emma is authenticated and is offered her teacher and parent
> accounts, **When** she chooses her teacher account, **Then** her welcome
> screen shows her selected applications and teacher management tools.

Un **Scenario** Gherkin est un **exemple concret**, plus étroit que le
scenario « récit » du début.

### Criteria, tests, Definition of Done

| Concept | But | Portée |
|---|---|---|
| **Acceptance criteria** | **énoncer** les résultats attendus | **une** story ou feature |
| **Acceptance tests** | **comparer** résultat observé et attendu | vérifications concrètes des criteria |
| **Definition of Done** | standard de **qualité commun** d'un Increment | **tout** le produit |

- Les criteria sont des **spécifications**, **pas des résultats de test**.
- Un Gherkin **exécutable** a besoin de **step definitions**.
- Le travail doit **aussi** respecter la **Definition of Done**.

### Les cas non résolus

La description de New Group précise la création, mais **pas** :

- un **nom vide** : rejeter ou nom par défaut ? **non spécifié** ;
- un nom **déjà existant** : autoriser, refuser, renommer ? **non spécifié**.

Une règle manquante doit être **clarifiée** avant de devenir un résultat
attendu.

## 7. Stories et Product Backlog

- Le détail d'une story **se développe à l'approche de l'implémentation** ;
  une phrase courte est un **rappel**, pas toute la connaissance.
- **Scrum ne prescrit pas** le format *As a… I want… so that…*.
- Le **Product Backlog refinement** ajoute du détail et **découpe** les items.

`User need and candidate feature` → `Discuss, divide, add detail` → `Select
feasible Sprint work` → `Develop and inspect outcomes` → feedback.

| Représentation | Apport à la décision |
|---|---|
| **Persona** | caractéristiques et capacités des users |
| **Scenario** | la situation et la séquence qui donnent du contexte |
| **Story** | un besoin précis ou un aspect d'une feature |
| **Feature description** | comportement, inputs, outputs, contraintes |
| **Acceptance criteria** | les conditions pour vérifier le résultat |

---

# Partie 2 — Lab : Two stories, checkable outcomes

**Résultat** : un document d'équipe `M2_story_slice.md` avec **deux user
stories**, **au moins deux acceptance criteria par story**, et un lien vers
l'**utilisateur** et le **scenario**.

| Temps | Étape |
|---|---|
| 0–5 | **Prepare** : relire M1, garder ou réviser un énoncé user / problème ; noter le feedback reçu (sinon « No feedback yet ») ; un **writer**, un **reviewer** |
| 5–10 | **Apply** : profil utilisateur bref + scenario de 2–3 phrases ; marquer **connu** vs **supposé** |
| 10–15 | **Apply** : deux stories (role, action, reason), dans un ordre provisoire justifié |
| 15–25 | **Apply** : deux critères vérifiables par story (**condition + action + résultat visible**) ; traiter un cas **alternatif / invalide** ou noter la règle non résolue |
| 25–30 | **Check** : un coéquipier lit les critères **sans aide** ; clarifier une ambiguïté ; sauvegarder |

**Exemple Meeting Helper** :

- *As a meeting organizer, I want to see common available times so that I can
  propose a time all members can attend.*
- **Critère 1** : Given 10:00–11:00 et 10:30–11:30 (même date, même fuseau),
  When on demande les créneaux communs, the displayed interval is
  **10:30–11:00**.
- **Critère 2** : Given 10:00–10:30 et 11:00–11:30, the result states that **no
  common interval exists**. (Le cas des **extrémités qui se touchent** reste à
  convenir.)

> **Règle du lab :** les criteria décrivent un **comportement futur** : ne
> jamais écrire « passed » si le test n'a **pas été exécuté**.

---

## À retenir

- **Persona** = type d'utilisateur imaginé (context, activity, skills,
  relevance). **Proto-persona** = sans recherche, hypothèses à vérifier.
- **Scenario** = récit d'usage dans une situation ; incomplet, pas une spec.
- **User story** = *As a [role], I want [action], so that [reason]* ;
  rationale **optionnelle**. Trop grosse pour un Sprint = **epic**.
- **Feature** = fragment de fonctionnalité ; description = **input, action,
  output, activation** ; propriétés : **independence, coherence, relevance**.
- Trade-offs : simplicity/functionality, familiarity/novelty,
  automation/control. **Feature creep** = expansion progressive.
- **Acceptance criteria** : clairs, testables, observables ; **Given / When /
  Then**. Criteria ≠ tests ≠ **Definition of Done**.

## Pièges classiques du quiz

| Affirmation | Vrai / Faux |
|---|---|
| Une persona est la retranscription d'un utilisateur réel interviewé | **Faux** : elle représente un **type** d'utilisateur |
| Une proto-persona repose sur une recherche utilisateur approfondie | **Faux** : sur les connaissances limitées de l'équipe |
| Un scenario est une spécification complète | **Faux** : il est généralement incomplet |
| La rationale (*so that…*) est obligatoire dans chaque story | **Faux** : utile quand elle aide à comprendre |
| Une story qui prend plusieurs Sprints est un epic | **Vrai** |
| Chaque action d'un scenario devient une feature séparée | **Faux** : c'est un indice, on peut regrouper |
| « The page loads fast » est un bon acceptance criterion | **Faux** : pas mesurable |
| Les acceptance criteria sont des résultats de test | **Faux** : ce sont des spécifications |
| La Definition of Done s'applique à une seule story | **Faux** : à tout le produit (chaque Increment) |
| Scrum impose le format *As a… I want… so that…* | **Faux** |
| Le feature creep réduit la complexité | **Faux** : il l'augmente |

name: Week 5

exercises.prompt: What does software architecture describe?
choices: The system's components, their relationships to each other and the environment, and the principles guiding design and evolution
exercises.explanation: Composants + relations + principes.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about requirements and architecture is TRUE?
choices: Requirements do not determine a unique architecture
Each feature maps to exactly one component
Each component supports exactly one feature
exercises.explanation: Une feature peut demander plusieurs composants, un composant peut servir plusieurs features.

exercises.prompt: Match each architectural concern with its meaning.
pairs: A named unit providing coherent functionality
The functionality and services assigned to a component
How components use, contain or share data with one another
A priority or constraint guiding the organization
exercises.explanation: Tableau 4.1 de Sommerville.

exercises.prompt: In Sommerville's terminology, does a 'service' imply a separate server or a microservice?
choices: No: a service is a coherent unit of functionality offered through an interface
exercises.explanation: Un composant offre un ou plusieurs services via une interface (API).

exercises.prompt: What should a component using another component's service rely on?
choices: Its interface, not its hidden implementation details
exercises.explanation: Information hiding : on dépend de l'interface seulement.

exercises.prompt: Match each quality attribute with its concern.
pairs: Returning results within an acceptable time
Delivering services when users request them
Protection against unauthorized access and attack
Using needed features with few errors
Updating and adding features at an acceptable cost
Continuing to provide services despite partial failure or attack
exercises.explanation: Les 7 quality attributes du tableau 4.2.

exercises.prompt: A system keeps serving users even when one of its databases crashes. Which quality attribute is this?
exercises.explanation: Continuer malgré une panne partielle = resilience.

exercises.prompt: Adding a feature to the product costs little effort. Which quality attribute is good?
exercises.explanation: Mettre à jour et ajouter des features à un coût acceptable.

exercises.prompt: C1 and C2 use one shared database. Changing its structure would make C1 faster. What is the risk?
choices: C2 uses the same structure, so it may need changes and its response time may change
exercises.explanation: La base partagée crée une dépendance commune.

exercises.prompt: C1 and C2 each have their own database with duplicated shared information. What extra mechanism is needed?
choices: Data reconciliation to keep the copies consistent
exercises.explanation: C3 réconcilie : délai, travail, stockage en plus, incohérence possible.

exercises.prompt: Which is an ADVANTAGE of separate databases over a shared database?
choices: Components can change more independently, and a database failure may leave part of the system available
exercises.explanation: Indépendance et disponibilité partielle, au prix de la réconciliation.

exercises.prompt: Match each architectural choice with its cost.
pairs: Detection and switching add cost and complexity
exercises.explanation: Améliorer une qualité en dégrade souvent une autre.

exercises.prompt: Several protection layers improve security. Which quality may suffer?
exercises.explanation: Trade-off security / usability.

exercises.prompt: Match each influence on architectural design with its consequence.
pairs: Long-lived products need an organization that can evolve
Saves work but constrains the surrounding design
Rapid demand changes may require scaling
Existing software and data restrict feasible choices
exercises.explanation: Plus les quality priorities, les compétences, le budget et le planning.

exercises.prompt: Why record the design rationale of an architectural choice?
choices: To make its compromises and assumptions understandable to other developers
exercises.explanation: Comparer les alternatives, dire le bénéfice accepté et le coût subi.

exercises.prompt: Is an initial architecture diagram evidence of the delivered system's structure?
choices: No: the implemented system may later differ from the model
exercises.explanation: Le modèle seul ne prouve pas la structure livrée.

exercises.prompt: Abstraction or decomposition?
pairs: Focus on essential elements and suppress detail
Represent a larger component as smaller parts with related responsibilities
exercises.explanation: Les deux outils pour maîtriser la complexité.

exercises.prompt: Match each relationship between components with its meaning.
pairs: Components reside in the same module or object
exercises.explanation: Les relations expliquent comment un changement se propage.

exercises.prompt: What mainly determines architectural complexity?
choices: The number and nature of relationships between components
The number of boxes in the diagram
exercises.explanation: Plus de boîtes ne veut pas dire meilleure décomposition.

exercises.prompt: Match each decomposition guideline with its meaning.
pairs: Group functionality around a coherent concern
Provide a service in one place
Hide internal details behind coherent, stable interfaces
exercises.explanation: Elles localisent les changements futurs.

exercises.prompt: The same date-validation code is copied into three components. Which guideline is broken?
exercises.explanation: La duplication oblige à coordonner les changements.

exercises.prompt: Component B changes its internal algorithm but keeps the same interface and behavior. What happens to component A, which uses B?
choices: A does not need to change
exercises.explanation: Une interface stable protège les appelants des changements internes.

exercises.prompt: Order the layers of the generic web application model, from top to bottom.
exercises.explanation: Figure 4.10 de Sommerville.

exercises.prompt: In this layered model, which dependency direction is NOT allowed?
choices: A higher layer using a basic service further down
A higher layer using the layer below
A lower layer depending on a higher layer
exercises.explanation: Une couche basse ne dépend jamais d'une couche haute ; les données peuvent remonter.

exercises.prompt: A product stores no data. Must it still have a database layer?
choices: No: the layered model is a starting point, adapted to the product
exercises.explanation: Une appli peut avoir plus ou moins de couches.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a cross-cutting concern?
exercises.explanation: Security, performance, reliability touchent toutes les couches.

exercises.prompt: Where should a security-critical field be validated?
choices: On the server (local checks may be added for responsiveness)
exercises.explanation: Les vérifications qui demandent la base, les permissions ou la sécurité vont côté serveur.

exercises.prompt: Why is a single security component a risk?
choices: If all checking depends on it, its compromise or failure removes the system's only protection
exercises.explanation: Point de défaillance unique : protéger dans chaque couche.

exercises.prompt: Match each iLearn design principle with its intention.
pairs: Extend or limit the standard system
Different interfaces for learners of different ages
Combine existing applications into new functionality
No extra work for users who do not customize
exercises.explanation: Tableau 4.7 de Sommerville.

exercises.prompt: In iLearn, replacing a service may break combined applications. What preserves existing combinations?
choices: Keeping the older service alongside the alternative
exercises.explanation: Conflit replaceability / programmability.

exercises.prompt: Decomposition or distribution?
exercises.explanation: Décomposition = composants logiques ; distribution = clients et serveurs.

exercises.prompt: In a client–server architecture, what does a load balancer do?
choices: Distributes requests across a set of server instances
exercises.explanation: Il répartit les requêtes des clients entre les instances.

exercises.prompt: In this MVC figure, which component is '?' (it handles user input and sends change requests to the Model)?
exercises.explanation: Controller → Model (change request) → View (change notice).

exercises.prompt: Match each MVC part with its role.
exercises.explanation: L'essentiel est de séparer le model de la présentation.

exercises.prompt: In the textbook's client–server MVC example, where is the shared model kept?
choices: On the server; each client can have several views
exercises.explanation: Le serveur maintient le model partagé.

exercises.prompt: Order the tiers of a multi-tier client–server system, from the user.
exercises.explanation: User interaction → HTTP and pages → product operations → data management.

exercises.prompt: In the theater booking example, which server supplies show information and seat-booking operations?
exercises.explanation: Un payment server spécialisé peut gérer les cartes.

exercises.prompt: Why did iLearn's designers choose a service-oriented distribution?
choices: To update functionality and add unforeseen services easily
To use a single shared database
exercises.explanation: Séparer en services facilite remplacement et scaling.

exercises.prompt: Stateless service instances can be replicated as demand changes. Does stateless mean the product has no persistent data?
choices: No: persistent data is stored elsewhere
exercises.explanation: Stateless = l'instance ne garde pas d'état entre les requêtes.

exercises.prompt: In the Week 5 lab, what does Architecture_v1.md contain?
choices: One structure diagram and one justified design decision
exercises.explanation: Diagramme (composants, responsabilités, frontière, flèches étiquetées) + une décision justifiée.

exercises.prompt: Meeting Helper, decision D1: keep the interval calculation separate from the UI. What is its cost?
choices: Defining and maintaining the calculator's input and result format
The calculator must run on its own server
exercises.explanation: Bénéfice : isoler les changements de la règle ; coût : un format d'interface à maintenir.
